en: With his footstool honored by the mass of rays from rubies, the Lord of the Holy Places, the conqueror of enemies, became like a bull;
he was the manifest, singular kinsman of the three worlds without cause. // 1 //
The meaning of the passage:
Having approached that Lord of the Tīrthas, whose form is encompassed by the power of true miracles and other such qualities, one should bow with the head.
Having performed prostrations with their three organs of action (body, speech, and mind) with great humility,
Bharata, the lord of the Bharatas, and the others questioned him thus regarding everything.
The essential meaning is this:
formerly, in the lands of enjoyment, people were born with excessive passion,
possessing all great objects of enjoyment provided by the wish-fulfilling trees.
Having experienced divine happiness, those of great merit went once more to heaven in human form, attaining their desired bliss. // 3 //
The meaning here is that those classes of embodied beings who have attained birth [in this state] possess superior merit and possess great lifespans that cannot be shortened.
Others in this world whose supreme lifespan was subject to reduction experienced great fear here due to the provocation of their own faults.
The essential meaning is this:
for those of agitated minds here in this land of action,
who are oppressed by cold, heat, and the downpour of snow;
In the course of time, they became intent on eating coarse food.
The essential meaning is this:
for us who do not understand the etymology of great food and medicine,
here [is set forth] the method for protecting the health of those who are afflicted.
Or what action, O Lord of the World, is there for those who speak? // 6 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
having informed the Lord for the sake of the welfare of the entire world,
the principal leaders, headed by the Gaṇadharas, remained silent.
In that great assembly, the goddess Varadevī uttered a melodious speech accompanied by divine sounds.
The essential meaning is that she [the Goddess] is, in brief, all medicinal herbs, the qualification of all times, and the entirety of the fourfold categories of existence.
He spoke this, which indicates that he is omniscient.
The essential meaning is that the Gaṇadhara directly learned in its entirety the entire collection of the ultimate truth as it was revealed by the divine voice.
Sages whose intellects were purified by half of the eighth part attained [this].
The essential meaning—

handed down through tradition, extensive, unconfused, profound in its significance, and heard directly from the Śruta-kevalins by those possessing the leaves of sacred learning— is thus [revealed]. // 10 //
We shall explain the essential meaning of that which is the sole abode of welfare for all the world, like the tiny, beautiful droplets issuing from the surging waves.
It is endowed with a meaning well-known as "the doer of what is auspicious. // 11 //
The essential meaning shall not be set forth here by means of demolishing the pride of other scriptures, nor having followed the path of other teachers. (12)
Others say the true meaning of existence is the study of sacred texts; indeed, I consider the root of all austerities to be primarily affection for the best of physicians.
It is correctly undertaken so as to bring about the happiness of both oneself and others. // 13 //
The meaning of this is as follows: here too, there are many who are crooked by nature,
of evil vision, double-tongued, and impelled by wicked intellects.
Those lowest of men, who delight in seeking out faults and who cause harm to others, are comparable to terrible serpents. // 14 //
The meaning of this is as follows:
some people, possessing virtues esteemed within their own homes, find fault with others; yet there is no fault in that, for they are not among those who possess complete knowledge.
Of those characterized by the marks of slanderous speech and harsh words. // 15 //
The essential meaning is this:
some who lack discernment, though renowned for their prowess, roam the world like manifest piśācas.
What need have I for them as they are?
For it is well known that envy is the foremost of the vices of the noble. // 16 //
Having reflected thus on the essential meaning and having relaxed my envy,
I shall set forth the scripture according to its proper application.
It issued from the mouth of the Omniscient One, was received by Gaṇadeva, and subsequently descended through the lineage of great sages. // 17 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
there is an alternative reading, "mātsaryaṃ āryagaṇavarjyam iti prasiddham," which means it is well known in this world that the stingy person is avoided by the assembly of noble ones.
"Vidyā" is the name for the true, manifest, and absolute eye;
those who know the distinctions of words and treatises call that noble scripture which is established within it "vaidya."
Having reflected upon this, those physicians also recite it. // 18 //

The meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is indeed the word that indicates the true nature of reality; however, those who know it declare that there is another term for the treatise (*śāstra*) based on the distinction of its constituent elements (*dhātu*). (19)
The meaning of the verse:
We shall now describe those who, by being vessels for duality, have been conceptualized as having strayed from the path entered upon by the Lord of Jinas. // 20 //
The meaning of the passage is:
the wise man, whose conduct is blameless, who is skillful and humble,
should approach his teacher in the morning and inquire according to the prescribed manner.
Thus, he shall become a partaker of the stainless discipline and the scriptures. // 21 //
The essential meaning is this: this foremost scripture should always be given to one who has undertaken the true vows in the presence of the Arhats.
"Those who know medicine say that this should not be given to anyone else. // 22 //
The essential meaning is: the teacher, the means of accomplishment, the companions, the dwelling, the consort, health, intelligence, discipline, diligence, and devotion to the scriptures.
Thus have been described for those seeking the scriptures the external, internal, and innate treasures of one's own excellent qualities. // 23 //
The essential meaning is as follows: this treatise is indeed for the purpose of benefiting the world;
furthermore, the purpose of the treatise is also twofold, exactly as it is.
Now, the preservation of health and the liberation from disease are both described here in their entirety and in brief. // 24 //
The essential meaning is that wherein, indeed, there are immediately the six categories of beings, such as the living soul and others, distinguished by the divisions of the stationary and the mobile.
This world, which is esteemed by the ancient sages as "the world," beholds its own collection of excellent qualities and the goodness of sentient beings. // 25 //
The essential meaning,
according to the established doctrine, concerns the five types of excellent sense-faculties known as "paryāpti," which are distinguished within the various classifications of living beings.
There too, the foremost among men will be devoted to the Dharma; and in that land, which abounds in righteousness, they will be born for the sake of the ultimate truth. // 26 //
The essential meaning is: lifespan, age, digestive fire, strength, constitution, favorable location, suitability,
the well-known types of constitution, medicines, the body, and diseases.
Having understood even the sequence of time according to its proper order. // 27 //

In that context, the sages have stated that "action" (kriyā) is the essential meaning; this very medicine (cikitsā) is characterized by the predominance of the qualities of these fourfold categories of entities.
Among them as well, the one with unimpeded intellect is the preeminent physician. // 28 //

The meaning of the term [bhāvārtha] is one who is endowed with intelligence regarding the meaning of the texts, proficient in other systems of thought, skilled in correct application, dexterous, and exceedingly steadfast.
Preeminent in the Dharma, well-conducted, and purified by many sacred fords, he becomes a physician worthy of the wise and the great. // 29 //
The meaning of the matter [is determined] by means of questions, the rules for omens, the arrival of portents, and the specific conjunctions of the lunar mansions, the zodiacal signs, and the moon.
Having ascertained the measure of the lifespan, the physician should apply himself [to treatment]. // 30 //
The essential meaning is this: in this world, death does not occur for a living being without the presence of fatal signs (riṣṭas),
whether through the transgression of its [allotted] lifespan or by means of something exceedingly subtle.
The physician should examine the symptoms here according to the prescribed method with diligent effort. // 31 //
The essential meaning is the reversal of the excellent characteristics of shadow and form,
as well as the abnormality of the objects of the five senses, and of feces and phlegm.
Furthermore, immersion in water is the cause of destruction for one who is distressed. // 32 //
The meaning of the signs is as follows:
one who has limbs that are deficient, excessive, emaciated, black, or parched; one who is afflicted by disease; or one who himself holds a weapon or a staff in his hand.
At the twilights, with tearful eyes and trembling with fear, the messenger becomes exceedingly like a messenger of Yama. // 33 //
A group of messengers who always arrives on horses, donkeys, excellent chariots, young camels, or superior vehicles is highly censurable;
for he who, standing at the front, cuts the grass or breaks [the ground] is not a messenger.
Whether it be wood, a clod of earth, or a piece of straw or brick. // 34 //

Having thus suddenly observed such an omen manifested in the messenger— a sign that is the sole cause for the patient's death— the physician who understands the meaning of the medical aphorisms should avoid treating him in this world.
Gentle, for the sake of auspiciousness, clad in clean garments, and of his own caste. // 35 //
The essential meaning is that there are great torments arising from rivalries, stumbling through anger,
and the fires of strife and assault within villages.
Indeed, these must be avoided by physicians at the time of departure. // 36 //
The meaning of the signs is as follows:
a fire, a boar, a buffalo, mongooses, and jackals; red garlands and soiled loads belonging to a washerman.
Those who have arrived from Samataka are to be avoided. // 37 //
The essential meaning is this:
when the quarters are tranquil, there are auspicious omens such as the sounds of kettledrums, large drums, conchs, clouds, excellent flutes, and clay drums.
The prince [beheld] parasols and banners, maidens in white garments, and gentle fragrant breezes favorable for song. // 38 //
White-eyed peacocks, blue-throated cuckoos, and white cocks; women graceful with playful charms; lordly elephants;
jars filled with clear water; and bulls and horses.
At the time of setting out for the further shore, they are auspicious when facing forward. // 39 //
The essential meaning is this: having thus ascertained the glory described in the section on great omens, one should approach the patient whose limbs are marked with excellent characteristics.
Having observed and reflected, even a physician here can see how much of the maximum lifespan has passed and how much remains yet to come. (40)
The essential meaning is that his two feet are exceedingly tender,
very fleshy, smooth, and resemble the sprouts of an Aśoka tree and lotuses.
His hands and feet here are endowed with various beautiful forms, possessed of deep, broad, and long lines, and are stainless.
Her ears are exceedingly delicate and supremely pure;
her eyes resemble blue lotuses,
and her teeth are like pearls or like the seeds of a pomegranate.
He whose forehead is glossy, elevated, broad, and clean; // 42 //
One whose sighs, glances, arms, and nourishment are long; likewise, whose fingers, nails, face, and nose are thick;
and whose tongue, sense organs, throat, belly, penis, and shanks are short [is of the *pittaja* type].
And their ankles are low-set, well-knit, and hidden within the folds of the skin. // 43 //
One whose chest is very broad, or the distance between whose breasts or eyebrows is wide, and whose network of veins is restrained and hidden;
one whose [body] is anointed and smeared here only upwards.
Then the body may wither, and afterwards even the head itself.
For he whose body has been free from disease since birth and gradually attains constant growth,
and whose intellect is exceedingly capable even regarding the entire range of training;
And whose firm faculties are all to be known. // 45 //
He whose mass of hair is exceedingly glossy, fine, and soft, and whose body hairs are generally sparse and emerge from minute pores—
his body is thus marked with irreproachable and auspicious characteristics.
He possesses abundant wealth and an exceedingly long life. // 46 //
Long life is that [period] beyond it; half of that is considered to be the duration of health, and half of that is considered to be the period of prime youth. // 47 //
Having understood the essential meaning [of the patient's condition], the illustrious physician should first examine the lifespan of that afflicted person; then,
while further displaying his expertise in the true nature of the disease, he should also exert effort in its suppression.
The physician, knowing the rules, should perform this daily while preserving his own stainless reputation. // 48 //
The essential meaning [is as follows]: from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued forth by the power of the Jinas,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.

For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. // 49 //
Having bowed to the Jina— the cause for the destruction of all karma— who is worshipped by the hosts of gods and asuras,
I shall therefore speak of that which is characterized by the investigation of well-being, as it has been defined by the wise through its true characteristics. (1)
The meaning of the verse:
Now, in this world, for a person capable of liberation, the Victors have declared that well-being is of two kinds:
the first is primary and is called ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); the second is other and arises from conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). // 2 //

The meaning of the term *bhāva* is that which is born from the total destruction of all karma—this great wonder which is ultimate, peerless, beyond the senses, and sought after by those who know the goal; this is what is called by the name "the ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*). (3)
Its essential meaning is the state of the fire-element, free from the delusion of defects; it consists of the purification of impurities and the perfect clarity of the sense faculties.
And for a person, there is always clarity of mind; thus has that which arises from worldly transaction indeed been explained. 4.
The essential meaning is that one whose self, senses, and mind are serene is designated as "healthy" (svastha); thus says Vāgbhaṭa.

Indeed, a state of great gentleness is called equilibrium (*sāmya*); appetite, digestion, and strength are its characteristics; a wholesome regimen of moderate diet is the means; and strength is considered the accomplishment of the fourfold aim of life. // 5 //

If the meaning of the state of being is not such-and-such in this way or that way, what is the use of verbal analysis for those who know the reality? Having observed the similarity in those who possess specific bodily strength and form, experts declare them to be equal.

What is meant by the meaning of "being established in one's own nature" (bhāvārtha)? It is characterized by a state of well-being resulting from inquiry. When a person’s body is freed from diseases, at that very moment he is proclaimed to be "established in his own nature"; according to the path of the scriptures, it is not otherwise than this. (7)
The essential meaning is as follows:

The Victors have categorized lifespan into four stages—the infant, the youth, the middle-aged, and the elderly. Thus, when endowed with ten decades [of years], a man in the Kali Yuga has a lifespan of one hundred years. (8)
The meaning of the verse: "Ten" refers to childhood; "increased" refers to the arrogant [stage]; "youth," and likewise whatever else exists together with it, such as the skin...

He surpasses those who possess the strength of bones, shells, and pure gold by means of his supreme power of intellect and senses, through the withdrawal of the primary elements and the faculties. // 9 //
The meaning of the verse:

Now, some child eats only milk; another eats milk with rice; and yet another eats a fine meal—such is the threefold rule of diet for young people. Among others, however, a full meal is indeed the best.
The essential meaning is this:

likewise, for those of middle age or even older, the physician should perform the treatment progressively better, having properly examined the digestive fire of the person's stomach, as well as its state of equilibrium or imbalance, according to the scriptures. (11)

Now, the meaning of the term *agni* is also explained here in three ways. It becomes irregular due to the defects of transformation (*vikāra-doṣa*), such as excessive sharpness; it may also be characterized by qualities (*guṇa*) through the presence of slow wind (*manda-anila*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*sat-kapha*). The treatment for each of these will be described here in sequence. (12)
The essential meaning [is achieved] through the actions of the *subasti* procedure, as well as by proper purgatives, emetics, and nasal medications (*nasya*) that are appropriate [to the condition].
This is the essential meaning.

The wise physician should always protect the *samāna* fire in this manner: by means of appropriate dietary regimens, and constantly with enemas, purgatives, and emetics suitable for the three periods of the day. (14)
The meaning of one's inner disposition may be weak yet still some man becomes powerful; conversely, there exists a disposition that is extremely feeble even in one who is very stout.
Strength is indeed the primary factor among all medical procedures; therefore, a wise physician should carefully consider it.
When treating men who possess superior strength in this world, a skilled action should be performed by one desiring a successful outcome. (16)

Through the subsiding, the destruction, or the partial destruction and subsiding of the fruition of one's own karmas, there arises in a person of excellent character who is ever-striving a supreme and constant goodness; such a person of excellent character endures the various hardships. // 17 //
That which properly digests food consumed in the appropriate quantity is called *samāgni*. (The essential meaning:)

He is a man of courage who, even in the face of prosperity or ruin, maintains a posture with a blossoming and serene lotus-like countenance; his mind, resting upon fortitude, is not pierced by even the most unbearable of specific actions. (18)
The essential meaning is that the land is designated by its own names as *jāṅgala*, *anūpa*, and *nijābhidhāna*; furthermore, another [classification] is the *pradhāna* and the *sādhāraṇa*.
Thus, the land is always proclaimed to be of three kinds. I shall now state the characteristics of these three in their proper order. (19)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: In some places there are harsh grasses, crops, and creepers; in some places there are *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *bhūrja* trees;
in some places there are *palāśa*, *asana*, and *śāka* trees; and in some places the ground is red, black, or pale. (20)
In some places there were mountains composed of harsh stones; in others, forests with thickets of bamboo and deep hollows;
in some places, fierce tigers, wolves, bears, and wild beasts; and in others, parched iron pyrites mixed with gravel.
In some places there were excellent priyaṅgu plants and kodrava grains; in others, o Śāntanu, there were mung beans and chickpeas.
In some places there were species of donkeys, horses, cattle, and camels; in others, flocks of goats together with sheep. (22)

And in some places, far outside of wretched villages, people labor with great effort using mechanical devices to draw water from large, bottomless, and most terrifying wells where water is always extremely difficult to find. (23)

In that region, people are naturally very emaciated, with prominent veins, firm and harsh frames, and bodies prone to stiffness; they are constantly afflicted by diseases caused by wind (vāta). Therefore, one should employ treatments that subdue the wind for them.
The meaning of what has been stated is as follows: that is the *jāṅgala* [region], and thereafter the rules for the *anūpa* [region] are described.
For in such a place, the earth is always cool with water and difficult to traverse due to mud, according to the sequence. (25)

By its very nature, there were grasses, shrubs, bushes, and spreading creepers that were exceedingly soft; there were banyan trees and pāṭalī trees towering with their branches, as well as pārijātaka trees strewn with heaps of blossoms. // 26 //

Where there are always species of *aśoka*, *kakkola*, *laṃvaga*, and *kaṅguka*; where there are varieties of *jāti* produced with grace; where there are *mallikā* and *mādhavī* vines, and *mālatī* creepers thick with swaying flowers. (27)
There, the mountains were adorned with great trees, their peaks washed by the gods;
there, the campaka trees trembled under the heavy rain-clouds, while the mango and ketaka trees were filled with the cries of peacocks.

There, the Tamāla, Tālīvara, and Nālikera trees, as well as rows of Kramuka trees, are always surrounded by groves of Tāla and Hintāla; and there are lakes and rivers, exquisitely beautified by their clear waters.
Adorned with clusters of swaying lotuses and water-lilies, where cranes, swans, and wild cocks move about. // 30 //
There, the spreading creepers of hanging betel vines, the rice fields on all sides,
the bright enclosures of great sugarcane, and the lovely groves of plantain trees abound. (31)

There, the food was delicious and abundant, consisting of ripe cow’s milk and buffalo curds as bright as ghee, along with jackfruit, mangoes, and jujubes; it was strewn with dates and coconuts, and abounded in molasses.
In that place, people are always characterized by an abundance of softness, with hands and feet as radiant as tender sprouts;
they possess exceedingly stout bodies, have a predominance of phlegm (kapha), and are afflicted by diseases caused by wind (vāta). // 33 //

Therefore, physicians here always perform treatments for those [beings] with regard to phlegm and wind; thus has the regimen for marshy lands been proclaimed, as well as the discourse on the characteristics of the intermediate region. // 34 //

The essential meaning is as follows: the ground was neither excessively red nor pale in appearance; it was neither too parched nor too dense. There was neither excessive cold nor harsh heat, neither excessive wind nor extraordinary rain. (35)

And here there is no counting of mountains, nor is there a forest of gods; nor does the ground here become entirely devoid of hills, nor is it excessively watery, nor is it possessed of waterless tracts; nor are there excessive thieves, nor wicked and evil beasts.

This world, abounding in good people and rich in excellent crops, exists through the proper application of seasonal foods and nourishment; because the digestive fire remains balanced, there is no provocation of the humors, and consequently, there is never any disease here.
Therefore, that which is common to both is indeed auspicious, since it is observed to possess the characteristics of both regions;
people dwell there in constant happiness, and now the sequence of wholesome suitability (susātmyakrama) is being described.
The essential meaning is this:

medicinal substances that are congenial to a person, as well as the primary factors of place, water, disease, and physical constitution—whatever else may conduce to well-being when practiced properly becomes harmful otherwise. (39)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

When even a very small amount [of a substance] is consumed gradually and digested regularly, it does not cause harm to a person at all; rather, within seven days, it becomes habitual (*sātmyaka*). (40)
Having explained with effort the characteristics of the best suitability for men— this being the essential meaning— their constitution (prakṛti) will now be declared,
after due consideration along with the characteristics of the womb and the causes such as the recollection of previous births. (41)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: During her fertile period, the woman who observes the vow of a sage should discard her garlands, ornaments, and ointments;
she should eat from a leaf-plate or with her cupped hands during the day, and even at night she should sleep upon darbha grass. (42)
The husband should avoid her for three days; thereafter, on the fourth day, by means of immersions in water, [she becomes pure].
She has been auspiciously consecrated, adorned with performed rites of blessing, radiant, provided with warm oil, and eating *kṛśara* rice.
Well-adorned and of virtuous mind, he [approached] that beautiful woman, Manoharī, who was herself captivating.
At night, one who is skilled should approach his wife; if there is a desire for a son, he should press against her right side and lie down, but for a daughter, the other side, for a moment. (45)
If,
due to ignorance, a woman conceives on the first day [of her period],
this offspring will die from within her womb on the second night, even amidst the impurity of childbirth. (46)
Or if he dies on the third night, or again becomes stammering, blind, deaf, or extremely mute,
or even if he becomes naturally more cruel, then on the fourth day one should sow the seed.
The meaning of the passage is as follows: When a woman is in her menses, the semen of the man enters it gradually with effort;
then, by means of his own past karma, the beginningless and endless Self, whose consciousness is conditioned by that act, enters [the womb]. (48)
The meaning of the term is that he lives here again and again, or rather, that very same one who lived previously will live once more;
therefore, it is specifically proclaimed as "the living being" (jīva) because of its continuous maintenance of the collection of vital breaths. // 49 //

The essential meaning is this: together with the powers of mind, speech, body, and the senses, and endowed with discernment, breath, and one's own life-span—these ten are proclaimed as the group of vitalities (prāṇas). Therefore, the separation from them is indeed the death of the embodied being. // 50 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

then, food, the body, its own sense organs, breath, mind, and speech—these groups of primary *paryāptis* (developmental capacities) are described in their proper order for the sake of the acquisition of a living being's body. (51)
The essential meaning is this:

indeed, the embryo, joined with the soul and consisting of semen and blood, sequentially attains the sixfold specific stages of development (*paryāpti*) within a period of one muhūrta; thereafter, it enters the state of a physical body in this world. (52)
The meaning of the verse: Now, from the tenth night, it attains the state of the *kalala* by its own nature;
through ten days at a time, it reaches turbidity and stability here by means of karma.
Furthermore, from month to month, it becomes a bubble and then a solid mass; and after five months have passed, there is the expansion of flesh.
For while in the womb, one indeed attains the differentiation of limbs month by month;
furthermore, the skin, nails, and body hair emerge month by month;
and after the head is formed with its apertures, one experiences frequent throbbing for a month.
Up until the ninth or tenth month, there is the departure of each respective [element]; beyond that, it is otherwise, resulting in deformities.
The meaning of the state [of existence] is as follows:
one remains within the womb situated in the midst of a vessel whose impurities have not yet ripened according to one's own desire;
it is enveloped by a moist placenta and rendered dull by the intense darkness of the womb.
Above, they fall incessantly, abounding excessively in bile and phlegm. // 55 //
Smeared all over with the foul-smelling excrement of the corpse,

the fetus drinks the fluids from all sides like a jar with a broken side; situated within the jar-like body along with the fluids, it remains there for seven months as previously described, after which it becomes like the stalk of a blue lotus.
For by means of this, one attains the navel-cord and from there enjoys the essences beyond.

Thus, having been led through an increase of suffering by means of various obstacles according to the sequence described, and further manifesting a fierce affliction of the limbs that has fully arisen, it is certain that there is no suffering whatsoever equal to that of birth within human existence. (57)
The meaning of the state [of the body] is as follows:
it is smeared with impurities, excrement, urine, blood, secretions, and the filth of private parts;
it is extremely difficult to traverse, being filled with a mass of hair that is most harsh, foul-smelling, putrid, and mixed with many [other impurities].
By the power of karma, the one born from a womb encounters a hollow opening situated near the anus, facing downwards, unbearable to behold, and unfit even to describe. (58)

The essential meaning has been thus understood; having explained with effort, through the logic of the great scriptures, the birth from the excellent womb, I shall now describe in due order his beautiful physical characteristics as proclaimed by the Lord of Jinas. (59)
The essential meaning [is as follows]:
from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina, which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence;
For this [teaching], which shines from both banks as it accomplishes the welfare of both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (60)

Having bowed to the venerable Vardhamāna, the Jina Vardhamāna— the established meaning of whose being is the sole cause of the bliss of the Great Siddhi— I shall explain the primary body as it is known through the traditional instruction. (1)
The essential meaning is this:
the bones, with their clearly manifest joints, the sinews, the veins, and the extensive masses of flesh—
this is the sequence according to their enumeration.
One should declare three hundred and ninety, as well as seven hundred and five, as being recognized [in the respective cases]. // 2 //
The meaning of the passage is that twenty vessels are said to surround the navel, and four are said to extend transversely.
Likewise, they say there are sixteen permanent cavities and six empty ones, along with the kūrcas. // 3 //

The meaning of the passage is as follows: here, three hundred bones and three hundred joints have been mentioned. However, how can there be as many joints as there are bones? For a single joint occurs when two bones are joined; therefore—

With that number of bones, it is natural for the number of joints to be fewer. Even in the Suśruta-saṃhitā, 300 bones and 210 joints are mentioned. Although in the three manuscripts available to us, the reading "tri-tri-navapratītam" [is found].
This very reading is found; nevertheless, this reading appears to be incorrect. It seems to be the fault of the scribes.
[The text reads: *sraḥstiryaggāḥ*.
Thus, the description of the twenty-four *dhamanīs* is complete; therefore,
the meaning of the word "samaṃtāt" is as follows:
In all four directions; even so, here only this much—above and below—should be understood. With this very intention, the eminent teacher himself stated:
"Four vessels are said to be horizontal."
This has been expressed by writing;
otherwise, it would be [only] on all sides (samaṃtāt).
The oblique [channels] are also included;
there are two cords of flesh and seven layers of skin. There are likewise eight channels, as well as the liver and spleen.
The stomach, the small intestine, and the large intestine (pakvāśaya) are constant; the series of the thick intestine (*sthūlāntra*) consists of exactly sixteen [parts]. // 4 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

one hundred and seven vital points (marmas) have been taught; furthermore, there are nine gates in this body; there are eighty thousand pores of the skin; and the three humors (doṣas) are designated by the specific term "pillars" (stambha). // 5 //
The essential meaning is as follows: here, the rows of teeth are thirty-two in number; the count of the nails is twenty;
and the fat, along with the semen and the entire brain-matter, each measures one añjali. (6)
The essential meaning is that there are three *añjali*s of blood, one *vasā* (fat), one *prasṛti* of bile,
and one *prasṛti* of phlegm in the body.
Each one here is prescribed as six; likewise, the red [substance] is joined with a measure of half an āḍhaka. // 7 //
The meaning of the substance is as follows: urine is measured by one *prastha*, while feces in the middle [of the scale] is half an *āḍhaka*.
These five winds, which abide eternally, pervade the body in their respective order.

The meaning of the term *bhāva* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as well as those known as *apāna* and *samāna*; *vyāna* and *udāna* are likewise designated as its meanings. This is the meaning of *bhāva*.
In the eyes, there is pain, tearing, and thick, sticky discharge; likewise in the ears, there is earwax and even excrement.
In this mouth, there is the filth of spittle, snot, wind, bile, and the impurities of the tongue and teeth. (10)
The essential meaning is this:
there is indeed mucus in the nose, specifically within the nostrils; likewise, excrement is produced therein.
Urine, semen, feces, and blood flow downward from the two openings. (11)
The essential meaning is this:
the body is like a leaking, broken jar, rich with impurities flowing from its nine gates;
it vomits sweat through its bristling pores, and lice, nits, and eight-legged insects are born therein. (12)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
Thus, for a human being, the body is a source of suffering, as are old age, death, separation, and the extreme hardship of birth; therefore, one should always direct one's mind toward Dharma. (13)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: Indeed, for some person born in this world, there occurs a certain recollection of past births (*jātismaratva*).
Therefore, its characteristics are indicated here in order to establish the existence of other lives. (14)

The essential meaning is that at the moment of death, there arise many causes for the recollection of past lives: a stainless state of intellect and being, knowledge of the scriptures, reverence for the investigation of the Dharma, and the manifestation of specific qualities acquired through non-crooked means. (15)

Having heard and seen [the teachings] in the past and having practiced them, embodied beings— through the exhaustion of karma and through tranquility— remember that supreme state of their own kind directly, by means of inference from dreams and from fears resembling those [experiences]. (16)
Having indicated the essential meaning, we shall describe the characteristics of one who remembers past lives and the nature of the elements in their proper order.
When the semen is joined with blood and the soul enters it, the nature of men arises from the predominance of the [three] humors (doṣas). // 17 //
The meaning of the state [of the asterism] is as follows:
a person born under that nature is intensely averse to cold, harsh, and possessed of prominent veins;
he remains constantly awake at night, prone to delirious speech, unfortunate, engaged in the conduct of a thief, and unpleasant [to others]. (18)
Possessing envy and shunned by the noble for his lack of virtues, with coarse and sparse hair, and gnawing at his nails and teeth;
burdened by disease, quick in movement, wicked, unstable, and devoid of friendship, the singer always runs about. (19)

One who has destroyed his realization, whose limbs are emaciated and harsh, whose feet are split and covered with prominent veins, who is devoid of fortitude, unstable in intellect, and insignificant, dreams of wandering upon mountain peaks or in the sky. (20)
The essential meaning is as follows: [the person] arises from a constitution dominated by bile (*pitta*); he is characterized by excessive anger, is very sharp, and is bold;
he perspires profusely, and his network of veins is yellow; for this reason, he is fond of copper-colored lips and palate. // 21 //
Endowed with intelligence, exceedingly brave, and invincible; eloquent, a poet, and a skilled reciter;
proficient in the arts, dexterous, and highly wise; possessing superior luster, devoted to truth, and of great fortitude. // 22 //
Yellowish, excessively red, with a body that is flaccid and hot; his pair of hands and feet resemble red lotuses;
he quickly becomes afflicted by old age and is overcome by baldness; though possessing good fortune, he is constantly intent on eating. // 23 //

In a dream, one should see golden ornaments, jasmine garlands, and [substances] the color of lac and flesh; blazing meteors, thunderbolts, and masses of flickering fire; and heaps of flowers, as well as *kiṃśuka* and *karṇikāra* blossoms. (24)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
A person of a phlegmatic (śleṣma) constitution will possess superior intelligence, be very stout, and be serene;
such a mortal has a slender body dark like a blade of dūrvā grass, is grateful, and is firm in enmity. // 25 //
The illustrious one possesses a voice like the sound of a drum, thunder, or a lion; he is affectionate, steadfast, virtuous, sweet, and beloved.
Endowed with sweetness, vigor, great fortitude, and compassion, he is patient and free from calamities.
Even though he was skilled in the arts of training, Subhaga, despite his beautiful eyes, was not able to understand it quickly.
While fast asleep, he sees ponds and flowing rivers filled with clusters of lotuses and water-lilies, abounding with swans. // 27 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

Having thus described the nature of the excellent site, we shall now explain the characteristics of the medicinal substances for the purpose of [identifying] a good field—one that is praised for its unimpaired qualities and free from pits, anthills, and poisons. (28)
The meaning of the passage:

[It is] a place of dissolution, an abode for hosts of hungry ghosts, overwhelmed by cold, heat, and extreme frost; submerged in water, waterless, and desolate, resembling sapless and parched shrubs and trees. (29)
A site that abounds in ravines, hidden recesses, and caves; that is thick with foul odors and densely packed with sand;
and which is always to be avoided if it is dark blue, white, or excessively red, or possesses the color of ashes, clouds, or a pigeon—these are the lowest qualities. // 30 //
It was filled with glossy, burgeoning, and blossoming creepers; it was known for its trees that sported with rows of playful fruits;
it was bound by sweetness, beauty, and fragrance; and it was preeminent in its clearly manifest and abundant essence.

A field that has sweet-tasting water, is very level, beautiful in appearance, common [to all], rich in all medicinal elixirs (rasāyana), very black, soft, and pleasant, should always be known as suitable for the collection of herbs.

The meaning of this is as follows: Even here, that which has become a great medicine should be avoided when it is being oppressed by forest fires, heat, and paths made like water, or by weapons, thunderbolts, bursting insects, and winds. (33)
The essential meaning is that which is small in quantity, beautiful in form, delicious in taste, fragrant, refined, pleasant, most wholesome, pure,
directly visible with immediate results, praiseworthy, and fully encompassed by the intended purpose. // 34 //
The meaning of the essence is that it quickly destroys even most terrible diseases; [if] deficient or excessive, it has defects such as being fruitless. // 35 //
The meaning of the verse:

Medication administered here in an excessive dose may cause fainting, intoxication, exhaustion, burning sensations, piercing pain, flatulence, distension, constipation, delusion, and so forth; it produces indigestion and irregularity of the digestive fire. (36)
The meaning of the intent is this:
what is deficient leads to ineffectiveness; therefore, it should be applied properly and equally.
Having given a small amount at a time over three days, one should establish the proper measure here for the sake of pacifying the defects. (37)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: Experts declare that all fresh and excellent medicinal herbs possess superior potency.
When combined with ghee, viḍaṅga, and long pepper, they become enriched with the highest medicinal virtues. (38)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: having explained the preparation of medicines according to the sequence of the aphorisms, [the author] now describes the classification of the body:
"It is gross, lean, and called middling; among these, that which is named middling is indeed the primary. (39)
The meanings of "excessive" and "emaciated" are both highly censurable; they should be avoided in relation to burdens, horses, vehicles, and so forth.
In all circumstances and in every way, one who possesses a body of moderate build is desired by everyone with their whole being. (40)
The essential meaning is this: here, one should effect the emaciation of the obese through dry medicines, food, drinks, and the like;
likewise, the nourishment of the emaciated through unctuous and strengthening remedies; and there should always be the preservation of the healthy through wholesome means. (41)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Emaciation is said to arise from the humors (doṣas) and from constitutional nature (svabhāva). They declare that emaciation caused by the humors is most curable, whereas that which is constitutional is extremely difficult to treat; therefore, one must exert great effort to nourish it.

Those who know the truth declare that the constant treatment for the gross [dosha] consists of purgatives produced from specific formulations, along with dry decoctions and groups of pungent and bitter substances; this is the desired method for food and medicine. (43)

The essential meaning is that water is therefore recommended for one whose digestive fire has been diminished; furthermore, after eating, milk should also be administered here, either as nasal drops, electuaries, or gargles. Thus, that digestive fire must be constantly protected.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

In the spring, one should administer the *vāsya* enema; that which is called *madhyama* (intermediate) should be administered during the rainy season; and its purgative (*vairecana*) procedure should be performed in autumn. This protection of the healthy is desired by the noble ones. (45)
The essential meaning is: one should constantly practice the service of a single rasa, while avoiding those causes that bring about faults. // 46 //
The essential meaning: Having properly described the sequence of the body, we shall explain diseases according to the method of the aphorisms.
Indeed, the well-known humors (doṣas)—wind (vāta), phlegm (kapha), and bile (pitta)—arise within the body. (47)
The essential meaning is as follows:
Vata is pungent, extremely dry, and mobile in nature; Pitta is liquid, very bitter, and hot-yellow; Kapha is unctuous, sweet-tasting, exceedingly dull, naturally heavy, slimy, and cold. (48)
The essential meaning is this:
residing properly in the stomach, the chest, the head, the throat, and all the joints, *kapha* performs all the functions of the body by means of the mobile vital air (*marut*). (49)
The essential meaning is this:

bile resides between the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) and the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya), or sometimes it is said to be located in the heart, liver, and spleen; it pervades the entire body, being carried by the movement of the wind (vāta). // 50 //
The essential meaning is as follows: The wind (vāyu) resides in the secret region of the hips and groins; it is the essence of the entire body.
By its very nature, it carries the humors (doṣas) and the constituent elements (dhātus); when itself corrupted, it corrupts the body here in this world. (51)
The essential meaning is this:
indeed, when a single humor (doṣa) becomes provoked, it vitiates those other humors residing within its own abode.
We shall now explain, according to the path of the scriptures, the purposes regarding the origin of diseases from the provocation of these humors. (52)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Through the conjunction with external, internal, and personal causes, or through the arising and activation of karma, or from the fourfold group beginning with the field (*kṣetra*), defects undergo provocation and subsidence. (53)
The meaning of the state [of the humors] is as follows:

from excessive physical exertion, or from excessive sexual intercourse, or from traveling a long distance, or from climbing [heights], or from suppression [of natural urges], or from the reversal of sleep patterns, or from immersion in water, or from the impact of wind. (54)

By means of coarse grains such as śyāmāka, nīvāra, and kodrava; by pulses such as niṣpāva, masūra, and māṣa; and by the consumption of dry and light substances such as mudga, āḍhakī, bitter and astringent vegetables, and other parched greens. (55)

Due to excessive joy, exposure to strong winds or heavy snowfall, yawning, injury, or the suppression of natural urges, or through dry food and drink that is excessively cold, the provocation of Vāta invariably occurs. (56)

The meaning of the state [of possession] arises from excessive grief, anger, fear, or extreme joy; from severe fasting or excessive sexual indulgence; and from the consumption of pungent, sour, sharp, or excessively strong substances, as well as heating agents mixed with mustard oil. (57)

In this world, the provocation of pitta in a living being occurs through oil-cakes, oil, sun-exposure, leafy vegetables, fish, the meat of goats, sheep, and cows, horse-gram soup, and sour liquids such as sauvīra and fermented gruel. // 58 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

[The humors become aggravated] by constant sleeping during the day, by lack of sexual intercourse or physical exercise, and by the consumption of heavy, slimy, and sour foods; by the excessive use of unctuous, very firm, or very sharp substances; and by diets consisting largely of flour-based foods, sugarcane products, milk, and black gram. (59)
Through the consumption of curd, fermented gruel, seasoned foods, the fruits of climbing vines, and undigested heavy meals,
as well as by drinking excessively sour liquids and very cold substances, an aggravation of phlegm (śleṣman) occurs in human beings. (60)
The essential meaning is that,
through the refutations of the individual, the combination, and the collection [of the senses], there are exactly ten defects pertaining to the person in this context.
And the blood, together with the humors (doṣas), is to be divided [into two parts], because of the relationship between the corrupting agent and the corrupted substrate (dūṣaka-dūṣya-bhāva). // 61 //
The essential meaning is this:
from their provocation, there arises pain within the abdomen, as well as shifting sensations, acidity, and the defects of burning heat.
Nausea and anorexia are the doshas; therefore, their characteristics are now stated according to their enumeration. // 62 //
The meaning of the [root] *bhū* consists of piercing, striking, and prodding; cutting, uprooting, and crushing; scattering, biting, and breaking; splitting apart, tearing out, and shaking. // 63 //

Separation, stiffness, lockjaw, breathlessness, contraction, and drawing [of limbs], as well as various extremely painful symptoms occurring without apparent cause, indeed arise when there is an aggravation of Vāta. (64)
The meaning of the verse: Excessive heat, parching, extreme delusion, burning sensations, a sense of fuming, loss of appetite, anger, and fever;
heat in the body, excessive perspiration, and much delirious talk—these are the diseases that arise when pitta is provoked. // 65 //
The meaning of the state [of kapha] is as follows: sleepiness, itching, heaviness of the limbs, excessive whiteness, coldness, enlargement, and drowsiness;
stiffness, loss of appetite, and slight pain—these are the diseases resulting from the provocation of phlegm (śleṣman).

The essential meaning of these is as follows: the *bhasman* (earth-element) is extremely coarse, clearly greyish-brown (*kapota*), or excessively black; *marut* (wind) is [characterized by its movement];
*pitta* is said to be blue, very yellow, intensely green, or exceedingly blackish-red.
Phlegm becomes oily and very pale; when all [the humors] are combined, it is of their respective colors.
At the time of the provocation of the humors, a sudden change of complexion occurs in men. (67)
The essential meaning is that one should diligently apply the prescription of medicines possessing superior qualities,
having understood the entire distinction of time as it pertains to the correct path of the meaning of the sūtras.
By a physician who is devoted to diligent action and possesses skillful qualities, [the healing] of the sick is undertaken with great care. // 68 //
The meaning of the subject matter [is as follows]:
from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issuing from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence;
For this [teaching], which shines from both banks as it accomplishes the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (69)
The essential meaning is this:
he who knows the entirety of the activity of the three times situated within the womb of the three worlds—
substance together with its modifications and inherent nature, which has not been tasted by others.
Having bowed to that Supreme Lord, the Conqueror who has vanquished his enemies, the God of gods, I shall, out of reverence, explain in due order this succession of time according to the Sūtra.
This time, which is the essential meaning of existence, is supreme and irresistible in its power, due to its drawing together of all beings.
Neither heavy nor too light, devoid of beginning and end, great,
distinct yet non-distinct from others, moving without transgression, subtle, and indivisible— this is time (samaya), which possesses formless qualities and is characterized by revolution. // 2 //

This is the essential meaning: it is twofold, being the object of inference; devoid of form and other qualities, inactive, and though densely packed in all locations within the space of the world, each atom is indeed singular.
Time is always understood as the supreme object beyond the senses;
worldly convention preceded by that [time] is said to proceed from the sequence of sunrise and so forth. // 3 //
The meaning of the term is that it is known as an *āvalī*, which is traditionally remembered as being beyond calculation and perceived as a conventional unit of time.
In this same manner, sixty *āvalikās* are declared to be endowed with the designation of one breath (*ucchvāsa*). Seven such breaths constitute a *toka* in its full extent.
From seven *tokas*, a *lava* arises; and from thirty *lavas* plus eight (*vasu*), a *nāḍikā* is formed. (4)
The meaning of the terms is as follows: two nāḍīs are said to constitute one muhūrta; thirty muhūrtas make a day;
ten days make a fortnight (pakṣa); and those two fortnights, the bright and the dark, are equal in duration.

Twelve months and six of those groups of seasons [constitute a year] in the order beginning with Caitra; and there are two solstices, for when these two are joined together, the designation "year" (varṣa) is applied.
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is as follows: the duration of time required for a single mental state is called one *samaya*.
Here, the first [state] is sweet, powerful, pure, and possesses the majesty of a mass of clouds.
The autumn causes constant torment; the winter is an accumulation of cold; and so is the cool season.
According to the rule of sequential enumeration, two months beginning with Caitra constitute each successive season;
this is indeed declared to be the eternal means for accomplishing all ritual actions.
The meaning of the [seasonal] states is as follows:
the period named Vasanta (spring) occurs in the forenoon; midday is Grīṣmaka (summer);
the afternoon is indeed called Prāvṛṣya (the rainy season); and the onset of the rains is the early night.
Midnight is declared to be the autumn season, while the time of dawn is winter;
thus, the progression of the six seasons occurs daily and constantly, following the same sequence as throughout the year.
The essential meaning is that phlegm, accumulated during the winter season, becomes aggravated during the period of late autumn and spring,
just as wind, always accumulated in summer, rises daily during the rainy season.

In autumn, when the activity of the clouds has ceased and bile (pitta) becomes excessively aggravated, one should then eliminate those humors (doṣas) according to the prescribed method for the accumulation and provocation [of pitta]. // 8 //
The meaning of the state is that those doshas, being specifically aggravated, spread forth either together with blood or individually.
Whether in pairs or in threes, or even as these four here, they attain mutual dependence; though dispersed, they once again descend into manifest individuality.
Subject to the power of time, they produce disease according to the stated strength of the six [humors]. // 9 //
The essential meaning here is the complete accumulation of the fifteen ascending aeons (*utsarpaṇa*),
as well as their mutual dependence, their manifestation through their own nature, and likewise the distinction between individuals.
Or he who knows the conduct characterized by all defects that brings suffering to living beings—he is the supreme physician; he should perform the treatment for the six [seasons] every day. (10)
The essential meaning is this: having thus understood the prescription of time, the wise and great physician should now apply the rules for drinks, diet, conduct, and medicine.
In that regard, one should always pacify the humors when they are in a state of accumulation and when they are provoked;
thorough purification performed with diligence is considered the protection of one who is healthy. (11)
The essential meaning is this:
in the spring, food consisting primarily of dry, alkaline, astringent, bitter, and pungent substances is beneficial;
likewise, drinks and even mouth-solvents (coṣaka) with similar qualities are prescribed here.
Water from a well, water from a village pond, water heated by fire, pure water, excellent cool water, nasal drops, and emetics—these are declared by the Lord of Jinas to be most worthy of honor. (12)
The essential meaning is this: in summer, food consisting primarily of milk and ghee is excellent, as is cool drink;
moreover, the consumption of honey, molasses, and sugarcane, as well as water from a well, is indeed appropriate.

In the rainy season, one should generally consume water that is intensely bitter, slightly pungent, and endowed with astringency; likewise, milk, sugarcane juice, and similar products are beneficial, as is boiled water.
The essential meaning is this:

in autumn, for living beings seeking their own welfare, all food should be accompanied by milk and enriched with ghee and sugar; it may also be bitter or astringent; and all water should be beneficial.
In the winter season, pungent, bitter, cold, alkaline, astringent, and similar substances are considered unwholesome;
whereas water mixed with ghee and oil, as well as sour and sweet [substances], are said to be beneficial.
The essential meaning is this:
in the winter season, food that is clearly sour, milky, astringent, bitter, and salty, along with an abundance of heat, is beneficial; likewise, water situated in ponds is said to be wholesome.
That which is wholesome and beneficial for a person should be given according to the time and the state of their hunger. // 15 //
The meaning of the state [of readiness] is as follows:
when feces and urine have been expelled, when the vital air (vāyu) has moved, when the body is light,
when the senses, speech, and mind are purified, and when the belly is relaxed yet weary from exertion.
One should prepare the great meal according to the scriptural injunctions; I shall now explain the sequence of the reasoning.
The essential meaning is this:
at the beginning of the meal, one should eat that which is unctuous and sweet;
in the middle, that which is accompanied by salty and sour foods; and afterwards, the remaining tastes.

Having understood the strength of one's constitution, being focused and steady upon a clean, comfortable seat, one should quickly [drink] water that is lukewarm, increasingly liquid, and suitable for all seasons. // 17 //
The essential meaning is this:
a mortal, while consuming boiled rice as food, should take it accompanied by those [liquids] as drinks;
likewise, among oily substances, that which is pure and warm, and for flour-based foods, cool water.
Having drunk this beneficial beverage that follows [the ritual], one becomes eternally happy; it is wholesome for all living beings. // 18 //
The essential meaning is this:
water drunk here before meals always brings about emaciation;
when drunk during the middle of the meal, it produces a moderate effect; and likewise, when drunk at the end, it causes nourishment.

Having understood the true nature of wholesome food, a person should follow the rules for eating; otherwise, dry food that has been consumed may lead to indigestion and cause suffering for embodied beings. (19)
The essential meaning is that rice grains possess sweetness and cooling qualities; because they are light in digestion,
they subdue pitta, increase kapha, and promote the daily passage of stool and urine.

The qualities of rice have been declared: they are astringent and sweet, they subdue pitta and vāta, they are characterized by a tendency to cause constipation, and they are heavy in their digestion. (20)
The essential meaning is:
they are hot, very dry, astringent-sweet, and possess great lightness in their post-digestive effect;
they destroy phlegm, excessively generate wind and bile, and are always constipating.

This description of inferior grains such as *śyāmāka* and others has been declared for men who eat them; now, out of great regard, the various groups of pulses, vegetables, and excellent juices are being described. (21)
The essential meaning is as follows:
all products of bamboo (vaidalaka) are parched, possess a hundredfold qualities, are astringent-sweet, are constipating,
increase wind (vāta), and when combined with astringents, they are prescribed for bile (pitta) and blood disorders.
These warm kulattha beans have been described as destroyers of diseases caused by phlegm and wind;
they break up abdominal tumors (gulma), stones (aṣṭhīlā), liver disorders, and splenic enlargements, and are beneficial for those suffering from internal hemorrhaging and bleeding disorders.
The essential meaning is that these juices are slimy, cold, and very sweet; they are aphrodisiacs and nourishing,
yet they cause heaviness upon digestion, increase phlegm, and provoke blood-bile (pitta).

Those whose feces, urine, and flatus are constantly broken apart are the best among those suffering from consumption; they are manifestly afflicted by vāta alone, whereas those beginning with the "king" (rājā) and māṣa types are composed of kapha.
The essential meaning is:
*āḍhakī* beans are most beneficial for phlegm and bile, though they slightly aggravate wind; *mudga* beans are similar to them, as well as fever-removing and beneficial in all types of diarrhea.
Among these, lentils (*masūra*) are said to be especially beneficial for those with wind disorders (*sūpa*); they are cooling (*hima*).
One should employ all [these grains] according to the individual's constitution (*prakṛti*), local climate (*deśa*), season (*samaya*), and the progression of the disease (*vyādhi-krama*). // 24 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
Sesame seeds are hot in potency; they are pervading, astringent, bitter, and sweet;
they are constipating and digestive stimulants; they are light in their post-digestive state; and when applied to wounds, they cleanse and heal them.
Wheat, sesame, and barley are cooling; they are beneficial for children and increase virility.
Having considered their defects and virtues, these should always be eaten by embodied beings according to the prescribed rules.
The meaning of the essential point is as follows: that which is utterly shattered, decayed, stale, or infested by insects and the like;
that which grows in a poor location in the forest; that which is produced out of season; and that which is slightly unripe or newly harvested.
Therefore, this unsurpassed grain should always be avoided by the lords of sages at all times. // 26 //
We shall properly explain their essential meaning from the very beginning until the conclusion of the results.
And others, such as the *ālukayuktapiṇḍa*, *madhu*, *gaṅgā*, *hastiśūka*, and so forth. // 27 //
If it were so, it would seem correct; by doing this, the meaning becomes "the breaking of the *āluka*. The intended sense is:
"Even though these [roots] such as the *ryādī* are heavy due to their ripening time and being from dogs, they are nevertheless cold."
Those things that increase phlegm should be consumed when bile and blood are in excess;
likewise, those that cause the discharge of waste and urine, as well as those that promote the emission of semen, should be employed. (28)
The essential meaning is as follows: *āraṇyā*, *luvarāṭikā*, *muraṭikā*, *bhūśarkarā*,
*māṇakī*, *bindu*, *vyāpta*, *sukuṇḍalī*, *namalikā*, and *amlīkā* destroy hemorrhoids and wind disorders.
Śvetāmlī, muśalī, varāhakaṇikā, bhūhastikarṇī, and others—when well-prepared, they promote nourishment, pacify poisons, and are beneficial for disorders of wind (vāta). // 29 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows: the tips of bamboo, śatāvarī, śaśaśira, vetrāgra, vajrī-latā,
śevālī, vara, kākanaśā, and the sprouts of mārdī are always [to be used].
They are cold, increase phlegm, are highly aphrodisiac and heavy, pacify bile,
remove external heat and impurities, and slightly aggravate wind.
The essential meaning is: jīvantī, taruṇī, bṛhacchagalikā, vṛkṣādanī,
pañjikā, cuñcu, and kunḍalatā, along with bimba— these are astringent and increase wind (vāta).
Jīvantikā, which produces tears and grows on two types of potsherds, is phlegm-increasing; when combined with cillī, vāstūka, and taṇḍulīyaka, they are pure and beneficial for bile.
The meaning of the substances is as follows:
śāṅgīṣṭā, paṭolapānikacarī, the creeper of kākādimācī, saptalā with maṇḍūkī, dravaṇikā, chinnodbhavā, and putriṇī.
Nimba and the others—along with kirātatikta, jharasī, śvetā, punarnavā, and sadā—remove pitta and kapha, pacify worms, and eradicate skin diseases. (32)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: *guhyākṣī*, *sakusuṃbha*, *śāka*, *lavaṇī*, *rājyā*, *ajigaṃdhā*, and so forth;
*gaura*, *amlā*, *amradala*, *akhalākulahala*, *gaṇḍīra*, and *veguṇḍikā*.

Śigru, uḍīcya, śatapuṣpā, and others that are fragrant; dhānyaka, musta, and sārjaka; as well as kāsaghnī, kṣavaka, and their like—these remove phlegm, are heating, and are beneficial in cases involving vāta. // 33 //
The meaning of the verse:
Having tied together bandhūka flowers, *bhṛguśoliphena* stalks, and *veṇyākhukarṇī* and *āḍhakī* seeds that have been crushed;

With *rhimakara*, *tuṭika*, *kuṣṭha*, and blooming *nāgapuṣpa* flowers.

The syllable *ṣaṃ* destroys phlegm.

The essential meaning is that it is not even the size of an atom, nor the measure of a grain,

The meaning of existence, characterized by transformation, is presented through its various synonymous distinctions.
