The characteristics described as "stench of the breath" (niśvāsapūti) manifest daily in bilious fever (pittajvara). // 56 //
The essential symptoms are: drowsiness, lack of appetite, excessive heaviness of the head,
mild heat, extreme sweetness in the mouth, and horripilation.
In this condition, there is obstruction of the channels, slight pain, and rapid onset; vomiting, excessive salivation, whiteness of the eyes, and impurity of the face. // 57 //
Coughing, nasal catarrh, the emergence of phlegm, and itching in the throat.
And all the symptoms manifested in phlegm-fever arise from the great universal fever. // 58 //
The meaning of the verse is:
by means of an exchange between those two, they will become musical instruments. // 59 //
The essential meaning regarding all fevers is that which has been described with its complete set of symptoms,
even when it is accompanied by all the various groups of complications.
With a feeble voice and distorted eyes, gasping for breath, he constantly falls to the ground accompanied by delirious cries. // 60 //
Accompanied by internal burning, it disappears upon being remembered.
The physician who knows the characteristics of fever here should avoid that [patient]. // 61 //
The meaning of the state [of affliction] is indicated by labored breathing, colic, retention of feces and urine, and burning sensations.
And those accompanied by these groups of complications are to be rejected. // 62 //
The essential meaning is this:
one should drink sharp purificatory ghee after it has been vomited.
This fever does not afflict one whose body is thoroughly purified;
when the fever is manifest, fasting alone should be practiced. // 63 //
The essential meaning is:
having observed the procedure for leaping over, one should give [water] to one afflicted by thirst.
One whose body is afflicted by phlegm and wind should drink water that is warm;
one accompanied by bile should drink it boiled and then cooled.
The meaning of the passage is:
if a man should be afflicted by hunger,
he might drink gruel or lie down to rest to alleviate his fever.
In the same way, one who seeks to eliminate the disorders of fever should also prepare a gruel with various lukewarm soups.
The essential meaning is:
one afflicted by wind-fever (pavanajvara) should drink a non-cold decoction of bilva, agnimantha, the two types of bṛhatī, and pāṭalī.
A cold decoction of kāśa, ikṣu, yaṣṭimadhu, candana,
and sārivā is here the destroyer of disorders caused by pitta.
The essential meaning is: one should drink *muṣaṇa* for the purpose of digesting a fever caused by *kapha*.
In this case as well, when the matter has ripened, there is mild fever and a relaxed abdomen.
The essential meaning is that,
having observed a mature fever,
one should treat it with unctuous purgatives or, alternatively, with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) as appropriate.
One suffering from fever caused by pitta, vāta, or associated with pain should be treated with emesis, cold applications, and purgation. 68.
The essential meaning is that in phlegm-fever (kaphajvara), emesis with fermented liquors (ariṣṭa) mixed with a large quantity of ground rock salt, vacā, and madana is desired.
It should be employed as a gargle, a broth, or a paste of bitter groups [of drugs]. // 69 //
The essential purpose for women is fulfilled through ritual actions employing methods of pacification.
One should honor those who possess superior qualities and those afflicted by the fever of suffering. // 70 //
The essential meaning [of this formulation] consists of vāsā, amṛtā, udaka, paṭola, mahauṣadha, pāṭhā, agnimantha, the two types of bṛhatī, and nāgara.
Or one should drink a decoction of ginger, nimba, and the king of trees (āragvadha) in all fevers caused by vāta. (71)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: [the preparation] of parched grain, water, *āmalaka*, *bālaka*, and *śerukā*;
and of *mṛdvīkā*, *nāga*, *madhuka*, *utpala*, and *śāribā*.
In cases of fever caused by all types of pitta, one should drink a decoction of kustuṃburu, utpala, payas, and payoruha.
The meaning of the verse is: [the decoction] of māragvadha, ambuda, mahauṣadha, and pippalī.
In cases of fevers characterized by an abundance of phlegm (kapha), one should drink a decoction here of bhūnimba, nimba, the two types of bṛhatī, and nāgara. (73)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: [the paste] of Musta, Niśā, Āmalaka, Candana, and Sārivā; and of Chinnodbhavā, Ambuda, Paṭola, and Harītakī.
One should drink a decoction of mūrvā, amṛtā, udumbara, bibhītaka, and rohiṇī in cases of fevers caused by all the doṣas. (74)
The essential meaning is that [the disease is cured] by the correct application of medicines prescribed according to the specific defects,
as well as by individual preparations of ghee, oil, milk, flour-pastes, and fermented acids.
It shall be the destroyer of irregular fevers such as those occurring at intervals of one day and so forth. // 75 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
[this applies] during the intervals between the third and fourth days in cases of fever caused by combined wind and great poisons.
One who desires their own welfare should drink the juice of the *kākāṅgī* plant mixed with snake’s milk. (76)
The meaning of the essence is [conveyed] by the leaves of the great medicinal herb that is stainless through its shedding.
Incense is the cause for the destruction of planetary fevers and piśācas. // 77 //
For the essential meaning is that the procedure for parching the corrupted matter is indeed prescribed in cases of fevers.
One should administer oleation therapy, along with appropriate excellent medicines and other measures,
in cases arising from excessive dryness.
The essential meaning is that one should perform the action of an enema in cases of chronic fevers.
Milk, ghee, and jaggery, taken together with long pepper,
should be drunk in cases of very chronic, dry, and high-grade fevers.
The essential meaning is:
[he perceives] the absence of longing, diminished sneezing, a lack of appetite, clarity,
all the sense faculties, and a state of physical equilibrium and coolness.
Observing that the patient’s nature of itching and impurities has ceased and the digestive fire in the stomach is kindled, one should determine that he is free from fever.
The meaning of the state [of being] arises from physical exercise, wind, heavy loads, leaping, and impact.
Even here, one who is free from fever through right conduct may still experience intense [suffering]. // 81 //
The meaning of the state is this:
just as a forest fire burns wood that is exceedingly dry,
so does this fever here burn one who has returned [to health] and is freed from fever.
Therefore, like one afflicted by fever whose limbs have been freed from it, he must be protected by means of his own conduct, food, medicine, and so forth. // 82 //
The essential meaning is this:
bile, when vitiated and combined with blood, phlegm, and wind,
reaches the receptacle of waste and suppresses the digestive fire of the stomach.
When it quickly discharges impurity that has become liquefied, the experts call that disease *atisāra* (diarrhea). // 83 //
The essential meaning is that there is intense pain in the anus accompanied by colic,
and the stool is mixed with phlegmatic foam, painful, and accompanied by a discharge.
When it discharges dry matter excessively and repeatedly in very small quantities, the sages call that *vātātīsāra* (wind-type diarrhea). // 84 //
The meaning of the state [of the poison] is as follows:
it is yellow, reddish, large, green, and always burning;
it is accompanied by fainting, thirst, fever, indigestion, and intoxication.
When one quickly voids very loose and clear feces, the sages call that *pittātisāra* (bilious diarrhea). // 85 //
The essential meaning is this:
[the patient's body] is white, abounding in phlegm (balāsa), copious, and very cold;
the slender frame of his body is afflicted by cold and is exceedingly heavy and chilled.
When the dull-witted person produces a large amount of phlegm but only a small amount of stool, the sages call that "phlegmatic diarrhea" (śleṣmātisāra). // 86 //
The meaning of the state of being (bhāvārtha) is that which consists of all things, endowed with every particular defect,
whether it be interrupted, pure, like a grain of rice, or without a grain.
That which is foul-smelling, even when submerged in water, and consists of impure, undigested matter, they call *āmātisāra*; the opposite of that is called *pakvātisāra*.
The meaning of the verse is:
[he saw him] emitting excrement accompanied by flatulence and colic pain.
Accompanied by afflictions such as thirst and loss of appetite, abdominal disease destroys one whose voice has been weakened. (88)
The essential meaning is that for children, the very elderly, the emaciated, the weak, and those suffering from consumption,
one should avoid administering *kṛcchra* in cases of diarrhea.
One should administer ghee equal in quantity to the spleen, honey, muscle fat, and liver; or oil, water, milk, curd, and buttermilk, each equal in measure, while it is flowing out.
Having understood the entire management for undigested fever,
this [treatment] should be properly administered in cases of diarrhea accompanied by excessive thirst.
One should induce vomiting by drinking warm water mixed with a paste of Madana fruit, Saindhava salt, and Pippalī. // 90 //
The essential meaning is this:
on that day, he vomited what was peaceful, free from burning, and devoid of defects;
being exhausted, he abstained from food and drink for the duration of the day.
One should praise him who possesses little greatness, or bestow upon him what has been prescribed.
The essential meaning is:
in cases of diarrhea caused by excessive sourness, sugar-cane juice, wind, or disease,
one should drink [the decoction] in the morning enriched with black pepper, rock salt, and ginger.
Or else, one may take excellent *amlīkā* cooked with abundant asafoetida, or with black pepper, *ajamoda*, rock salt, and ginger. // 92 //
The essential meaning is:
either goat's milk boiled with a decoction of yaṣṭī,
or a decoction of jambu, ambu, āmra, kuṭaja, and ativiṣā.
Likewise, a paste of sesame seeds with curd-juice and yellow myrobalan quickly pacifies the disease of diarrhea caused by pitta and ama. (93)
The essential meaning is:
[a decoction] of dārvī, niśā, trikaṭu, ambuda, and citraka;
of pāṭhā, ajamoda, marica, āmalaka, and abhayā.
Likewise, one [dose] should be given in diarrhea caused by phlegm and associated with disease. // 94 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
mango stone, lodhra, madhuka, sesame, and that which is called padmaka; along with dhātakī flowers and śālmalī bark.
Bilva, priyaṅgu, kuṭaja, ativiṣā, and samaṅgā,
when drunk with curd-water, pacify chronic diarrhea.
The meaning of the essence is: [these substances] produced from trees, ground with water and abundant rice-grains.
Enclosed within a leaf-cup of the *raṃbhā* plant and burned, it is squeezed out and drips with fragrant red juice. // 96 //
Having drunk that cool [mixture] combined with a paste of Madhuka,
a person very quickly conquers abdominal disease.
Or, having boiled ambashthika, sarasa, pomegranate, and tinduka together with buttermilk, drinking it here immediately [yields the same result]. // 97 //
The meaning of the verse is:
having brought down the water that remains after one-eighth has been subtracted, one should dissolve it.
Having cooked *pāṇitaka* here with a spoonful of paste, a person will overcome diarrhea in no time by licking it. (98)
The essence of milk, quickly ripened with *trivṛt* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
when strongly seasoned with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), pacifies diseases of the abdomen.
Or else, it may be combined with ginger or with śatapuṣpā. // 99 //
The meaning of the essence is that which remains after the portions have been extracted, being distinguished and desired.
A person should quickly drink this together with *ambaṣṭhikā*;
it stops even the Ganges, let alone a minor case of diarrhea. (100)
The essential meaning is:

when one is afflicted by abdominal tumors (aṣṭhīlā), gravel-like stones (śarkarā), menorrhagia (asṛgdara), thirst, burning sensations in the body, vertigo, loss of semen, or fainting, this [medicine] should be drunk; how much more so when it is administered in combination with drugs appropriate to those conditions? (101)
The meaning of the passage is:
it should be thoroughly seasoned with a mixture of ghee, rock salt, and black pepper.
It is beneficial for people in cases of heavy meals, chronic diarrhea, and chronic fever. (102)
The essential meaning [is as follows]:
from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence;
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (103)
The essential meaning is this: that by which the entirety of living beings, non-living beings, and so forth— divided into their various categories— is explained according to rule,
has in this very moment attained a manifest transformation characterized by the nature of persistence, arising, and passing away.

Having bowed to that unconquered Lord of Jinas, who is worthy of salutation by the lords of gods and has attained the true miraculous powers, I shall set forth the complete therapeutic procedure for all diseases caused by phlegm. // 1 //
The essential symptoms are: unctuousness, moisture, discharge, loss of appetite, vomiting, heaviness of the head, and excessive sleep.
Weak digestion, indigestion, a salty taste in the mouth, numbness, and so forth.
Having fully understood the true nature of diseases caused by phlegm, one should administer the appropriate medicines. // 2 //
The therapeutic principle consists of alkaline substances, hot groups of drugs, very light and clear foods and drinks in small quantities,
along with soups of *kaula-stha* beans, mung beans, or the juices of extremely pungent peas and *āḍhakī*.

Through intense sweating, fasting, the consumption of sesame seeds, massage, and sexual intercourse, as well as by pungent, bitter, very dry, and astringent substances, the excess of phlegm (śleṣman) attains pacification. // 3 //

The meaning of the passage is as follows: [One should perform cleansing] with mouthfuls of water containing mustard seeds and the like, using salt, pungent, astringent, extremely bitter, or hot water;
and with tooth-sticks made of neem, karañja, and other such woods, mixed with the three pungents (trikaṭu) and salt.

By means of these applications— namely, oranges, various types of cane-juice, chickpeas mixed with pomegranates and sour substances, along with the three pungents (vyoṣa), rock salt, and so forth— a mortal attains the pacification of phlegm (kapha).
The meaning of the passage is as follows: bhārṅgī, hiṅgu, ugragandhā, marica, biḍa, yavakṣāra, sauvarcala,
elā, kuṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, pāṭhā, the fruit of kuṭaja, the seeds of mahānimba, and ajamodā.

Having powdered cavya, ajājī, śatāhvā, dahana, gaja-kaṇā, pippalī, granthi, and sindhu, and having repeatedly stirred it with the group of sour substances (amlavarga) and dried it, one should powder that [mixture] again. // 5 //
Phalasā, nimbu, jambīrī, dāḍima, and likewise karamarda—this is declared to be the group of sour substances (amlagaṇa), joined with vetasāmla. [From] the *Rasendrasārasaṃgraha*:
sour vetasa, jambīrī, nimbu, bijaurā nimbu, cane, khāra, nāraṅgī, tintiḍīka, and the fruit of imalī.
Lemon, hog plum, sorrel, sour pomegranate, and tamarind— these are called the group of acidic substances (amlavarga).
When drunk mixed with Sauvīra, it destroys liver disease, costiveness, abdominal tumors, and weak digestion;
it also cures cough, upward-moving breath (hiccup), pain, vomiting, diseases of the stomach and abdomen, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, and so forth.
This [application], combined with lukewarm water and oil, immediately and infallibly pacifies disorders born of Vāta.
The meaning of the verse: Having drunk a large quantity of lukewarm neem decoction mixed with the three pungents (trikaṭuka), one should induce vomiting;
then, equal parts of khadira, kuṭaja, pāṭhā, paṭola, and niśā [should be taken].
He who drinks daily this powder, enriched with the three acrids (vyoṣa) and mixed with hot water, pacifies leprosy, hemorrhoids, scabies, and all diseases born of phlegm (kapha). // 7 //
The meaning of the essence is as follows: either *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) combined with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, enriched with *saindhava* salt and taken in equal parts;
or else, the alkali obtained by straining the ashes of the scrotum (*muṣka*) through water, cooked until it becomes a reddish powder.

The powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) or *mārkaṇḍa* (Eclipta alba), taken repeatedly with cow’s urine and an equal amount of ghee, destroys all diseases of phlegm (*śleṣman*) without exception and immeasurable ailments of excessive urination (*bahumūtra*). // 8 //
The essential formulation consists of asafoetida, long pepper, cumin, chaba pepper, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), yava-kshara, and sauvarchala salt;
or else, musta, the three pungents, ajamoda, amalakī, salt, pāṭhā, abhayā, and citraka.
Śigru, granthi, akṣa, pathyā, marica, magadhaja, nāgara, elā, and viḍaṅga—these, ground into a powder and drunk with warm water or combined with ghee, destroy kapha. (9)
The meaning of the passage is: *narkālarka*, *ugragandhā*, the three pungent spices (*trikaṭuka*), turmeric (*rajanī*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), *uṣṇīkā*, and *karañja*.
One should utterly uproot them, just as an immeasurable forest fire consumes vast expanses of water.
The essential meaning is:
or by means of *cakramarda*, *āmalaka*, salt, excellent *bākucī*, and *bhūśirīṣa* seeds.
When used as an ointment, it destroys all types of skin diseases, including ringworm and scabies, without exception. // 11 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows: [A plaster] made from *dhātrī*, *akṣa*, *hāridrā*, and *abhayā*, along with *trikaṭu*, *rajanī*, *cakramarda*,
*adrikarṇī*, *nimba*, *vyāghātaka*, *agnidruma*, and the group of salts, ground with *kāñjika* and buttermilk.
It instantly pacifies severe scabies and all diseases of phlegm without exception. // 12 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

or, by means of smoke from the paste of *granthi*, *hiṅgu*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *kunaṭī*, *bhavya*, *bhārṅgī*, and *niśā*; or by means of [smoke] applied from within the stalks of large castor plants (*eraṇḍa*) wrapped in fine cloth and smeared with that same paste.

Through gargles, mouthfuls, sprinklings, and plasters made with *siddhārtha* (white mustard), *sarṣapa* (mustard), black pepper, *magadha* (long pepper), *nāgara* (ginger), and the roots of *śigru*, the excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*) comes to pacification.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
Elā, tvak, nāgapuṣpa, uśīra, māgadha, and nāgara,
taken in increasing proportions and reduced to powder, when combined with an equal amount of sugar, is an excellent and desired remedy that destroys kapha.
It destroys knots, dyspnea, vomiting, fever, abdominal ailments, severe cough, and heart disease. // 14 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
one part of strong *satpippalī* bark, with a large amount of inner bark, measuring five parts in total.

Having made a powder and prepared boluses (*modaka*) with jaggery and *āmalaka*, by eating them one destroys cough, upward breath (*ūrdhvaśvāsa*), hiccup, fever, vomiting, intoxication, and diseases of phlegm (*śleṣman*). // 15 //
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:
[one should prepare a mixture] with the fruits of śārṅgeṣṭā, naktamāla (the two types), and khadira;
with the horns of a goat and a sheep; and with pippalī, elā, the two types of haridrā, kuṭaja, vacā, kuṣṭha, mustā, and viḍaṅga.
By means of those [decoctions] enriched with *arbuda*, *nimba*, and *āragvadha*, one obtains the pacification of *kapha* in all its forms. // 16 //
The essential meaning is: whatever is bitter, whatever is dry, and also whatever is pungent, whatever is astringent and parched;
whatever is alkaline, whatever is sharp, and also whatever is clear and light substance that is hot.
Having thoroughly tasted all those various qualities of taste that subdue *kapha*, one should apply them in foods for the benefit of patients, after understanding this sequence of the *doṣas*. (17)

*tugām api bahulām* is an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*). According to this, one should take *vaṃśalocana* (bamboo manna) in place of cinnamon (*dālacīnī*). However, the word *tugā* denotes *vaṃśalocana*; it is not *tuga*.
No other medicinal substance is understood by the word *tuga*. Furthermore, *vaṃśalocana* is included in the *Tālīsādi-cūrṇa*.
It is astringent and it also destroys phlegm (kapha); therefore, one may take this. The intended meaning is:
the trees known as khyāta, arka, alarka, tarkāri, amarataru, mayūra, ṭuṭūka, and vṛkṣa.
Mūrvā, Koraṇṭa, Pīlu, Snuhī, Tilaka, Tilvaka, those called Keṃbuka, Varṣābhū, and Pāṭalī bring about the pacification of diseases caused by the wind (vāta). // 18 //
The essential meaning is this: whatever substance is sharp, unctuous, hot, salty, excessively heavy, or combined with extreme acidity;
whatever is properly slimy; and whatever possesses the inherent natures of the various categories such as sweet, pungent, bitter, and so forth.

Having understood the properties of the tastes that are said to pacify various types of vāta, one should employ them for the sake of the patient's health in drinks, massages, poultices, emesis, affusions, and immersions. (19)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: [one should prepare a paste] with bimbī, nimba, indrapuṣpī, madhuka, sahasa, viśvā, and the rest of the devīs;
vidārī, kākolī, vṛścikālī, añjana, madhukapuṣpa, uśīra, and the essence of mango.
Through *nyagrodha* and *aśvattha* trees, and through white and blue water lilies, the bile returns to tranquility. // 20 //

The essential meaning is this: whatever is unctuous, whatever is cold, whatever is sweet, astringent, or very bitter; whatever is directly slimy, whatever is exceedingly soft, and whatever is said to be a heavy substance.

Having thoroughly tasted all those substances which have been described as pacifiers of pitta according to the rules for the qualities of tastes, they should be employed in food, massage, external applications, abundant affusions, and nasal therapy.
The meaning of the verse is as follows: cinnamon bark, cloth (musk), long pepper, sweet fragrant root, and extremely white sugar—
each subsequent substance possessing twice the quality of the preceding one— all of these should be powdered together in that numerical order.
[It cures] thirst, dyspnea, vomiting, hiccup, fever, intoxication, cough, anorexia, and excessive burning sensations. // 22 //

Thus, the entire nature of the arrangement of the three defects has been stated; having understood the subject matter through these few verses as they have been explained, one may comprehend the immeasurable diseases.
By means of the application of medicines that are suitable for those [humors], according to the logic of their predominance and combination. // 23 //
In common practice, this is called by the name *sītopalādi-cūrṇa*.
The essential meaning is: other [formulations] not mentioned here, which possess even greater qualities and are marvelous, exist though they are not included in this small treatise.
Even one who possesses the single eye of grasping-cognition and is all-knowing is utterly deluded; how much more so, then, someone like me? 24.
The essential meaning is this:
having examined the defects through the reasoning of the specific qualities and faults [of medicines], one should apply even excellent medicines to those characterized by great maladies.
The essential meaning is this:

by all these excellent medicines—whether used in full, in half-doses, or according to availability—and through appropriate, antagonistic applications that are peerless and unfailing, diseases are pacified. (26)
The essential meaning is that one should eliminate pervasive diseases through various therapeutic procedures.
Having drunk [the medicine], the physician should avoid those things that ought to be avoided. // 27 //
The essential meaning [is extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of all extensive categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (28)
The essential meaning is the Lord of all fortunes, the Supreme Sovereign Jina, who proclaims the systems of valid cognition, the categories of designation, and the philosophical perspectives.
Having prostrated together with Lakṣmaṇa, who is free from all ailments, he shall proclaim the Siddha system of medicine in its proper sequence. // 1 //
In reality, there is no occurrence of any modification whatsoever here without all the causes of defects.
Nevertheless, I shall describe all diseases, examined according to their names, forms, and characteristics, along with their treatments. // 2 //
The meaning of the [preceding] section is thus;
hereafter, I shall describe the groups of minor diseases along with their treatments for head diseases and poisons. (3)

The meaning of the term *bhāva* is "great illusion" (*mahāmāyā*), which surpasses all other maladies, such as urinary disorders (*prameha*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), abdominal enlargements (*udara*), and diseases born of vitiated wind (*duṣṭavāta*).
Those who know all things declare that it [the *mūḍhagarbha*] includes hemorrhoids, sprouts of growth, urinary stones, and fistula-in-ano. (4)

I shall explain the essential meaning of all the great ailments according to their sequence, characteristics, and treatments; including the primary causes for the occurrence of diseases that are incurable or curable, and the methods for warding them off through proper care and other means. (5)
The essential meaning is: [the condition arises] from eating heavy, liquid, unctuous, cold, or excessive food, and from being sluggish due to excessive daytime sleep and exhaustion.
One should quickly diagnose that a man will indeed suffer from prameha by means of its specific characteristics. // 6 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
thirst is caused by the injury to one's own hands, feet, and limbs; and due to the excessive oiliness of the body, it becomes very slippery.
Excessive sweetness of the mouth and overeating here are the premonitory signs of prameha. (7)
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
Now, when the phlegm, bile, and wind have become active and, having reached the bladder along with the fat, undergo suppuration;
The essential meaning is this: all those very things are considered difficult to conquer by oneself, like actors who possess the nature of manifold sentiments. // 9 //
The essential meaning is this:
when much water flows from the premonitory symptoms, one should diagnose the man as suffering from prameha (urinary disorder).
One who has *prameha* characterized by *pramīḍha* is called a *prameddavat*; such a person suffering from *madhuprameha* is accompanied by eruptions (*piṭakā*).
The essential meaning [of the diseases] consists of śarāvikā, sarṣapikā, sajālinī, saputriṇī, kacchapikā, and masūrikā.
Vidārikā, Vidradhikā, and Kālajī are considered [to be varieties]; these ten types of pustules (piṭakā) occur in those suffering from urinary disorders (pramehin).
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
[the tongue] is even-colored, moist, accompanied by excessive sensation, and possesses lips that are sunken in the middle and elevated at the edges.
That which has the shape of a shallow bowl and possesses excellent proportions is designated as *śarāvikā* by the wise. // 12 //
Its essential nature is that it ripens quickly, is extensive, accompanied by pain, and is equal in size to a mustard seed.
That [mixture] is said by experts to be of two kinds: the *sasūkṣmikā*, which has very little density, and the *sarṣapikā*. // 13 //
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is as follows:
it is covered by a network of a mass of equal-sized channels (*nāḍī*), possesses great cavities, and is accompanied by excessive pain and piercing sensations.
Furthermore, it is described as being very smooth, exuding moisture, possessing subtle pores, rigid, and even webbed.

Its essential meaning is as follows: accompanied by very small pustules, it is called Mahatī; it is associated with daughters, is large, deeply rooted, and joined with excessive, dense pain; it resembles the back of a tortoise and causes intense piercing pain. // 15 //

That which is always characterized by very soft qualities and extreme distress is called *kacchapikā* by the wise; that which has the excellent size and shape of a lentil (*masūra*) and is slightly painful is termed *masūrikā*. (16)
The meaning of the term is as follows:

*vidārikā* refers to a hard, round mass; it is accompanied by piercing pain (*vedanā*). This abscess (*vidradhi*) is classified as fivefold, having been previously produced by all the *doṣas* acting together. (17)
I have described the two types of *savarṇaka*, which causes rapid suppuration and is accompanied by abscesses;
it rises up intensely, burns the skin, and is covered with eruptions that are very blackish or deep red. (18)
It causes thirst, delusion, and intense burning pain; it is accompanied by fever, is extremely distressing, and is characterized by the absence of suppuration (alajī).
It is located in any one of the well-known sites such as the back or the abdomen, and being large in size, it is accompanied by piercing pain. (19)
Accompanied by intense pain and discharge, and marked by a bluish tint—this Vinatā, thus described, is distinguished.
The essential meaning is that [the diseases] beginning with *śarāvikā* have well-known names corresponding to their meanings, and *savidradhi* is also accompanied by an abscess (*vidradhi*).
The essential meaning is that in cases of Kapha-type urinary disorders (kaphaprameha), complications such as the crawling of flies and the sliminess of the mouth occur. // 22 //
Sour substances cause inflammation, discharge from the urethra, pain in the bladder, burning sensations, difficulty in urination, colic, thirst, and an acid taste in the mouth.
Fever, excessive fainting, intoxication, and jaundice are the complications that arise in cases of urinary disorders associated with pitta. // 23 //

In cases of urinary disorders associated with Vāta, the following complications arise: retention of the heart and the abdomen, restlessness along with insomnia, severe tremors, colic, constipation, excessive coughing, hiccup, labored breathing, and emaciation of the body. // 24 //
The essential meaning is that those which flow like fat, ghee, and honey, like a stream of water from an elephant blinded by rut and intoxicated by its own scent; [these are the secretions].
Those who constantly emit turbid urine and are afflicted by the aforementioned complications; // 25 //
They are afflicted with carbuncles arising from their vital points (marmas) located in the anus, shoulders, heart, back, head, neck, and abdomen.
Those who drink while dreaming, and those who swim in the waters of rivers, oceans, and the like; // 26 //
Men with shattered limbs who suffer from urinary disorders die soon; one should not treat them. // 27 //
The essential meaning is this:
by virtue of the predominance of that [knowledge], a physician who knows everything should perform the treatment for all those suffering from prameha. // 28 //
There are two types of patients suffering from prameha: the emaciated (*kṛśa*) and the obese (*sthūla*), who [become so] either due to their own birth or due to the consumption of unwholesome food.
For those two, one should perform treatment for the emaciated by means of increasing nourishment, and for the other by means of reducing it. // 29 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

one suffering from urinary disorders (prameha) should avoid liquor, fermented spirits, *ariṣṭa*, milk, ghee, and sour gruel; one should also abstain from eating abundant food, sweets, curd, and sugarcane products. Furthermore, such a person should even avoid meat and should be intent on a diet that promotes dryness (*virūkṣaṇa*). // 30 //
The essential meaning is this:
immediately after the purgation, one should treat that person with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) using the appropriate medicinal drugs for nirūha.
The essential meaning [of the rite] is through meals consisting of the flours of *priyaṅgu*, *koddālaka*, and *śāli* rice, along with *kaṅgu*, wheat, and barley.
This is the essential meaning.
Having ground the *niśā* (turmeric) and mixed it with *āmalaka* water, one should pour it into a consecrated jar and seal it.
When consumed gradually according to one's strength, it deposited in a granary well destroys urinary disorders. (34)
The meaning of the process:
having carefully boiled *niśā*, *samustā*, *triphalā*, and *surendhana* here to produce a decoction—
this is the meaning of the process.

One should have those suffering from urinary disorders born of pitta drink a decoction made from the *sacada*, *naṭa*, *indrāśana*, and *tinduka* trees, along with clusters of milk-exuding trees and the three myrobalans (*phalatraya*), mixed with a thick paste (*ghanakalka*). // 36 //
The meaning of the verse:

One who has conquered the senses should drink a decoction prepared from *kapittha*, *bilva*, *asanadha-vani*, *niśā*, *harītakī*, *kṣāmalaka*, and the bark of the *arjuna* tree; this will conquer all types of urinary disorders (*prameha*) along with their complications. // 37 //
The meaning of the term *bhāvārtha* is as follows:
*bhāvārtha* refers to ghee boiled with a decoction of the three fruits (*phalatrika*) and *śilājatu*; by drinking this, one completely eradicates all types of urinary disorders (*meha*).
One shall conquer all types of prameha, along with their well-known complications and accompanied by carbuncles (piṭaka). // 39 //
A person who desires to eliminate all diseases should always be intent on the practice of *bhāvārtha* (the essential meaning).
This is the *bhāvārtha*.
One should speak kindly to a man of noble birth who is distressed, destitute, or afflicted with urinary disorders, even if he has transgressed against you.
Having wandered constantly through villages, cow-pens, mines, and ports, go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
The essential meaning is that one should dig wells, tanks, and ponds, as well as cultivate the earth, and always protect it;
this is the essential meaning.

As stated, for a person who lacks the proper application of the prescribed path, medicines, and other treatments, various types of boils—specifically those described as occurring in the lower part of the body—become difficult to bear in a patient suffering from urinary disorders (pramehin). (43)
The essential meaning is that a patient suffering from madhu-prameha should indeed employ very sharp purgatives, for such a person is difficult to purge.
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:
one should take good mustard seeds combined with radish seeds, along with rock salt, uṣṇīṣa, and madhuśigru.
All medicines that are pungent, trikaṭu, and hot are digestive and dissolve the āma humor. // 45 //
By the power of which [the mind] overcomes specific medical treatments such as squeezing, applying ointments, and bandaging.
When the pustules have ripened on their own, the excellent physician should incise them and overcome the condition with purificatory and healing treatments. 46.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
*karañja*, *kāñjīra*, *niśā*, *sārivā*, along with *nimba*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and *iṅgudī*.
Sarā, rājīvṛkṣa, indrayava, indravāruṇī, paṭola, and jātī are beneficial for purifying wounds. // 47 //
The essential meaning:

Sesame seeds with *lodhra*, the bark of *madhuka* and *arjuna*, the tender leaves produced by *palāśa* and milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*), as well as *kadaṃba*, *jambu*, mango, *kapittha*, and *tiṃduka*—these, along with *samaṅgā*, are beneficial for the healing of wounds. (48)

A medicinal wick (varti) prepared with the milky juices extracted from the *vajravṛkṣa*, *arka*, and *kuraṇṭaka* plants, combined with *karañja*, *lāṅgalī*, *saindhava* salt, *aṅkola*, and *śilājatu*, destroys malignant ulcers and sinus tracts. (49)
Having purified the essential meaning [of the wound], one should immediately fill the opening of the ulcer with clarified butter or with a healing paste.
Alternatively, it is desired for the purpose of subduing the heat of the wound with well-ground yaṣṭīmadhuka added [to the mixture]. // 50 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

after applying the medicinal paste, the physician should carefully wrap the wound with a very fine cloth. He should always treat it while keeping it bound, taking into account his own physical condition, the nature of the wound on the body, and the time of day. (51)
The essential meaning:
then, on the second day, having performed the release from the bandage and having removed the pus by means of compressions;
this is the essential meaning.

Through bandaging, it becomes purified; the wound heals, attains softness, and becomes free from pain. Therefore, constant bandaging alone is beneficial for all wounds; this indeed is the correct method. // 53 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

the preparation of decoctions, pastes, clarified butter, sesame oil, and so forth, using the aforementioned groups of wholesome medicinal substances, is prescribed by one who knows the means and the goal, according to the specific nature of the most extraordinary disorders. (54)
The meaning of the internal state is stable, intent on non-outflow, free from sensation, endowed with the color of a dove at its extremity, and exceedingly fleshy.
When a wound has healed, it possesses the characteristic of extreme purity; having become fully grown, it becomes equal in color [to the surrounding skin]. // 55 //
The essential meaning is this:
when a patient suffering from prameha passes urine that is clear, extremely bitter, parched, alkaline, and pungent-hot;
If at times he voids only a small amount that is not turbid, then it would possess the characteristics of being free from meha.

The essential meaning is as follows: having thus recognized this ulcer, the physician should cleanse it thoroughly with purifying agents, and then heal it with medicinal pastes and decoctions combined with healing remedies.
Therefore, this very injunction is prescribed here with care regarding all things composed of the elements. // 57 //
The essential meaning is that leprosy (kuṣṭha), generally characterized by signs produced by all the vitiated humors (doṣas) combined,
consists of eighteen types according to the various combinations of the primary and secondary qualities of those humors.
And others as well.

I shall explain these in brief here, according to the characteristics of the diseases, their remedies and so forth, along with the sequences for complications, and matured by the investigation into what is curable and incurable. (58)
The essential meaning is as follows:

due to improper conduct or unwholesome causes, the vitiated wind (vāyu), having seized the provoked bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha), casts them wherever it directs; there, according to the specific differentiation of the aggravated humors, it produces the most agonizing leprosy (kuṣṭha). // 59 //
The essential meaning is that when leprosy is about to arise, symptoms such as harshness and trembling first appear. (60)
"Consisting of three [humors]" is an alternative reading.
The meaning of the term is as follows:
that which arises from wind is called *kṛṣṭha* (scraped) here, known by the name *aruṇa* (red), characterized by eruptions (*visphoṭana*) that are reddish in color and accompanied by pricking pain.
The meaning of the verse is:
[this disease] arises from the provocation of phlegm (*śleṣman*); it is characterized by ringworm, *sapuṇḍarīka*, itching, excessive whiteness, abundance, and long duration.
Due to the excessive entry into the bodily constituents (dhātu), seven great types of leprosy (kuṣṭha) are said to be incurable in this world. // 62 //
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is as follows:
*kṣudra*, *aruṣka*, *kuṣṭha*, and also *sidhma*; these, along with blood associated with phlegm (*śleṣman*), constitute the thousand [types of skin diseases].
Sidhma occurs on skin that has been previously marked by a rash, is characterized by a strange itching, is white, thin-skinned, and rough.
The meaning of the verse:
There are pustules on the body that exude [fluid]. They perish daily and then arise again.
Accompanied by itching, minute, of many varieties, and oily, they are seen to be caused by an excess of phlegm (kapha). // 64 //
The essential meaning is that one [type of] swelling arises from wind, another from bile, and the remaining one here is caused by the three humors combined;
this is the essential meaning.
The entire body becomes a dense black color,
or it becomes reddish in luster and accompanied by pricking pain.
A constant eruption on the palms of the hands is called vicarcikā; when it occurs on both feet, it is known as vipādikā.
The essential meaning is:
from pitta arise pustules accompanied by burning, which are extremely intense, characterized by discharge, and mixed with blood; these they call parisarpa. This is the essential meaning.
Those who are very learned say that *kiṭibha* is a circular patch that exudes a discharge, is very glossy, and is extremely black;
they describe it as having a strong layer of skin on the palms of the hands, accompanied by heat, dryness, and a pricking pain. (68)
The pustules arising on the pair of feet are those caused by the *piṭika* [demon].
It arises on the hands and the buttocks; that which is abundant is taught by the experts of the scriptures as *kacchū*.

The essential meaning is this: indeed, even that which is called "other" here is leprosy (*kuṣṭha*); moreover, the nature of leprosy is superior [to other diseases] insofar as it is produced by the three humors (*doṣa*).
The essential meaning is as follows:
from Vāta arise emaciation, wasting, and hoarseness of voice; during sleep, there occur great disorders such as leprosy (kuṣṭha);
and there is injury to the eyebrows, ears, and nose, as well as redness of the eyes. From Pitta, there is the falling off of the toes and feet, as well as ulceration. // 71 //
The essential meaning is that these symptoms occur here in leprosy (kuṣṭha): when it resides in the skin, there is a discoloration of the natural complexion and a state of roughness. (72)
The essential meaning is that when [the disease] named "all forms of leprosy" has resorted to the blood, there is perspiration, sleepiness, deformity, and swelling.
In cases of severe leprosy (kuṣṭha), there are clusters of blisters accompanied by discharge that are not intensely painful, yet they are extremely powerful at the joints.
The essential meaning is this:
leprosy (kuṣṭha) located in the fat, vessels, and ligaments indeed makes even the state of a malignant ulcer more grievous. // 74 //
The essential meaning is that there are powerful disorders such as acute eye diseases, the occurrence of worms, tearing and other ailments, as well as impairment of the nose and the voice.
When a terrible leprosy has reached the marrow and bones, those previously mentioned symptoms subsequently appear. // 75 //
The essential meaning is this:

leprosy (kuṣṭha) that has reached only the skin, blood, and flesh is curable, provided the prescribed medicinal regimen is followed. That which has reached the fat is considered palliable; beyond that, it is declared the worst type of leprosy and must be avoided. // 76 //
The meaning of the essential nature is as follows: that which resembles a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), like the *bandhūka* flower, and has the luster of gold.
One should avoid from its very birth a *kākaṇaka* that resembles a reflection and is accompanied by bile, even if it has arisen [as a natural mark]. // 77 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
one should avoid all flour-based foods, thick sour fruits, meat, salt, and food or drink that causes corpulence. (79)
The meaning of the term *bhāvārtha* is as follows: food consisting of pulses such as mung beans and *āḍhakī*, prepared with broth, or dry foods such as *śyāmāka*, *kaṅgu*, and *varaka*.
The meaning of the underlying intent:
regarding those dependent on passion, the previously mentioned [remedies] apply— namely, the removal of passion and the cultivation of the astringent [antidote].
Having first performed the rites for one situated in the flesh, he subsequently accomplishes the great application of various medicinal formulations. // 83 //
The essential meaning is this:

leprosy (kuṣṭha) that has reached the fat (medas) is extremely difficult to treat in this world; it may become manageable through the application of abundant medicinal measures, but otherwise, it must be abandoned by physicians, as it proceeds even after undergoing the five purificatory therapies (pañcakarma). (84)
The essential meaning is that,
having drunk either matured ghee or well-refined oil, the patient must perform the purification of the body.
Having understood the essential meaning and performed venesection in this case, one should administer these formulations which remove all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha):
dantī, dravantī, trivṛt, haridrā, kuṣṭha, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī, and pāṭhā. // 86 //
All these, having been dried, weighed accurately on a scale, and ground into a powder, should be thoroughly saturated with a decoction of nimba, āragvadha, and dhāvanī. // 88 //
Furthermore, even with the juice of *brāhmī*, [the pills] should be prepared repeatedly until they reach the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*).
Beginning from that point until it reaches the size of an eye, one should then eat it according to the well-established measure of the eye. // 89 //
It cures skin diseases, urinary disorders, all types of abdominal enlargements, hemorrhoids, worms, fistula-in-ano, and malignant sinus tracts.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
the essence of neem wood, along with powdered viḍaṅga, combined with the seeds of bhallātaka and the two types of haridrā (turmeric).
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
for here the mandalas are exceedingly high; having rubbed them with weapons and with a sharp whetstone provided with foam.
The essential meaning is this:
it should be properly strained here as well, having been boiled again in the ashes of *pālāśa* wood mixed with water.
The meaning of the state,
the meaning of the state, the meaning of the state.
The aforementioned great plasters are also to be applied for vitiligo (śvitra), as is the treatment frequently mentioned by many authorities. The essential meaning is as follows:
the kernel of the bhallātaka fruit, agni, bilva pulp, *bhṛṅga*, *arka* latex, yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
Likewise, having burnt either a leopard skin or an elephant hide and reduced it to powder, a plaster mixed with sesame oil [is applied]. // 97 //
The medicinal application consists of *kāñjīra*, *dhāmārgava*, and bitter *tumbī*, along with the burnt seeds of *nimba*, mixed with oil. (98)
The meaning of the verse is:
even when a fault remains, [remedies] may be applied again; therefore, a person should be intent on providing a counter-measure for leprosy and other such ailments. // 99 //
The essential meaning is that, from the perspective of the [two] sides, one should vomit from the side alone; for those afflicted by leprosy, a superior purgation should be administered once a month.
And for those [patients], one should administer blood-letting once a month, or even every six days.
The meaning of the state,
the meaning of the state, the meaning of the state.
Or wheat, rice, barley, or other grains—once crushed, stripped of their husks, thoroughly cleaned, and dried.
Furthermore, they should be repeatedly sprinkled with cow's urine and fried in fresh, clean vessels that have been deemed worthy.
One should take bhallātaka, āvalī, mārkava, arka, mustā, and viḍaṅga, adding a fourth part of powdered kṛtavedhana.
Reduced to powder in the measure of a single *akṣa*, they were mixed together as a paste of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances. // 104 //
One should drink together with water the [powder] of *sāla*, *ajakarṇa*, *arjuna*, and *śiṃśapā*, along with parched grain flour (*sakthu*). 105.
The meaning of the verse:

Having prepared those very barley-grains according to the described procedure and mixed them with the powder of the three aromatics (trijātaka) and great medicinal herbs, one who is entirely free from dullness and hesitation should drink those various decoctions of heartwood-tree barks along with rock salt. 107.
The essential meaning is:
with those very same heaps of roasted flour, he prepared various foods such as cakes and full vessels; this is the essential meaning.
In this manner, for each [ingredient], there should be a powder the size of a *kuḍava*, with half that amount consisting of the extremely fine dust of *amalaka*. (109)
Having firmly tied it externally with a thread around the thighs, one should then throw into it the powder of the aforementioned medicinal herbs. (111)
Having placed half a *tulā* of jaggery into that [vessel], it should be mixed with eight *kuḍava*s of heartwood-water.
Having properly covered the mouth of this jar, one should place it in a large pit filled with an abundance of grain and barley.
In this way, one should apply all the applications of nectar together, exactly according to the path that has been described.
This entire ritual procedure has been declared; it should be performed with a jar containing all medicinal herbs.

Having extracted it, after seven days, a fortnight, or a month, one should consume it—possessing abundant fragrance and flavor, along with its potency—in accordance with the strength of one's digestive fire; this is the cause for the destruction of leprosy, urinary disorders, and abdominal enlargements. // 114 //
The essential meaning is as follows: the ashes of *āragvadha*, *aruṣkara*, *muṣkaka*, and *nimba*; and the auspicious ash of the blossoms of *raṃbhā*, *arkatāla*, and sesame.
Droṇa [of the substance] cooked with four droṇas of water yields a red juice when wrapped in a clean cloth. (115)
Into this, one should throw one āḍhaka measure of pure jaggery, along with trikaṭu, triphalā, and viḍaṅga.
The powder is heavily saturated with a great abundance of cloves and *balā*.
Having placed it in a jar according to the many methods described, it remains in the grain for a period of one month.
Desiring in his mind to destroy them briefly, he should consume those kings of inexhaustible diseases. (117)
The essential meaning is as follows:
it is the essence-powder even of the most excellent trees, dried after being infused with the natural juices of those same excellent trees.
When the essence-medicine is drunk together with a decoction of heartwood, it becomes an essence-remedy that destroys great diseases.
The meaning of the procedure is as follows:
having burnt [the substance] with a *puṭa* in a fire of good cow-dung, one should extinguish it with the juice of the three fruits (*triphalā*) of the *sāra* tree. (119)
In this manner, having again burned it as before and extinguished it likewise, one should do so here for exactly sixteen times.
Afterwards, once it has been burnt with khadira wood and extinguished, one should grind it into powder and place it here upon a cloth. // 120 //
That powder, mixed with clarified butter and blood from a rabbit, should be consumed constantly, taking into account one's own physical strength.
Having destroyed leprosy, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, and anemia, it brings about youthfulness, strength, physical well-being, and happiness. // 121 //
The essential meaning is this:
when one has digested this great iron-based medicine, one should consume food that is free from salt and sourness, according to the requirements of the disease.
Having consumed this [medicine] equal in weight to the body, and having employed it here, one shall live for a hundred years endowed with a healthy body. // 122 //
The essential meaning is this:
that powder, mixed with sugar and clarified butter, when consumed, quickly pacifies even excessive disorders. (123)
The essential meaning is as follows:
having prepared and employed, according to the prescribed method, this renowned medicinal compound known as "nine metals" (navāyasa) in its various forms;
Ghee extracted from sesame seeds, cooked with the paste and decoction of the various medicinal herbs that destroy leprosy, constantly destroys [the disease].
The essential meaning is this:
even one whose body has been consecrated with anointment, if afflicted by severe leprosy, may drink a single decoction of the heartwood of the khadira tree with his whole being.
With his body made perfectly pure by short nails and fine hair, he immediately becomes happy, with the great pain of his illness stilled.
The essential meaning is this:
through unwholesome food and improper conduct, the vitiated vāyu corrupts the nutritional essences (annarasa) of the body.
It causes piercing pain, flatulence, various pricking sensations, a greatly distended abdomen, and dark veins. // 128 //
The meaning of the state is always characterized by being withered by the fever of craving, accompanied by parched urine and the spreading of the vessels.
It makes bile manifest as a large, rapidly spreading mass, corrupted by its own specific causes. (129)
Its essential meaning is:
heavy, stable, very unctuous, well-cooled, large, white, and bound by white veins.
Corrupted by itself, phlegm (kapha) produces a gradually enlarging abdomen accompanied by swelling. // 130 //
The meaning of the state is this very thing;
it constantly undergoes a particular transformation during the thick clouds and dark storms of delusion.
Following that, he faints from thirst; his body, overwhelmed by burning heat, is consumed by flames. (132)
The meaning of the verse is: when there is excessive enlargement of the liver and spleen, it is *mahodara* (ascites) with swelling on the right and left sides. // 133 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Because it is obstructed by hair, stones, and grass, and because the filth within the intestines has accumulated excessively, it produces a large abdomen known as *baddhaguda*, which is filled with the stench of impurities and the like. (134)

The essential meaning is that food eaten unknowingly while containing a foreign body (śalya) causes a perforation of the intestines; consequently, due to the flow of abundant secretions, a large abdominal swelling arises characterized by discharge, known by its own name [mahodara]. // 135 //
One who drinks an excessive amount of cold water [with such intent] produces ascites (jalodara) according to its true etymology. // 136 //
The meaning of the verse: That vast expanse, which is imagined as being filled with abundant water, trembles and is agitated;
it wastes away and becomes bewildered here, its state one of thirst and aversion toward food. (137)
The essential meaning is that there is always the fainting caused by the ego, the filling of the stomach, the fire [of digestion], and the excessive obstruction of wind and feces.
Swelling, emaciation, and bodily afflictions—all these occur in cases of abdominal enlargement (mahodara). // 138 //
The meaning of this is:
one should avoid those [fetuses] that are attached to that [organ], as well as those whose bellies are bound together or distended by fluids. 139.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
furthermore, those remaining types of *mahodara* (abdominal enlargements) are difficult to cure.
The physician, having approached, constantly performs the appropriate medical treatment there. // 140 //
The meaning of the term is that even half of that [distance] among those with eight great bellies is to be accomplished by means of excellent medicines; then the other half is likewise.
All treatments involving weapons arise from the influence of time; likewise, the applications of weapons and medicines [arise] from the same source. // 141 //
The meaning of the passage is:
[one who is] afflicted by loss of appetite and broken ribs, with limbs tormented by diseases of the abdomen accompanied by swelling.
Even one who has been purged should be quickly replenished with nourishment; however, one suffering from abdominal disease should be avoided [for such treatment]. 142.
The meaning of the verse is: having drunk here ghee with the decoction and paste of *biḍa*, *ugragandhā*, and the bark of *madhuśigru*.
One should administer a purgative using tilvaka and kṛṣīpa, and one should also give him a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) with cow's urine.
The meaning of the verse is as follows: A large pot smeared with oil should be heated quickly by means of wind, using milk, curd, and boiled [substances].
In the case of Mahodara caused by Vāta, fomentation should always and repeatedly be performed.
With great medicinal herbs, rock salt, and roots of the śigru plant, as well as meals consisting of well-prepared milk and other such items. // 145 //
The meaning of the verse: Having caused him to drink ghee, one should purge him as desired with *trivṛt* mixed with an equal amount of sugar. (146)
The essential meaning is:
one should treat a patient suffering from abdominal enlargement caused by pitta with non-unctuous enemas (nirūhaṇa) prepared with appropriate medicinal drugs. // 147 //
The meaning of the verse: Prepare a vessel with a very clean interior, smeared with ghee and fitted with a lid, and fill it with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Let meals consisting mostly of lukewarm milk, along with bitter vegetables, be prescribed for him. (148)
The essential meaning:

[One should prepare a decoction] with cow urine, cow milk, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), and so forth, along with groups of drugs such as the three fruits (phalatraya) and those containing bitter substances (satikta).
The essential meaning is that fresh ginger always produces beauty when combined with the juice of ripe milk and floating rice.

The essential meaning is as follows: for the great abdominal swelling caused by the aforementioned poisonous venom, one should proceed by means of the specific medicinal path that treats the three *doṣas*.
The meaning of the passage is as follows: [one should prepare a decoction] with the waters of *nidigdhikā*, *nimba*, *karañja*, *pāṭalī*, *palāśa*, *nīlī*, and the tree *kuṭaja*.
One suffering from poison-induced abdominal disease (viṣodara) should cook ghee with viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, and snuhi, mixed with milk, and then drink it.
The essential meaning is:
[one should take] rock salt mixed with powdered ginger, or indeed oil produced from various seeds.
One should lick [the medicine] which is the cause for destroying all abdominal ailments, or one may even drink it thinned with warm cow’s milk.
Likewise, for abdominal enlargement (mahodara), one should prepare [a medicine] with the juice of bhārgī and the juices of punarnavā. (155)
