The essential meaning is as follows: one should cook separately one *prastha* each of the juices known as *bhṛṅgarāja*, *rājā*, and *āmalaka*, along with oil, four *prasthas* of milk, and one *pala* of *yaṣṭikā*. This nasal medication (*nasya*), when prepared, conquers many diseases. (113)

Oil cooked with the decoction and paste of *sahā*, *ari*, *medā*, *āmalaka*, *abhayā*, *asanā*, turmeric (*rajanī*), and the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), along with milk, thoroughly overcomes diseases when administered as nasal drops (*nasya*) or mouth gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*). (114)

One who drinks, along with cow's urine, the medicinal substances *surendrakāṣṭha*, *kuṭaja*, *pāṭhā*, *rohiṇī*, *ativiṣā*, and *dantikā*, each measured in portions of one *dharaṇa*, shall conquer various diseases of the mouth caused by *śleṣman* (phlegm). (115)
What is the essential meaning? It is said to be the medicine for the disease residing in the mouth; one should constantly employ that which destroys phlegm and wind.

The essential meaning is that [the patient] should be treated with soups made from various vegetables, along with ghee and salt, or with medicinal preparations containing pungent herbs mixed with soups.
Thus,
with effort, the sixty-six types of mouth diseases have been described here according to their own enumeration.
Among those [afflictions of the lips], three—those arising from the three doṣas, from flesh, and from blood—are to be excluded as they reside in the lip itself. // 118 //

The essential meaning is that even in the roots of one's own teeth, two other conditions— characterized by the symptoms of the three *doṣas* and consisting of displacement and cavitation— should be avoided.
Likewise, others there have teeth produced from the *ālana*, *śyāmala*, and *bhañjana* trees; such are the twice-born. (119)
One should avoid the great disease known as Alasa in the organ of taste, as well as a tumor (arbuda) located on the palate.
A constricted ring in the throat causes loss of voice; likewise, a large goiter and a mass of flesh [indicate] Rohiṇī.
Even the flood of disease, more fierce than a *śataghnī* weapon, which is terrifying, all-pervading, and wandering everywhere.
One should carefully examine and avoid those ten and eleven defects pertaining to the face. // 121 //
The essential meaning consists of the specific characteristics [of diseases], their treatment, those that are incurable and those that are curable, all presented in their complete sequence. (122)
The essential meaning is this:
the primary [beauty] is half the body, and then the entire face; they say that even within the face, there is a preeminence in the eyes.
The essential meaning is this:
therefore, it is indeed excellent to protect that [mind], just as one would guard against the impurities that afflict the sense organ of the eye.
Their number is exactly seventy-six; the physician should treat those who are afflicted with these difficult diseases. 124.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: from entering the water, from having a body that is excessively heated, from sitting in a steady posture, and from the transition [of breath], there arises the summer heat.
Because of suppression. // 125 //
From headache, from eating excessively dry food, and from the suppression of the urges of feces, urine, and wind;
Therefore, their essential meaning consists of three kinds of bases, as well as mandalas and other junctions therein.
There are five types of *paṭala*s in the eyes; they are indeed five, six, and again six respectively. (127)
And the meaning is "from walking," which is an alternative reading.

"Bindughaṭṭanāt" is an alternative reading. Furthermore, there are junctions (*saṃdhi*) at the junction of the two [eyes], and likewise two others located at the corners of the eyes (*kāminikāpāṅga*). (128)
The meaning of this is as follows:
these [eyes] are directly on their own path within the chapter, and likewise, all four are the sockets of the eyes.
And in those [eyes] where there is a terrible darkness, I shall specifically describe all-pervading eye diseases. 129.
I shall now describe the various types of *abhiṣyanda*, which are the basis for all causes of eye diseases.
The meaning of the term *vicā* is the intense perception of a multitude of distinctions among existing things, characterized by particular harshness and causing the hair to stand on end.
The falling of cold tears accompanied by non-cooling exhilaration constitutes that very condition known as abhiṣyanda caused by vāta.
The meaning of the term is "having set aside"; "vyapohya" is an alternative reading.
One should quickly apply a lukewarm fomentation and then plaster the area with these non-cold substances mixed with rock salt.
The essential meaning is this:
therefore, one should purge a person whose body is very unctuous by means of venesection as well as by the administration of enemas.
One should conquer [the disease] with nasal drops (puṭapāka), saturating therapies (tarpaṇa), excellent fumigations, sudation, and the application of medicinal leaves as bandages. // 133 //
The essential meaning is that one should feed [the patient] with preparations well-concocted from sour fruits and spices, along with unctuous substances (khalas) and ghees prepared with boiled milk.
After eating, he should drink fragrant ghee while it is still lukewarm; if thirsty, he should drink a small handful of water. (134)
The essential meaning is as follows:
take citron, sour tamarind, and rock salt, along with ghee, oil, and cow's milk.
This collyrium, rubbed together with *nīlikā* and always fumigated with the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), should be applied as an eye-salve at all times. (135)
The essential meaning is that one should cure all diseases produced by wind (vāta) arising from the two eyes according to the prescribed method.
The essential meaning is that thirst, hunger, and a state of not having drunk occur in the Pitta-type group of Abhiṣyanda. (137)
The essential meaning is this: having first administered ghee to soften [the patient], one should purify [the body] therein and then release the vein.
The meaning of the verse is as follows: there is an alternative reading, "bhāvārthaḥ sadvayaghṛṣṭamiṣṭataḥ.
One should apply a plaster made from [drugs] ground with milk and mixed with ghee and sugar; or one should administer an extract (rasakriyā) prepared with them. // 139 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
having finely ground conch shell here with breast-milk, one should rub it in two iron vessels.
One should always apply [this] well-fumigated with sugar repeatedly to eyes afflicted by pitta. (140)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
buffalo milk itself, mixed with the paste of liquorice, strained, cooled, and combined with camphor.
One should apply [this] again with ghee or with the juice of *puṇḍra* sugarcane when there is pain from the burning sensation in the eyes. (141)
The essential meaning is that one should drink gruel well-prepared with milk, saturated with ghee, and combined with sugar.
One should eat mudga-bean soup mixed with milk-rice and ghee, or simply rice with mudga-bean soup. (142)
In this case, one should feed the person with boiled vegetables that are astringent, bitter, sweet, and very cooling.
One should drink water that is fragrant with the scent of sandalwood, beneficial, moderate in quantity, and perfumed with thick clusters of flowers. // 143 //
To what extent do things that have come before the eyes of men constitute their true meaning? They are merely perceived as arising from bile and causing a burning sensation.
Then, one should treat them with cooling measures for all procedures, or by means of the therapeutic regimen for pitta.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
his face was blood-red, and his eyes were likewise red, surrounded by spreading lines like a halo.
Where blood appears along with the symptoms of pitta, it is proclaimed as abhiṣyanda. // 145 //
The clinical significance [of this condition] consists of thick ointment-like coatings, coldness, excessive heaviness, swelling, very intense itching, and a craving for cold things.
The essential meaning is this:
one should repeatedly treat that [condition] with head-purgatives, bloodletting, and excessively drying applications.
One should apply a plaster made from triphalā, trikaṭu, and fresh ginger, ground with warm cow's urine.
Furthermore, one should irrigate eyes obstructed by phlegm with juices derived from the roots of *punarnavā*, mixed with rock salt. (149)
The essential meaning is this:

the procedure for gargling should always be performed with well-ground *satsa*, *sarṣapa*, and warm water; immediately thereafter, one should employ excellent mouthfuls (*kavala*) consisting of *śigru* root, fresh ginger, *kuṣṭha*, and rock salt. 150.

The essential meaning is that [the purification] is achieved through *puṭapāka* (herbal steaming) using substances produced from extremely sharp and parched sources, as well as by groups of astringent and alkaline substances and cow's urine.
With the well-ground paste of *niśā*, the two types of *trivṛt* (*dvaya-trivṛt*), the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *kuṣṭha*, and mustard seeds, thoroughly stirred and well-strained; 151.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
[this preparation] is combined with citron, sour *amlaka*, and rock salt, along with turmeric, *abhayā*, ginger, and the three types of *pippalī*.
One should stir [the substance] repeatedly in a shining copper vessel that has been well-perfumed with *harītakī* oil.
The essential meaning is this:
likewise, one should rub together this well-smoked *sad-añjana* for those suffering from eye diseases caused by phlegm (*śleṣman*). (153)
The meaning of the intent:
every three days, one should feed the man—who has fasted since the morning—once a day a small amount of light food consisting of ghee and rice. (155)

One suffering from eye disease should drink a small amount of water boiled with *kuṣṭha*, *harītakī*, and *ghana* (musta), while it is still warm; or likewise, water prepared with pungent, hot, and excellent medicinal herbs; or the beneficial and pleasing milk of the *āḍhakī* plant. (156)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

These [faults], which are like diseases in the eye, are difficult to conquer; they produce through their own various defects other [faults] that are known by specific names such as *pratīta*, *sat*, *syanda*, and *viśeṣa*, which cause the churning and splitting of the intellect of others. (157)
Having violently uprooted that very eye, they are now being churned again and again.
Even half of the head may experience extremely intense pain; this is the specific characteristic of Adhimantha. (158)
The essential meaning is that the types caused by phlegm (kapha), wind (vāta), and blood (rakta) are characterized respectively by seven, six, and five [symptoms], or even by three.
Those devoid of ritual action destroy their vision; the powerful one, like a person of bilious temperament, [consumes it] in that very instant. // 159 //
Therefore, having reflected upon those [teachings] which possess the quality of destroying the mental afflictions and which are the cause for the destruction of views, this is the essential meaning.
The meaning of this is:
This incurable disease, renowned on earth, is afflicted by excessive pain and has destroyed the vision; it is known as Adhimantha. // 161 //
Its essential nature is associated with oozing, itching, discharge, and burning; it is large and resembles a fully ripe bimba fruit.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: When the wind (vāyu) moves excessively within the pair of eyelashes and takes hold of the eyebrows and eyes to a great degree, it produces pain in turn; that condition here is known as *paryaya* due to the provocation of the wind.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

When the eye has constricted eyelids and appears harsh, extremely dry, and turbid in nature, and is unable to see due to the provocation of the wind (vāyu), one should diagnose it as *viśuṣkapāka*. (164)
The essential meaning is as follows:

Wind (vāyu) accumulated in the eyebrows and located in the eyes causes piercing pain in the head, the ears, and the jaw, as well as intense pain in the neck (manyā); they call that continuous condition *anyatovāta*. (165)
The meaning of the state is this:
for when the lords of the eyes become red, they may be accompanied by pain or even devoid of pain.
When blood is repeatedly discharged due to intense provocation, it is declared to be the disease known as *śirotpāta*.
The meaning of the passage is this:
when a headache is neglected by men, it becomes here known by the name "vein-excitement" (śirā-praharṣa).
Then a clear flow pours forth incessantly; a person is unable to perceive it for even a moment. (168)
The essential meaning is this:
by means of the number seventeen (ten and seven), one should diligently remove all diseases residing in the eyes and other locations.
I shall state the essential meaning according to its specific characteristics, having examined each one individually by its own number as it occurs during the junctions (saṃdhi) and so forth. 170.
The essential meaning is this:
there are exactly nine diseases arising from all the joints of the eyes; I shall describe them along with their treatments in their proper order.
In this joint, a swelling that is mobile, very soft, painless, and extremely red is considered a *piṭaka*; however, when it occurs at a joint (*parvan*), it is called *parvaṇī*. 171.
The etiological meaning is that it is associated with excessive discharge from phlegm, accompanied by intense pain, blackish in color, and hard; this is the type arising from the joints.
An excessive glandular swelling here is the disease called alajī; that very same swelling, when it has reached suppuration, is [known as] śopha.
When accompanied by pain and bursting, with much pus flowing out, that other [type] is known as pūyālasa.
In this case, there occurs what is known by the name *kaphopanāha*; that very same condition, when it has suppurated due to the profuse discharge of pus, [is called *vidradhi*].
It is characterized by the specific name "flowing with pus"; it is white, dried out, abundant, and extremely slimy. // 174 //
From this [condition], a constant discharge born of *valāsa* (phlegm) flows; here, that born of *pitta* (bile) flows with the appearance of a liquid like turmeric;
and that born of blood flows accompanied by blood; since these are the four types of discharges mentioned, they are thus declared to be fourfold. // 175 //
Then, worms born from one's own channels or born from phlegm produce a knotty growth that is extremely itchy.
Those originating from all the joints are proclaimed by their own names and characteristics at the respective locations of those joints. // 176 //
This is the essential meaning;
hereafter, I shall describe the diseases located on the pathways according to their own specific humors, types, forms, names, and numbers.
The essential meaning is this:
this carbuncle has openings between its internal cavities; one opening extends outward, while others are deep-seated and thick.
Therefore, by its very nature of clinging to the light of its own path, it becomes a transformation agitated by manifold sensations. // 178 //
The meaning of the state is that the pustules arising on one's own path are painless; they themselves are like the fruit-stones of the *kuṃbhīka* plant.
Because it repeatedly distends and then bursts again due to phlegm (kapha), this disease is therefore called kumbhīka. // 179 //
The clinical meaning is that there occur itching,
discharge, heaviness, and various pains, along with numerous pustules arising from its own path.
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is a severe,
very gross corruption, covered by other pustules on its own tracks.
Accompanied by subtle itching and clusters of pustules, this condition arises here from phlegm and wind; it is known as *vartma-śarkarā*. (181)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: likewise, they resemble the seeds of the urvāruka fruit; though as hard as thorns, they are exceedingly smooth and devoid of sensation.
There arise deficiencies in observing the path; for those embodied beings on the path, there is always a lack of vision regarding that [path]. (182)
The essential meaning is that the sprout of harshness is exceedingly long and most terrible; it is a disease of malignant sores that withers away in its own path.
Always reddish-brown like copper, with very tender pustules, it is painless and is known as Sāñjananāmikā. // 183 //
The essential meaning is that it is covered with pustules dominated by phlegm,
which are uniform in color, even, and continuous.
On all sides there would be a path known as "thick"; because of its own heaviness, it does not permit one to look upon it.
Its essential nature consists of swelling and itching, accompanied by slight pain, and it obstructs the vision of the eye when the eyelids are closed.
At that time, a man traveling on a path who is bound by a tether does not perceive everything clearly. (185)
The meaning of the verse is as follows; there is a variant reading: *samābhiratyantasa-varṇasaṃcayāt*.
"Equal" (*sama*) means having a uniform color (*savarṇa*) accompanied by mild pain, or always possessing a slightly greater coppery hue (*satāmra-varṇādhika*).
If blood should flow suddenly from its own path, this would be a case of an afflicted and specific disorder of the channels. // 186 //
The meaning of the state is this:
through neglect, one's own blood here becomes afflicted; from that, it undergoes putrefaction and then turns black.
From there, they proceed; here they are said to be those whose eyes are pierced, who perceive their own [nature], and who are joined with Kṛṣṇa and Kardama. (187)
The essential meaning is that,
both externally and internally, there is a flower upon the path, endowed with a dark-blue color.
They call that disease by the name Śyāmalavartman; it arises especially from blood and bile (rakta-pitta). // 188 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows: when there is pain and swelling here outside the eye, and always an internal discharge of slippery fluid;
Those who know the truth declare that this condition, arising from phlegm and blood, flows here with a moist and distinct track. (189)
The meaning is this:
even that path which has been washed again and again here is now being smeared with filth all at once.
That which is uncooked, not properly treated, arising from phlegm (kapha), and characterized by moist eyelids is named klinnaka-vartman. // 190 //
The essential meaning is this:
its activity is utterly destroyed, its joints are liberated, and its path is completely closed.
The wise, having investigated thoroughly, declare that this condition known as *vātahata-vartman* is born from wind (*vāta*). 191.
The meaning of the state is:
slightly reddish, uneven, slow, moving with a circular motion, situated within, without sensation, and dense.
The wise, who understand the onset of the humors (doṣas), declare that this arbuda is like a knotted tumor. // 192 //
The essential meaning is this:
having taken refuge in a vein originating from its own joint, that wind quickly moves along its path.
They recognize this disease as "nimeṣa," which arises from wind and throbs repeatedly.
Its essential nature is that which is known here by the name "red hemorrhoid"; even when cut, it grows back again in this world. (194)
The essential meaning is that it is painless, a knot-like growth, not subject to suppuration, located on the eyelid margin, thickened, and composed of phlegm (kapha).
Furthermore, the *lagaṇa* is proclaimed by those who know the specific distinctions of defects as being of two types according to its name. // 195 //
The meaning of the state of being is like the sprout of a lotus root in water—extremely subtle and deep-seated; it is just so on this path as well.
If water flows out continuously and repeatedly like that from a lotus stalk, one should designate it by the name *bisavartman*.
The meaning of the passage is as follows: whenever the eyelashes, due to the excessive provocation of wind (vāta), are constantly shaken and enter into the eye;
Then, arising from the agitation of intense fury, that terrible twitching of the eyelids occurs here. (197)
This is the essential meaning: here follows the discourse on diseases based on the pathways [of the humors], according to their own specific types, forms, names, and characteristics.
Now, having enumerated those belonging to the white [path] according to the count of twenty-one as they have arisen, I shall describe the diseases associated with them. (198)
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
Now, the *ārma* (cataract), being extensive, is blue-black; on its own white portion, it becomes thin and spread out.
In the same way, the *śuklārma* (white film) grows slowly; it is white, soft, and located in the white part [of the eye], while the other is likewise. (199)
The essential meaning is this:
when the flesh has increased sufficiently, it becomes like the petal of a red lotus.
Situated near the liver, it is thick and very extensive; this white-based structure is named *adhimāṃsa*. (200)
The essential meaning is that the flesh is stable, composed of many sinews, extensive, covered by vessels, and serves as the support for the white [fat].
The droplets are reddish and very smooth; when they are white, it is called *kṛśaśukti*. 201.
The meaning of the term *bhāvārtha* is as follows:
it is single, rabbit-marked (the moon), white and elevated, resembling flour, resting upon the white, known by the name *supiṣṭaka*, and characterized by discernment. // 202 //
The meaning is as follows: "Just like hemorrhoids" is an alternative reading.
A large, reddish, hard, and vein-covered mass, appearing as a network of veins and so forth, occurs here from the white [vitiated humors].
The pustule covered by veins and resting upon the vessels is called *sita*; it arises from the head and destroys men along with their heads. // 203 //
The meaning of the [term] *bhāva* would be "bound by phlegm" (*balāsagrathita*), arising from ten [factors]. Beyond this, I shall describe the diseases pertaining to *kṛṣṇa*. // 204 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

that which is free from ulceration, white, even, thin, easily curable, and located on the white part (śukla) of the eye near the black part (kṛṣṇa)—that very same condition, if it is sunken and flows with discharge all around, is incurable; however, this is understood to be [the case] when accompanied by an ulcer (savraṇa). // 205 //

One should treat that condition arising from the three humors (tridoṣaja), which is characterized by inflammation of the eyelids (akṣipāka) and is incurable, after having identified the specific nature of the humor involved. // 206 //
The meaning of the symptoms is as follows:
it resembles the back of a cowrie shell, is extremely painful, is reddish in color, and has a discharge resembling blood.
Having pierced the region of Kṛṣṇa, it increases;
that disease, known as Ajaka, causes terror to the eyes. // 207 //
The essential meaning is this:
these four aforementioned diseases are characterized by one's own defects within one's own dark circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala).
The essential meaning is that,
through one's own actions, there arises a cooling remedy the size of a lentil, born from the region of tranquility.
Those who have known all remedies say that vision must be protected with great effort, for it perishes very quickly. (209)
I shall now describe the diseases caused by the defects residing in the visual faculty, which are of twelve types and divided into many sub-varieties.
"Sabhājakākhya" is an alternative reading;
[it denotes] the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and the essential meaning (bhāvārtha).
But when the humors are established in the first layer of the eye, then the person [suffers].
One does not perceive here every object as it truly is; rather, due to one's own affliction, one sees what is distinguished as indistinct. // 211 //
The essential meaning is this:
a man's vision becomes utterly bewildered; he never perceives that which is pleasant yet hollow.
Or else, when there is an accumulation of faults through effort, and the second stage (paṭala) has likewise been reached; 212.
The meaning of the state is this:
he does not look downward, but then looks upward; thus, when the third membrane has been pierced through all its parts.
Within that accumulation of faults, he sees mosquitoes, flies, and gnats, along with their swarms, within his mass of hair. (213)
The meaning of the verse is:
one whose eyes are favored by the sun may see during the day due to the state of being depleted of phlegm. // 214 //
The meaning of the passage is this:
when [the breath] has entered the fourth petal, it obstructs vision due to the defect known as *timira*.
The essential meaning is that this destruction of the *liṅga* becomes *nīlikā* here; it is proclaimed as being known by the name *viśeṣakāca*.
The meaning of the state [of existence] is this:
one perceives various forms that are utterly overwhelmed by this very manner [of perception] arising from one's own internal derangement.
That very glass, consisting of wind and reddish in color, becomes stable, appearing as a red radiance within the field of vision. // 218 //
The meaning of the state is as follows:
from bile (pitta), there arises that which is called "excessively blue," as well as that which is withered and of a tawny nature.
In this condition, the circle of vision becomes white due to phlegm (kapha), and it completely dissolves when rubbed. (219)
The essential meaning is as follows:

moreover, the visual field (maṇḍala) may appear red or other colors resembling a sprout, being perfumed; it may be variegated in color all around and produced by the three humors (tridoṣa). These are proclaimed as the six types that destroy the vision. // 220 //

Now, I shall describe the six types of eye diseases caused by one's own vision being afflicted by vitiated *pitta*. One whose vision is scorched by *pitta* sees all things as intensely yellow; even though the object itself is not yellow, it appears so due to the corruption of the visual faculty. (221)
The meaning of the state [of existence] perceives with great clarity all moving and stationary beings, which possess the stainless luster of the moon, a conch shell, and crystal.

The essential meaning is as follows: when the head is afflicted by heat, fatigue, sorrow, and pain, and the entire vision here on earth is oppressed, one sees intensely smoky forms; the wise call such a person a "smoke-seer" (dhūmadarśin). // 223 //
When a letter of a different class joined with a short vowel occurs as the *bhāvārtha*, it indicates that men will suffer from disease seen in their vision. This is according to Satya.
They see those standing directly in front of them as being very far away; at that time, due to their defect, they perceive tall objects as if they were short.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

When a man’s vision on earth becomes brilliant at night—like the sight of a mongoose—he certainly sees various objects during the day; this disorder is known as *nakulāndhya* (mongoose-blindness). 225.
With her gaze fixed upon wealth, oppressed by the wind, overcome by pain, and her form utterly distorted,
she may possess a deep and specific consciousness, yet be endowed with a corrupted and extraordinary vision. (226)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
likewise, there are two types of external diseases—those with a cause and those without a cause.
Among these, that which arises from a cause is produced by a great trauma and is characterized by swelling and discoloration. // 227 //
The true meaning is that which is free from defects and possesses the nature of the primordial substance; even this transformation is characterized by the absence of a [external] cause. // 228 //
Thus, all diseases located in the eyes have been examined individually according to their manifested characteristics; this is the essential meaning.
One should also accomplish those [medicines] here according to the prescribed ritual by means of medicinal herbs. // 229 //
In that case as well, there are three additional meanings arising from *kapha*.
From the blood as well, there are ten, six, and all [the elements] born from it; furthermore, here, twenty enter, including two born from the external. (230)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: all those diseases number seventy-six;
among them, first are the diseases of *hatā*, *sahitā*, and *adhimanthara*.
The disorders caused by wind (vāta) would thus be fourfold in their variations. // 231 //
The disease known as *kāca* is reddish in nature; it should be treated with measures for wind (*vāta*).
It causes dryness of the eyes, inflammation, and impairment of vision due to wind.
Syanda is also declared to be the disease Adhimantha; those caused by Vāta are curable, except for Ativāta.
The meaning of "bhāva" is discharge; thus, those [two] mentioned as arising from pitta are incurable.
Even one called "glass" (kāca), designated as "blue" (nīla) by convention, which is withered and worn out, is merely something to be endured. // 233 //
The essential meaning of this [condition] is also called *syanda*,
and it is designated by the names *adhimanth* and *śuktyamla-adhyuṣita-vidagdha-dṛṣṭi*.
And together with one who observes [the signs] manifested by smoke and so forth, all six of those disorders born of bile (pitta) are to be diagnosed. // 234 //
This discharge (srāva) born of phlegm is indeed incurable;
however, that which is called kāca, produced by phlegm alone, may be palliable.
Syanda is that which causes its own specific *adhimantha* (painful inflammation of the eyes);
it is known as the condition where the vision is congealed by phlegm (*śleṣman*) and other humors or is corrupted (*vidagdha*). // 235 //
Pothakī is characterized by raised patches accompanied by itching and primarily infested with worms;
Granthi is marked by knotty growths; and Parivartma is characterized by the thickening and hardening of the eyelids.
Those associated with an upanāha caused by the predominance of white phlegm (kapha) and those arising from phlegm (śleṣman)—ten of the former and one of the latter—are curable. // 236 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows: hemorrhoids, ulcers, and white leprosy are mentioned;
excessive bleeding, and diseases such as those born from goats are of an incurable nature.
Even for her, there may be a cataract produced by that same [cause],
as well as a disease called syanda, which arises from excessive rubbing of the eyes. // 237 //
This afflicted [growth] described along its path is *lohitārma*; that which is well-known as being devoid of injury and located in the white [portion] is called *arjuna*.
On the festival day, she whose name was Añjanakṛtā [prepared] a net for the veins;
furthermore, there was a sudden outburst of joy. // 238 //
These are the diseases caused by blood;
others are also established as being characterized by a single [specific] symptom.
The meaning of the verse is:
there is blindness located in the eyes of the mongoose among all [the animals], and there is also a discharge accompanied by manifest pus. // 239 //
This inflammation occurring in the eye is called alajī by its own name; four such conditions have been described, and they are to be avoided.
A cataract manifested with visible eyelashes and an inflammation situated on the eyelid—
both of these conditions here must be managed conservatively.
The essential meaning is that which is moistened, even though it is directly before you, O Pillikākṣī.
That which is described as one's own cyst (piḍikā) arising in the vessels, or a fleshy growth (kārma) properly joined with the sinews, skin, and bone; 241.
*Kṛṣṇa* is an alternative reading. Now, the pair of *pāka* [medicines] beginning with *prastādi* is for hemorrhoids (*arśas*) that are dark-colored, thick, painful, and accompanied by discharge.
Furthermore, that which has a path accompanied by other poisons, is rich in gravel, and is characterized by white hemorrhoids, tumors, and slough, preceded by pus; // 242 //
Then, those known as *utsaṅginī*, *piṭaka*, and *kumbhapūrvā* are to be treated when all the resulting defects have been identified.
The two external [types of dreams], those born from manifest signs and those born from no signs, may be either curable or characterized as incurable. // 243 //
The essential meaning is this:
having understood here these seventy-six types of eye diseases along with their complications as curable, palliable, or incurable, one should then act accordingly.
One should properly treat it with surgical excision and other measures, through the application of potent medicines, and by means of pacifying therapies. (244)
The essential meaning is that in this world,
eleven eye diseases are to be excised,
nine others are to be incised, and the remaining ailments are to be scraped.
Thus, twelve have indeed been revealed; seven of them are palliative. // 245 //
Fifteen types of patients must be rejected by physicians;
those who are external [to the medical system] may sometimes be merely palliable, but they are incurable.
The meaning of the terms is as follows:
*armāṇi* (calluses), the five *piṭakas* (boils), those arising from the vessels (*sirā*), *jāla* (networks), *arbuda* (tumors) arising from the vessels, and furthermore, *darśa* (warts). // 246 //
When one's own channels have become dry due to a disease of the joints,
these disorders are declared by physicians to be treatable by excision.
The bhāvārtha, granthi, krimiprabhava, ekakaphopanāha, añjanākṣigata, gaṇa, bisavartman— these are the conditions that should be excised. // 247 //
The meaning of the state [of existence] is that it consists of the thick and excessive mire of afflicted bonds,
and it is characterized by transformations such as attachment and the aforementioned "book-worm" (pothakikā).
These have been declared by the ancient sages to be the types of written documents. // 248 //

The meaning of the verbal roots *vap* (to sow), *pac* (to cook), and *pūy* (to putrefy) is indeed [the same as that of *syand*]; however, in this context, only those [roots] designated by the grammarians as *ṣyaṇdī* (meaning "flowing") are intended to be pierced. // 249 //
The meaning of the term is:
one whose vision is impaired by phlegm and bile that have moistened the visual pathways and caused their digestion.
Dry ophthalmia (śuṣkākṣipāka), as well as śukla, amlakādi, and the disease characterized by a moistened eyelid and congealed phlegm (praklinnavartma-kaphasaṃgrathita), are [the conditions]. // 250 //
Having removed the effects of the weapon's blow, one who knows the procedure should treat them according to the rules with specially selected, excellent medicines.
As long as there is no affliction from the disease of the eyes, one should treat it even by means of non-surgical methods. // 251 //
The essential meaning is that all six types of *kāca*, when associated with an aggravation of the eyelashes (*pakṣma*),
are declared to be palliable; furthermore, they may also become incurable.
One should avoid those born from the combination of wind and blood, as well as those born from each of the [other] three humors individually, of which there are four types each. (252)
One should avoid those hemorrhoids that arise from phlegm (kapha), as well as the two types produced by bile (pitta),
and the two types born externally, excluding the one caused by wind (vāta).
The essential meaning is:
having placed a measure [of it] smeared with ghee, one should then [proceed] with continuous recitations. // 253 //
The essential meaning is this:
having averted the divergent [view] and having the eye remain steady,
it should be treated precisely according to the previously mentioned procedure for existing ulcers.
Even when afflicted by nourishing treatments, it attains pacification. // 254 //
The essential meaning is this:
I shall set forth the excellent procedure for briefly pacifying all eye diseases produced by the humors, such as wind and the others.
In that case, one should first treat the disorder caused by the reversal of wind (vāta), and then, depending on other factors, treat it according to the prescribed methods for wind.
The meaning of the verse is:
[this] powder, together with pūrakarasa and rock salt.
That most excellent collyrium, when ground dry, is beneficial for the process of healing and provides nourishment for the eyes when mixed with clarified butter and oils. (256)
The essential meaning is that there should be sprinkling with oil and lukewarm milk.
One should diligently treat all disorders affecting the eyes that have arisen from wind (vāta) by means of this method. // 257 //
One who knows the methods of treatment should treat all diseases arising from pitta with every kind of cooling remedy.
"Bhinna" is an alternative reading meaning "exudation," specifically that produced from the *narakiṃśuka* tree; it is ground here with milk and mixed with sugar. (258)
It instantly destroys even that which has been inhabited by one suffering from a wasting disease.
Likewise, water boiled with the three myrobalans (triphalā) and mixed with clarified butter should be drunk; it destroys impurities, but not in cases of śuktikā.
The essential meaning is that cooling ointments and other remedies are for the purpose of warding off acidity;
[the remedy] is enriched with fine gold, silver, sandalwood, and sugar.
One should mix this, well-ground, with goat's milk. // 260 //
The essential meaning is that he who observes the smoke-therapy should constantly drink cow's ghee and apply it as nasal drops; with that very substance, he should properly perform the treatment.
One should also quickly conquer diseases of phlegm through the application of dry and pungent substances, and by means of extremely sharp head-purgatives (śirovireka). // 261 //
The meaning of the procedure is as follows: having dried grains of śālī-rice, barley, and black sesame seeds,
one should repeatedly saturate them with well-boiled goat's milk.

Having been thoroughly cauterized according to the procedure for applying alkali, the ripened morbid matter (pāka) situated within the sinus, thickened by abundant phlegm, becomes like collyrium (añjana). // 262 //
The meaning of the essence is that it is desirable when well-ground with lime produced from *luṅga*.
That powder, when used as a constant collyrium, quickly destroys all various diseases of phlegm (kapha) without exception.

The meaning of the practice is as follows: one should grind together green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), rock salt (*siṃdhulavaṇa*), and the product of the ocean (*jaladhīprasūti*); this mixture is then combined with *tāla* (minium) ground with sour fruit juice.
This, when ground with an alkaline substance, destroys pilla. // 264 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
having repeatedly dried white *marica* from the Nādeya region and realgar,
one should prepare a medicinal wick for use as an eye-salve.
It destroys itching and all disorders born of phlegm (kapha). // 265 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
[one should treat] all the disorders arising from blood that have spread to the eyes,
including those resulting from excessive lacrimation (*ṣyanda*), *adhimantha*, and the dilation of blood-filled vessels (*bahurakta-śirā*).
One should conquer [these disorders] by means of sudden applications of ghee plasters, gentle bloodletting from the veins, as well as emesis and head-purgatives (śirovireka). // 266 //
The meaning of the passage is:
[the application of] fumigation, eye-drops, ointments, and medicinal plasters.
If one administers it with very unctuous and cooling ingredients combined with excellent jaggery,
even when warm, it will conquer even the most intense pains.
The meaning of the state [of reality] would suddenly cause the two eyes to meet together from all sides.
Clarified butter and honey-ointment are also well-known for treating varicose veins;
furthermore, white sugar combined with freshly expressed milk overcomes these diseases.
The essential meaning is this:
this powerful *arjuna* (Ficus religiosa) conquers all;
it is honey-colored (*mākṣīka*), white (*arjuna*), leafless (*apattrana*), and has flowers like eyes (*akṣipuṣpa*). 269.
The essential meaning is that [it is prepared] with powders of all types of salt, garlic, and karañja.
Collyrium made from *rlekhyā* would be a scraper for diseases of the eyes. // 270 //

One should overcome this condition, which has the nature of inflammation with swelling and other symptoms, by means of head-evacuants (śirovirecana) and purificatory therapies; furthermore, this collyrium should be used.
In this case, [the water] that has been rubbed and kept in a vessel for ten nights [is pure]. // 271 //
Jātī flowers, viḍaṅga essence,
ginger combined with rock salt, and long pepper;
This great substance known as añjana, when rubbed with oil, repeatedly and completely cures inflammation of the eyelids. (272)
The essential meaning is that in the case of *pūyālasa*, one should quickly perform bloodletting,
and also apply a poultice (*upanāha*) with the juice of fresh ginger.

One should conquer all eye diseases, including those involving the moistened eyelids, by using a collyrium prepared from green vitriol (kāsīsa), rock salt (saindhava), and antimony (añjana). // 273 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows: [one should offer] pieces of cloth soaked in warm water and smeared with ghee.
One should diligently accomplish those [goals] by means of the edge of a weapon sharpened by fire and heated,
using all the aforementioned heated yogas.
Having dissected the swelling and carefully wiped the track with a cotton pad,
one should incise the lines of the ulcer and rub it with salts.
Having divided those who are to be divided by means of snares, and having gathered those who are to be won over;
and having severed those who are to be cut off, including all those states that have resorted to the peripheral [views]. // 275 //
Having incised the veins and opened them according to the appropriate method,
he— the most excellent among those who know the Vedas— should conquer the targets to be pierced.
Even later, by means of reasoning that reveals specific defects, one should treat [the patient] with all appropriate medicines, collyriums, and so forth. // 276 //
The meaning of the verse is:
one should bind it so that the beautiful forehead-band is knotted.
Observing the growth of the eyelashes, the wise man should, for the sake of comfort, release all the bonds formed by the stalks.
Having written out its essential meaning, one should pacify the irritation of the eyelid here— whether by burning it with fire to remove the heat, or by excising it.
One should also constantly apply treatments for diseases of the eyes that produce clarity of vision, after having carefully examined those conditions that are curable. // 278 //
The essential meaning is this:
having recognized that even the destruction of its characteristic signs has arisen from intense phlegm, one should massage it and cause it to dissolve suddenly.
While the man gazes directly at his own nose, he should carefully examine the cavity within the white region with great effort. // 279 //
In this [body], which is marked by the characteristics produced by its own deity,
one should pierce it gradually and very slowly, following the proper sequence.
One should draw out that [disease] with the sound of a lion's roar, following after the humming [of the breath]. // 280 //
When the entire collection of objects standing before him has been seen,
the physician should withdraw the probe in due order.
Lying on one's back is always beneficial for him,
as is nasal medication (nasya) prepared with excellent pungent and dry medicines that destroy phlegm.
The essential meaning is this:
either goat's urine with *kataka* and two *nakta* fruits ground together is desired here as a collyrium that brings about vision.
Red sandalwood, likewise, should be rubbed in succession with fermented gruel-water,
water, clarified butter, oil, sour fruit juice, and buttermilk.
The meaning of the term *bhāva* refers to the substances: mercury, copper, elephant-ivory, and gold;
these are the rods, which are smooth and have been treated with a thick application of the king of fluids (mercury).
Like the purification by means of *sauvīra* salt, they are exceedingly pure and cool;
through their contact, they bring about stainless vision for human beings. // 283 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
a powder made from the three myrobalans (triphalā) mixed with sesame oil is for [timira] arising from vāta;
when arising from kapha, it should be taken with ghee; and in cases of pittaja and raktaja [timira], it should likewise be combined with ghee.
But it would bring about a view that is exceedingly satisfied, highly nourished, and indeed possesses great excellence. // 284 //
The essential meaning is this:
milk-rice (pāyasa) cooked with ripe āmalakī fruits and the auspicious roots of śatāvarī, combined with cow's ghee, should always be consumed.
Like the lord of birds [the peacock], he casts his long gaze upon the pair of eyes;
the juice of the three fruits (triphalā) is a bestower of virility and longevity, with the drinking of cool water being the most excellent. (285)
The essential meaning is this:
flour that has been ground and kneaded is placed within these two large, very dark bronze vessels.

When applied with oil and clarified butter, and further mixed with a large amount of lamp-soot (añjana), it suddenly pacifies all eye diseases born of the humors, including those caused by excessive secretions and inflammation. // 286 //
The essential meaning is:
[one should apply] *śītāñjana*, known as *himarśātala*, which has been ignited by fragrant cow-ghee formed into wicks, to the eyes. (287)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
gold, copper powder, silver, pearl, or coral;
and [the powders] of dhātrī, akṣa, abhayā, udadhi, kapha, niśā, śaṅkha, tuttha, and amṛtā, each held in equal measure.
A powder made from equal parts of yaṣṭi, pippalī, nāgara, and excellent marica, ground with a decoction of yaṣṭi and formed into pills, pacifies all eye diseases without exception. (288)
The essential meaning is that all these— emerging, the essence, the most excellent, the moon, and the serpent— are equally measured.
This, applied with a snake-stick and anointed, bestows good fortune and a pleasing appearance. // 289 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
this foot-massage, honoring and worshiping the feet, as well as nasal drops, cooling applications, and collyrium, are prepared by the Siddhasenas.
The sprinkling of the eyes and the head with those known as the Śrījaṭās, which are renowned for the time of withdrawing the gaze, [is prescribed]. (290)
The meaning of the essential nature, the meaning of the essential nature—
thus [is it extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issuing from the mouth of the Jina.
From that which is agitated by a multitude of waves expanded by all categories of objects.
For this [teaching], which shines upon the two banks that accomplish the welfare of both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (292)
The meaning of the text:
Having paid homage to the Lord of Jinas, whose limbs are beautiful, and having prostrated before him who is worthy of veneration and honored by Indra;
I heal the diseases rooted in their beautiful faces and restore them, endowed with all auspicious marks. // 1 //
The essential meaning:
having characterized all the various types of signs, one should accomplish [the goal] through the corresponding rites.
One who knows the sequence of the authorized [rites] should apply those things that are to be accomplished, those that are concomitant, and those that are to be avoided. // 3 //
The meaning of "bhāva" is said to be breath (śvāsa), which is reversed; the vital air (prāṇavāyu) has moved upward.
When that [wind] is further oppressed by phlegm, it is called *śvāsa* (asthma); thus, this [condition] is fivefold.
The meaning of existence becomes trivial when one is born into action; its cessation also occurs upon the cessation of that [action].
Accompanied by a rattling sound and associated with phlegm and cough, this tamaka occurs in the weak and is incompatible with food.
The meaning of the condition is that the digestive fire is extinguished; it is characterized by a distended abdomen, a burning sensation in the bladder, and severe pain throughout the entire body.
The meaning of the state is that one,
suffering from pain arising from a vital wound, breathes heavily with all sound lost.
The types of breath-holding (bhāvārtha) are kṣudraka and tamaka; tamaka is curable, yet for one who is weak, even tamaka is extremely difficult to treat.
Those remaining who were avoided by the hosts of sages—[this] beautiful medical treatment is for those suffering from asthma. // 8 //
The essential meaning is that one should first administer emesis and ensure the purification resulting from the oil enema.
One should apply the medicinal formulations for pacification to those who are strong, the weak, and those suffering from dyspnea.
Clarified butter cooked with the group of pippalī and salts pacifies even excessively digested food.
The meaning of the procedure is as follows:
the oil should be cooked with twenty parts of *bhṛṅgarāja* juice, or alternatively, with the addition of the medicinal paste (*prativāpa*).
It very quickly cures dyspnea and cough, just as water boiled with the three myrobalans (triphalā) combined with clarified butter does.
The meaning of the verse is:
by licking these [medicines] together with sugar and ghee, one quickly overcomes even intense asthma. 12.
The essential meaning is this: the root itself, grown from a small bulb, should be smeared with long pepper, salt, oil, and ghee.
This [practice], when elevated, would destroy that [obscuration] which robs one of breath and inhalation in a mere instant. // 13 //
This reading is not found in manuscript Kha. The vital breath, conjoined with the upward-moving breath (udāna), produces a sound resembling the resonance of a cracked bell.
Therefore, one who has approached a wicked person brings about the disease of consumption (*kāsa*), which also consists of five varieties. // 14 //
The essential meaning is:
when [the vital breath] is obstructed in the chest by excessive study and other such activities, there occurs a cough due to injury accompanied by thick blood. (15)
The essential meaning is this:

when one who is weak, with a blood-red complexion, constantly spits [phlegm], and is afflicted by severe coughing, that cough born from all the *doṣas* is called "wasting cough" (*kṣayakāsa*), which they declare to be difficult to treat. (16)
The meaning of the essence is that it quickly pacifies excessive cough born of wind, as well as vomiting and the purgation of ghee.
The unctuous enema (snehabasti) should also consist of the renowned and excellent six-pala ghee that has been properly processed by decoction.
The essential meaning is that it removes the smoke of affection arising from the wind, just as [one removes it] with the milk of the *arka* plant for cough. 18.
The essential meaning is that one should drink either lukewarm cow's ghee, or indeed oil mixed with salt and pungent spices.
A gruel made with the three pungents and sour agents, as well as milk from a *kṣīrikā* cow, [are beneficial] for wind and cough. // 19 //
The essential meaning is:
either ghee naturally prepared with the juice of *vyāghrī*, or [ghee] with the juices of *kāsamarda*, *vṛṣa*, and *bhṛṅga*.
Cooked oil, or salt together with *abhayā*, destroys cough arising from [an imbalance of] wind.
The essential meaning is this:
one should repeatedly lick clarified butter mixed with sugar to pacify pitta-type cough. // 21 //
The essential meaning is that one should drink even long pepper, ghee, and jaggery, combined with buffalo milk.
Or, by grinding [the drugs] with honey and sugarcane juice, it very quickly cures cough caused by pitta. // 22 //
The meaning is "sweet sugarcane";
there is an alternative reading: "maṣṭamadhurekṣu."
Emetics, excessive purgation of the body and head, strong fumigations, mouthfuls [of pungent substances], and bitter electuaries; // 23 //
The meaning of this is:
just as one who subsists on milk exhausts everything [in the way of impurities] here, so too does one initiated into the Jina’s doctrine exhaust all evil. (25)
The meaning of the verse:
In this case, one should have the patient drink buffalo milk mixed with clarified butter and jaggery for the treatment of wasting cough caused by consumption. (26)
The meaning of the state of being arises; a powerful thirst is born in the heart, and that, like a cough, consists of five types of conceptualization. // 28 //
The essential meaning is one who knows the own-characteristics of all defects, [perceiving] form as characterized by sensations.
One should quench the greatly increased thirst here by means of drinking various medicinal decoctions of three kinds. // 29 //
The meaning of the state [of thirst] is that which may arise from a wound, from the depletion of blood, or else from painful sensations or even from dryness.
The essential meaning is this:
even when the belly is completely filled with water, thirst does not abandon the body.
One who knows the ritual procedure should induce vomiting with cold water mixed with a paste of *pippalī* and *madhuka*.
The meaning of the passage is that one should likewise smear it with acidic fruits, or purify it with heated iron, sand, and so forth.
One should cause [the patient] to drink boiled water that has been processed with groups of sweet and cooling substances, or else water that is very fragrant.
The meaning of the state [of existence] is not found through the path, because those [states] are devoid of the defect of bile (pitta). // 34 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows; "rocayet" is an alternative reading.

One should cause him, who is tormented by thirst, to drink here either a decoction of cinnamon bark mixed with sugar, or the juice of the *jāti* flower made from milk-tree wood, or the excellent juice produced from a large *udumbara* tree. (35)
And as for the ritual meaning: one should place [the vessel] at night in the open space of the sky, mixed with sandalwood water and thick *vālaka* grass. // 36 //
The fragrant water is indeed exceedingly cool; it is that [water] combined with grapes and sugar.
One should cause [the patient] who suffers from excessive burning and thirst to drink it; it quickly brings comfort to the mortal. // 37 //
This essence, when cooked with water and enriched with very cold sugar-candy, when drunk, removes excessive thirst. (38)
The essential meaning is that one should also cure vomiting arising from wind, bile, or phlegm by means of the specific medicinal formulations prescribed for each.
The essential meaning is this:
having approached [the patient], one should treat him by means of procedures that expel all his own accumulated morbid humors through emesis. 40.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
A physician who understands the subject matter should avoid administering emetics here to one whose body is afflicted by vomiting and who suffers from excessive fainting. 41.
The essential meaning is this:
when vomiting is accompanied by excessively aggravated doshas, emesis is beneficial for achieving purification from below.
One who knows the sequence of the Jina’s doctrine should apply the medicines prescribed for the aforementioned defects. // 42 //
The essential meaning is that a diet of dry, wholesome, and light food is desired, as is gruel (yavāgū) combined with sour substances and rock salt.
When milk, water, and snow are drunk together, they quickly pacify vomiting arising from wind (vāta). // 43 //
The meaning of the verse is:
one should cause [the patient] to drink fresh ghee combined with honey during vomiting episodes accompanied by strong wind. 44.
The meaning of the ritual is as follows: a decoction of pure *āmalaka* fruits mixed with clarified butter, combined with sugarcane juice and milk.
One should administer [emetics] with groups of substances that are exceedingly cooling in cases of vomiting associated with powerful pitta. // 45 //
The essential meaning is that, along with *pāṭhā*, the root of *nṛpāṅghri* (musta), *niṃba*, *siddha*, *mahimā*, and *kaṭukā*— abundant with pungency— [should be used].
The essential meaning is this:
one should pacify the fever with a decoction enriched with ginger; one should cause the person to drink it repeatedly for the sake of the ultimate goal. // 47 //
The essential meaning is that one should consume [the medicine] with all types of aromatics and sugar; nasal administration (nasya) is also highly beneficial in cases of vomiting. (49)
The meaning of the passage is: various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, many drinks and syrups, diverse in their pleasant scents and stages of ripening.
The essential meaning arises for living beings from the deficiency of fire; it is produced as that which is characterized by its own specific qualities. // 51 //
The essential meaning, the essential meaning, the essential meaning.
The true meaning of existence is that which is eternally favorable even to one's own mind for those people afflicted by the loss of appetite for the Dharma. 56.
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is that it consists of six types, including modifications of fat and blood. // 57 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
due to an excess of wind (vāta), there is a voice that is suppressed and choked;
due to an excess of bile (pitta), there is a voice like that of a donkey or a mule with broken thighs.
Due to burning sensations, dryness of the mouth and throat, and the affliction of thirst, as well as from the presence of phlegm that obstructs the throat, the voice becomes impaired. (58)
The meaning of the state is that this tone of the gender-sign must be avoided.
And the sages say that this change of voice is also incurable. // 59 //
The meaning of the verse is: A person whose throat and palate are overwhelmed by fat speaks with difficulty, slowly, and with faltering, heavy words.
From the depletion of fat, a man loses his good voice. // 60 //
The essential meaning is this:
having directly beheld all men afflicted by disease,
[the physician] acts out of affection with appropriate medicinal applications suited to each case.
By means of the primary groups of medicines that bring about the pacification of the breath. // 61 //
The essential meaning is that for those men whose voices have been impaired by the derangement of Vāta, the daily drinking of ghee after meals is desired when Pitta is involved.
In cases of *balāsa*, one should drink milk mixed with a large quantity of ghee and jaggery;
or alkaline water blended with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
The essential meaning is this:
one who understands the disorders of the voice should administer oil according to the procedure for nasal medication (nasya),
combined with appropriate groups of drugs, for one suffering from vocal affliction.
The meaning of the passage is as follows: having eaten milk-porridge prepared with a decoction of yaṣṭīmadhu and mixed with abundant ghee and mung beans.
Within seven days, this wise one shall quickly become like the beautiful-voiced Kinnara, having directly eliminated all defects of the voice.
The essential meaning is this:
having duly applied the prescribed regimen for phlegm (*kapha*), the wise man should overcome the various types of hoarseness caused by disorders of the fat (*medas*).
Having excluded that which is produced by the three humors and blood, and having also considered its curability, the physician should apply himself [to the treatment]. // 65 //
The essential meaning is this:
one should consume black sesame seeds mixed with sprouts called *bhaṅga*,
along with black pepper and well-prepared chickpeas.
One who suffers from hoarseness of voice should drink milk here, enriched with cow's ghee, made warm, and mixed with sugar. (66)
The wise man should properly accomplish the essential meaning through effort, by means of causes, characteristics, and verbal remedies.
Equanimity toward that very thing swiftly destroys it. // 67 //

The essential meaning is that [the afflictions] such as wind and the rest, arising from the suppression of natural urges and so forth, are comparable to the lord of serpents, a thunderbolt, fire, and a weapon.
The essential meaning is this:
therefore, speed must certainly not be restrained; those who desire long life should act in exactly that way.
It causes colic, flatulence, dyspnea, heart disease, and hiccups; the obstructed apāna wind produces these very instantaneously. (69)
The meaning of the verse is:
the apāna-vāyu, having deviated from its path, forcefully obstructs the feces and may discharge it through the mouth.
The essential symptoms are abdominal pain, distension, dyspnea, constipation, hiccups, or the expulsion of feces through the mouth.
When feces are obstructed due to ignorance, a sharp piercing pain arises here in men, as if from a rising knife.
The meaning of the term is as follows:
there is excessive swelling of the urinary passage, the anus, and the scrotum; there is a painful discharge of urine mixed with semen;
and seminal stones (śukrāśmarī) arise here when the flow of semen itself is obstructed during its impulse. (72)
The essential meaning is this:
when the force of vomiting is suppressed, leprosy (kuṣṭha) arises; likewise, food is digested with difficulty by those very networks of humors (doṣa).
When the shedding of tears caused by grief, joy, and so forth is suppressed, diseases of the head, eyes, or nose arise. (73)
The meaning of the verse is:
those diseases arising from the nose, mouth, eyes, and head occur when the force of hunger is suppressed.
In those seven types of Udāvarta, one should understand the treatment for the disease and perform the correct medical therapy. // 74 //
The essential meaning is this:
a passionate woman, exceedingly beautiful, should first delight a mortal man—who is afflicted by the obstruction of semen—with her touches.
In all types of upward-moving disorders (udāvarta), the physician who knows medicinal drugs should administer whatever is appropriate in each specific case.
The meaning of the passage is as follows: when the wind repeatedly enters the mouth with great force,
excessively afflicting the spleen, liver, and other internal organs.
Because it destroys living beings along with the sound of cattle, those dear to the Jina declare that [the year] consists of irregular hiccup-like afflictions. (76)
The meaning of the state is that the wind thus described produces all five types of hiccup.
Then, there is likewise the [suffering] produced by food, as well as that which is paired, the minor, that called the great dissolution, and that which is exceedingly vast and profound. (77)
When the wind is itself driven downward by very pungent and bitter foods,

a person whose body is afflicted by insanity due to the humors (doṣas) should first be treated with oleation (snigdha),
and then have his body purified through both types of cleansing procedures (vibhāga).
Therefore, one should treat [the patient] with hundreds of sharp compressions on the head, purgations, and fumigations containing putrid substances. (108)
The essential meaning is that here, nasal medication and ointment are also beneficial to be employed,
combined with oil produced from very pungent mustard seeds.
And also by well-trained elephants skilled in all tasks. // 109 //
The essential meaning is this: in this well, which is filled with many most putrid and terrifying corpses,
one should cause him to lie down in that exceedingly thick and dense darkness.
Having properly licked [the area] on the surface of the forehead and all over the head,
the physician should also perform bloodletting here.
The essential meaning is that sleep-inducing factors consist of unctuous, well-washed, sweet, and very heavy types of food and drink, as well as eating and drinking in great quantities.
One should constantly administer purificatory therapies, which bring about intelligence and are the sole cause for the pacification of excessive intoxication, in order to eliminate the humors.
The meaning of this is:
here there is danger in the waters because one is deprived of life;
even the memory of that very [danger] necessarily perishes there through fainting.
In an instant, he falls to the ground, possessed by spirits that are yellow, green, and white. // 112 //
Falling to the ground, gnashing his teeth, vomiting phlegm, and gasping for breath,
with his eyes bulging from his head, he himself makes many moaning sounds.
Having died here, a man dies again; having died, he lives here with great difficulty.
The essential meaning is this:
why does this [mind] go forth so suddenly, having itself repeatedly returned;
it is stirred up by the qualities and defects that have been described through its exceedingly rapid coming and going?
In this case, that which arises from the humors (doṣa) known as epilepsy quickly subsides;
yet most ignorant people generally say it is caused by a seizing spirit (graha). // 114 //
The essential meaning is this:
in this world, some people become afflicted with excessive diseases solely due to their faults,
while others, after a very long time, [become so] by their very nature.

Just as a collection of seeds, even when endowed with the totality of all its qualities, produces on earth various individual sprouts according to whether they are slow or quick to grow; so too does the soul manifest. (115)
The essential meaning is this: here, due to great defects, diseases arise either quickly or after a long time.
Even though the ocean exists, masses of lofty waves arise by themselves, appearing individually and manifoldly at various times. (116)
May this entire collection of remedies for intoxication, whose essential meaning has been explained here,
always pacify the disease of epilepsy for one who knows the ritual procedure.
And by means of extremely potent medicines employed according to the methods for pacification. // 117 //
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is that which is to be enjoined;
it applies to states such as intoxication, excessive pride, and various mental afflictions.
One should always produce a sneeze here according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtra. // 118 //
The essential meaning is that it is sweet and fragrant, having been transformed by the mendicant.
Having placed it in a jar in the midst of much grain, if one drinks it repeatedly, it quickly pacifies epilepsy. (119)
The essential meaning [is extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent teachings issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (120)

This is the seventeenth chapter from the beginning, titled "The Treatment of Minor Diseases," within the section on therapeutics in the *Kalyāṇakāraka* composed by Ācārya Ugrāditya; this is the essential meaning.
In my mind, I hold the Lord of Jinas, whose pair of glorious lotus feet is the cause for men to attain the happiness and prosperity of the three worlds. // 1 //
The essential meaning is this:
I shall describe the state of being afflicted by powerful and severe wasting diseases, which serves as the sole abode for all the various ailments pervading the entire body.

By means of those very forms of his own, which were fashioned from his own qualities, which were initially most beautiful, which were like his own self, and which were highly desired by the gods, [he manifested] the various distinctions and subdivisions of faults. // 2 //

The essential meaning [is found] in the manuscript belonging to the Deśīgaṇa, within the lineage of the illustrious Kundakunda, which is marked by the cluster of deep and stainless roots, and follows the illustrious Panasogavali branch.
I perform service at the feet of you, the most excellent of teachers, whose fame is radiant and who possess the renowned eye of the Āgamas, and who enjoy the splendor of the lion throne.
Thus, an additional reading is found in manuscript *ka*:
"Bound on all sides by various and manifold diseases,
with the expansion of his banner raised, having manifested his own form."
Difficult to overcome in its transformation, hard to restrain, and exceedingly powerful, King Śoṣa, desiring victory, overcomes this world. // 3 //
The meaning of the term is that this "withering" results from being dried up day after day by extreme torments.
The king Śoṣa shines forth, possessing many names derived from the word *dadhi*.

The essential meaning is that this disease of consumption (śoṣa) has been described separately according to its various specificities and its divisions into primary and secondary types, arising from its own respective humors.
This [self] consists of a specific conjunction with that which possesses distinction. // 5 //
The meaning of the state [of the disease] is that,
due to the ten types of virasabhāva (vitiated states) and the obstruction of phlegm within the vessels.
This extremely painful disease of irregular wasting occurs. // 6 //

The meaning of the state [of existence] is like fire accompanied by smoke; through the distinction between the sign and the bearer of the sign, they are described as having many transformations and are endowed with their prior forms.
Thereafter, that abode of fire manifested its true characteristics;
likewise, diseases endowed with their own multitude of qualities appeared there as well.
The essential meaning is:
excessive and abundant phlegm, severe dyspnea, exhaustion of all limbs,
vomiting, dryness of the throat, extreme loss of digestive fire, and insanity.
Whiteness of the eyes and excessive sleepiness—these indeed are the premonitory symptoms of consumption (śoṣa). // 8 //
The meaning of one's state of being is conveyed during the time of sleep by parrots, peacocks, and those birds of the owl species, as well as by crows, vultures, troops of monkeys, and lizards.
Or he who might see a river that is harsh, rough, and parched, or withered trees scorched by forest fires and covered in smoke. (9)
The meaning of the symptoms is:
a sunken and emaciated flanks, contraction of the chest,
fever accompanied by burning sensations, blood disorders, and diarrhea.
In this context, those whose natural forms have reached a state of decay are born from bile (pitta). // 10 //
Furthermore, there is loss of appetite, cough, and injury produced in the throat;
these, along with heaviness in the head, manifest in many forms caused by phlegm.
Thus, one who seeks fame should avoid a person afflicted by consumption with ten, eleven, five, or six of these characteristics.
The meaning of the term *bhāvārtha* is one who, being emaciated, eats excessively;
such a person suffers from edema arising in the feet, abdomen, and private parts, as well as diarrhea.
With his mind attached to the curiosity of young women who are fierce as Yama, he proceeds without regard for anything else, quickly afflicted by destruction. (12)

One should purify that patient suffering from wasting, whose body has been lubricated with a collection of combined ghee preparations and whose head has been softened, by means of mild purification therapies.
The meaning of the verse is:
[he offered] barley grains possessing every excellence of sweet quality,
or wheat preparations of many kinds that had been prepared as food and were clearly visible.
One should feed him with plenty of ghee, jaggery, and milk, along with mung bean soups, various fruits, savory dishes, and well-nourished, desirable vegetables. (14)
The essential meaning is:
having risen in the morning, one should lick a fine powder of the three pungents (trikaṭuka), costus (ghana), chavya, and double-vidanga, either mixed with ghee or with jaggery.
Then, by constantly consuming long pepper (pippalī) together with grapes mixed with ghee and jaggery after meals, there shall be a destruction of consumption (kṣaya). // 15 //
The essential meaning is that, having drunk the dust from the scent of a similar horse with clarified butter;
A mortal who is anointed daily with milk mixed with jaggery and the fine paste of *vājigandhā* attains corpulence.
The essential meaning is:
one should drink boiled ghee prepared with vṛṣa, flowers, and roots; or one should eat cakes made from barley, sesame, jaggery, māṣa beans, and rice flour.
One should eat cooked foods with roots [ground] on a whetstone sharpened with a hundred blades. // 17 //
The meaning of the substance is as follows:
[it is prepared] with portions of the decoction of amṛta, khadira, mūrvā, and tejinī.
Or one should lick it after it has been cooked together with those [same ingredients] along with trikuṭa and madhuka. // 18 //
The essential meaning [is obtained] from *takana*, *nṛpa*, *bṛhatī*, *sairaṇḍa*, and the pair of *kārañja*.
One part of ghee is cooked with six parts of water boiled with barley, jujube, horse gram, ugrā, agni, and mandāgni. (19)
That ghee, when cooked with the milk of Snuhi and with Harītakī, Āsurāhva, and Cavya, pacifies the disease of consumption once it has fully developed.
[They sever] the knots of bondage consisting of many various, uneven, and fierce calamities. // 20 //
The essential meaning is that [the medicine] is cooked with clarified butter and portions of water boiled with *rasana*, *khadira*, *dhātrī*, *śāla*, and *gāyatrikā*.
By means of four [factors]. // 21 //
Then, thirty *pala*s of sugar and six *prastha*s of *tugākṣīrī* of manifest quality are added to the clarified butter that has been prepared.
Having given two *prasthas* of the decoction of *viṣatara*, *suviḍaṅga*, and *kvātha*, all thoroughly churned with a churning stick, into that aforementioned jar; 22.
When half a month has passed, having carefully extracted that [substance],...
Having licked one part daily here every day, one should take milk as an after-drink in a quantity of one pala.
This ghee is extremely pure, aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and a promoter of strength;
it pacifies consumption as well as diseases of the spleen and anemia.
There is no escape from this; by employing this very [practice], whether one is a mortal, a tīrthaṃkara, or a youth, day by day [one attains the goal]. 24.
The meaning of the formulation is as follows: one *prastha* of oil, an equal portion of ghee and jaggery, and an amount of *āruṣkara* [oil] equal to that.
Having quickly applied the oil that has been cooked until it is gently ripened.
A person possessing straightness and happiness shall weigh one droṇa.
The essential meaning is that by daily anointing one's own limbs with oil cooked with *kṣuraka*, *pippala*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruits, and through such acts as massaging the body;
Having removed the disease of decay, the person shall possess a robust body. // 26 //
The meaning of the passage:
Now, in a mixture of boiled milk and sugarcane juice combined with the six transformations [of milk],
and prepared with the powder of the extremely pure Varṣābhū plant;
On that day, the person suffering from consumption should eat with fragrant curd.
The essential meaning is that this is delicious, pleasing to the mind, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and refined.
One who suffers from consumption should constantly be provided here with food and drink of many various flavors, along with desirable and distinguished vegetables. (28)
This is the meaning of the ritual action. // 29 //

Due to the obstruction caused by the offering of oblations with well-known mantras, or from the wrath of hosts of sages, various types of *masūrikā* (smallpox) arise, appearing red, black, yellow, or pale-white, and possessing many different forms. (30)
The essential meaning is as follows: due to the distinction of one's own defects, *masūrikā* eruptions appear shaped like sand, mustard seeds, or lentils;
they may resemble all types of grain or the entirety of split pulses (*vaidala*).
Likewise, those that are yellowish-brown are like the fruit. // 31 //
The meaning of the term is "bhāva"; "gharma" is an alternative reading.
It is like the fruit of the *pīlu* tree when it is ripe.
Likewise, other hosts of special eruptions arise, resembling the excellent fruits of various trees;
they are terrifying to living beings due to their own karma, and they differentiate between those who are turned outward and those who are turned inward. // 32 //
The essential meaning is this:

where minute circles of white, deep red, reddish-brown, and black appear closely joined together without any intervening space, with their centers submerged and their peripheries dark, the physician should avoid treating those cases which are incurable in form. (33)
The essential meaning is as follows:

the premonitory symptoms of the onset of smallpox (masūrikā) are high fever, loss of appetite, horripilation, a burning sensation, excessive thirst, pain in the head, limbs, and heart, loosening of the joints, and profound sleepiness. (34)

Incessant delirium, fainting, vertigo, and dryness of the mouth; delusion of one's own mind, colic, and yawning; along with swelling, itching, and extreme heaviness of the limbs—these occur continuously, like those of one afflicted by poison. (35)
The essential meaning is this:

when [the fever] is accompanied by sharp pain, extreme delusion, hemorrhaging, burning sensations, and so forth, along with swelling, confusion, excessive incoherent speech, intense thirst, and fainting, it quickly destroys the vital breaths. (36)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: Then, diseases arise in one's own tongue, ears, eyes, nose, eyebrows, lips, throat, feet, hands, and head;
they occur throughout the entire body in various forms as numerous *masūrikā* eruptions. // 37 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

these eruptions caused by wind (marut) arise from powerful excess of pitta, or are observed to have the symptoms of other aggravated doshas; they are pigeon-colored, irregular, painful, black-faced, and are known as masūrikās. (38)
The essential meaning is as follows:

Masūrikā eruptions arise from the predominance of pitta; they are characterized by a determination of yellow, red, and black colors, are afflicted by fever, extreme thirst, and burning heat, ripen very quickly, and are soft, numerous, and abundant. (39)

Their essential nature is that they arise from phlegm (kapha), are dense, very thick, extremely cold, and take a long time to ripen; they are accompanied by fevers occurring in the cold season, are as red as coral, originate from an abundance of blood, and involve all the humors (doṣas) with intensely agonizing pain throughout the entire body. // 40 //
Their essential meaning is as follows:
those [vessels] which have downward-facing openings like shallow bowls, possess a central navel, and are adorned with circles like burnt offerings;
and those which are thick, excessively red or black at their mouths and wide—these are associated with fever, diarrhea, and the onset of piercing pains.
