Those afflicted by the aforementioned complications—burning sensations, tremors, excessive pain, diarrhea, extreme anorexia, flatulence, thirst, and violent hiccups—as well as by breathlessness, cough, and harshness, become incurable. (42)
Having reflected upon the meaning of the matter according to the previously mentioned characteristics, immediately after the excessive straining has ceased,
one should purge with the best *trivṛt* mixed with water of nimba and yaṣṭīmadhu, along with rising sugar. // 43 //
For the purpose of nourishment, one should feed [the patient] with *ṣaṣṭika* rice along with soups made from various pulses, accompanied by bitter and sweet vegetables;
or alternatively, one should have them drink a very cold gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with cooling substances, or one saturated with clarified butter.

A person afflicted by thirst should drink very cold water, or water that has been boiled and then cooled, at its source; likewise, one suffering from *masūrikā* (smallpox) should always sleep on a bed covered with the leaves of the rising plantain tree. 45.
The essential meaning is this:
when [the patient] is afflicted by the heat arising from that [fever], one should pierce the veins and let out the blood.
One should apply a plaster made of blue lotuses, red lotuses, and filaments, along with sandalwood and the sprouts of the *niba* tree.
The essential meaning is this:

one should apply a plaster made from the sprouts and roots of the *kiṃśuka*, *śālmalī*, and sugarcane trees, ground with milk, to ward off heat and to alleviate its pain; likewise, other sweet substances may be used for the same purpose.
The essential meaning is that one should apply a paste made of śaivala, uśīra, kaśeru, kāśa, excellent kuśa grass, and the juice of sugarcanes.

By these, cases of smallpox (masūrikā) and those born of poison are treated; specifically, for the latter, one should use a collection of anti-venomous medicines according to the specific type of poison.
According to the variant reading "vidvān," the meaning is as follows:
one should drink the water boiled with liquorice, bael fruit, sandalwood, and water, along with sugar.
With *masūrī*, grapes, *harītakī*, *amṛtā*, *paṭola*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and *ghana* (musta); // 49 //

One who knows the specifics should always drink a decoction boiled with *aruṣkara*, *āmra*, *ambu*, *sadhānyā*, and *rohiṇī*, or a cold infusion (śītakaṣāya) of these, mixed with sugar and sugarcane juice, which destroys eruptions and *masūrikā*.
Regarding the meaning of the verse:

When the *masūrikā* eruptions are ripening, the physician should apply a plaster for those arising from *vāta* and *kapha*, prepared with all the drugs of the *māṃsī* group; likewise, another [plaster] may be made with oils and clarified butter (*ājya*) processed with the same ingredients. (51)
The meaning of the verse:

At the time of ripening, having administered light and sour food so that it has reached full maturity, the physician should, in this case, pierce it with sharp, auspicious needles and irrigate it with oil from the *sūcaka* plant. (52)
The essential meaning is as follows:
even when they are afflicted by the ripening of their maturation like a festering wound, one should treat them like a traumatic ulcer or erysipelas;
being constantly accompanied by discharge, one should repeatedly apply compresses of mung beans and barley. // 53 //
The wise practitioner, having scattered fine ash or dissolved powder [over the seeds], should thoroughly dry them;
should they ever be eaten by emerging worms, he should treat them with groups of vermifuge medicines. (54)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: one should continuously fan [the patient] from all sides with the tender leaves of the Aśoka, Nimba, Āmra, and Kadamba trees;
or else, one should burn fine incense made from molasses, Sarja-resin, Guggulu, Dhyāmaka, Kuṣṭha, and Sandalwood. // 55 //

The meaning of the passage is as follows: Having washed [the vessel] with water and finely ground sesame seeds, the knower of the scriptures [should do so] for the sake of thoroughly pacifying its great heat. (56)
The essential meaning is this:

he should feed him only a single meal at a time, following a light dietary regimen, using soups and stews made from excellent lentils, mung beans, and *pravarāḍhakī* pulses, enriched with ghee and acidified with fruits. (57)
The essential meaning is this:
having properly applied the treatment for the ulcer, one should also treat the complications with appropriate remedies;
and one should have the patient lie upon a bed smeared with ghee and covered with fine skins or the leaves of the lotus and water-lily. (58)
The essential meaning is as follows:
even in cases with swelling and inflammation, one should apply the procedure as for a swelling and bandage it with leaves and tubes;
once it has suppurated, the wise physician should quickly incise it and treat it like a sinus ulcer as previously described. (59)
The meaning of the passage is: one should always smear it with trees and creepers that are cool and fragrant, along with ghee and sugar.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

One should apply an ointment made of *kapittha*, *śāli* rice, unbroken grains, and water from young trees, along with the leaves of *kalāya*, *kāleyaka*, and *mallikā*, rubbed together with milk, sesame seeds, and sandalwood, mixed with cow's ghee. (61)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: One who knows the mantras and tantras should ward off all diseases arising from great calamities by means of mantras and rituals;
one should worship the two lotus-feet of the Jina with primary substances, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and sandalwood paste. (62)
The essential meaning is this:

swellings, leprosy, fever, eye diseases, as well as complications arising from infectious contagion, and smallpox—these quickly pass from one person to another through contact with their limbs, living together, or sharing food and drink. (63)
The essential meaning is as follows:
Then, protected by the syllables of the *sumatra* mantra, the physician himself shall ward off the hosts of death-bringing spirits;
having paid homage to the Gurus and the Lords of Jinas and others, he should accomplish his purpose through the application of the most excellent mantras. // 64 //
The essential meaning is this:

the physician should apply the Bhūtatantra, Viṣatantra, and Mantravidyā along with their corresponding medicines for men afflicted by spirits or those distressed by poison, according to the specific characteristics of their appearance and symptoms. (65)

The *vyaṃtara* spirits dwell constantly upon the earth and afflict men according to their own will, whether out of anger born from enmity in previous births, for the sake of sport, or with the intent to kill. (66)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

In that place where they do not constantly worship the five kinds of true gurus with flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings; where the sinful follow the wealth and wives of others; and where they eat while disregarding the one who is worthy of honor—[that place is devoid of merit]. 67.

But those who dwell in dilapidated or empty houses, avoiding the giving of alms-bowls, offerings, and begging, and who eat meat and drink honey-wine and liquor—into them the enraged great grahas enter. (68)
The meaning of the verse is this:
those planets overcome children here who have been repeatedly threatened and beaten in many ways, terrified, and raised in impure or empty houses. (69)

I shall describe those sons who possess their own characteristic forms: those whose conduct is devoid of purity, who are inauspicious, whose sons are overwhelmed by the faults of their mothers, and who are resorted to by excessive kinnaras and other such beings. (70)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

That infant, whose gaze is fixed and whose limbs are supple, who possesses a fragrant scent and whose single eyelashes quiver upon his curved face; whose eyes are moist with flowing milk and whose complexion has the luster of a clenched fist—[such a child is long-lived]. (71)
The essential meaning,
summarized in its many forms, is that one should treat the child with the conduct of a prince;
a wise physician should treat a child afflicted by Kinnaras with red garlands and sacrificial offerings.
In this case of a son seized by the Kinnara-graha, anointing and bathing are recommended. (73)
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:
one should fumigate with resin, ghee, and molasses, and bathe [the image] at night and during the day at a crossroads.
The essential meaning is as follows:

one should construct a city out of rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, and barley; one should offer oblations with honey, *kuṣṭha*, and cow’s ghee, using the names of all the Tīrthaṅkaras without exception, along with the five salutations. (75)
The essential meaning is:
one should cause the child to wear a strung garland consisting of *bhūdhara*, *śravaṇa*, *somavallikā*, *bilva*, *caṃdana*, *indravallikā*, the root of *śigru*, and *gavādanī*. (76)
The meaning of the verse:
Here, the infant, though unconscious due to the sensations [of pain], repeatedly regains consciousness with his hands and feet;
he seems to dance, emits copious amounts of feces and urine, and stretches out while yawning intensely. (77)
The terrifying seizure known as Apasmāra-Kimpuruṣa vomits foam;
one should bathe it here with water boiled with the juices of Śirīṣa and Bilva.
The essential meaning is that oil cooked with all types of fragrant substances is beneficial for massage;
this ghee, prepared with milk-trees and sweet drugs and combined with milk, should be administered as a drink. // 79 //
The essential meaning is this:

one should fumigate even a child afflicted by a *graha* with the hair, body-hair, and nails of a bull or a human, combined with the dung of an elephant, a vulture, and an owl, and soaked in clarified butter. 80.
The meaning of the verse is as follows: Then, one should bathe the child at a crossroads and cause an offering (bali) to be given here at a banyan tree;
furthermore, he should hold a female monkey along with a hen and an egg, together with a *biṃba* creeper. // 81 //

This child, whose bodily humors are accompanied by foul odors and many ulcers, who suffers from the bursting, harsh ripening, and burning of boils, and whose limbs are withered— he is terrified on all sides by the affliction of the Garuḍa-graha.
The essential meaning is as follows:

one should bathe [the patient] with water cooled after being boiled with mango, neem, plantain, wood-apple, and rose-apple; furthermore, an ointment made from oil cooked with those same ingredients is also recommended. (83)
The essential meaning is this:

whatever treatment has been prescribed for wounds, whatever ghee is mentioned in the section on "Puruṣa," and whatever protection, fumigation, and so forth are described, that is beneficial for an infant afflicted by a bird-omen. 84.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

[One should avoid] a person suffering from jaundice, whose face is extremely red, who has yellow urine and severe fever, or one with a dark-complexioned body, or another afflicted by disease, whose nose and ears are repeatedly impaired. (85)
The essential meaning is this:

for that child afflicted by the malignant planetary influence (graha) of Bhrukuṭī, who belongs to the lineage of the Sugandharva, [one should treat him] with preparations made from the roots of Aśvagandhā, Śr̥ṅgī, and Punarnavā, combined with the substance known as Sāri. (86)
One should rub [the child] with all the best medicinal oils and have the infant drink matured ghee. // 87 //
The meaning of the verse: Furthermore, one should always fumigate during the two twilights with vulture and owl excrement mixed with clarified butter.
One should cause the child to wear the bark of the *varuṇa* and *nimba* trees, which wards off the *revatī* graha. 88.
The meaning of the verse is that there will be a child seized by the Pūtanā spirit, who possesses an excessive stench like that of a crow. // 89 //
The meaning of the ritual:
one should sprinkle [the plant] with the decoctions of *pāribhadra*, *varaṇa*, *arka*, *nīlikā*, and *āsphota*. // 90 //
The essential meaning is that one should apply an ointment made from kuṣṭha, sarjarasa, tāla, ugragandhā, and other ingredients cooked with sesame oil;
furthermore, one should have the child drink ghee prepared with the eight purgative drugs, yaṣṭikā, and tugākṣīrī. (91)
The essential meaning is that one who knows the ritual procedure should always bathe even an infant with water from the remnants of his meal,
in an empty house, in a secluded place not crowded by people, or near a mountain peak.
The best of physicians. // 92 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

At both twilights, one should fumigate the child with sandalwood, agallochum, tamāla leaves, tālīsa, kuṣṭha, and khadira, combined with ghee, as well as with hair, body hair, nails, and human bone. (93)
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:
one should carry variegated seeds, white mustard, *iṅgudī* seeds, and *kākavallikā*;
and one should always place an offering of well-prepared *kṛsara* (rice and sesame) in the middle of the *utkurūṭa* for the sake of the child. 94.
What meaning is there in this?
A child who has been tormented by these [beasts], whose body is foul with the stench of fat and marrow, and whose complexion and voice are lost. (95)
Having examined that [child] afflicted by the diseases of Pūtanās and the fierce seizing spirits (grahas) as previously described,
one should bathe him repeatedly with water boiled with the leaves of bitter trees and consecrated many times with mantras.
The essential meaning is:
one should apply a plaster made from kuṣṭha, sarjarasa, tāla, kāśa, parasa, sauvīra, and oil extracted from sesame seeds;
or one should have the patient drink ghee cooked with pippalī, dvika, viśiṣṭa, and the mṛṣṭa group of drugs. // 97 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
one should fumigate [the child] well with hair, chicken droppings, skin, and snake slough mixed with clarified butter;
furthermore, one should always wear a hen and a *biṃba* creeper around the neck of the infant.
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:
one should constantly present offerings such as water-libations, edible foods, and abundant meals, and worship [the deity] well;
furthermore, one should bathe the child within the house in a city made radiant by the application of pigments.
The essential meaning is as follows:

with his body trembling from the cold, the child weeps day and night; he sleeps huddled up, suffers from diarrhea accompanied by gurgling sounds, emits a foul-smelling discharge, and becomes afflicted by the winter chill. (100)
The essential meaning is this:

one should always apply a plaster made from sesame oil cooked with water boiled with *kapi*, *thasa*, *rasā*, *āmra*, *bilva*, and *bhallātaka*, along with the group of urines (*mūtravarga*), *suradāru*, and all the fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*). // 101 //
The meaning of the verse:
One should cause the infant to drink daily ghee cooked with water thoroughly boiled with the roots of *rohiṇī*, *khadira*, *sarja*, *nimba*, *bhūrja*, and *arjuna*, along with buffalo milk. 102.
Having thoroughly fumigated the child here with incense, he should hold him while accompanied by the sweet resonance of a *bimba* fruit and *guñjā* berries. // 103 //
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:

one should honor the child near a body of water with offerings such as food accompanied by mung-bean soup; furthermore, the knower of mantras should bathe the child according to the rules with water that has been thoroughly cooked and consecrated with mantras. // 104 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

A child with a very beautiful face, who eats excessively and has prominent veins, suffers from wasting; though his hands and feet are like tender sprouts, he smells of urine and is afflicted by a Piśāca spirit. (105)
The essential meaning is this:
having sprinkled the child with water from the Kubera-eye (Tagara), Arka-vaṃśa, Gandharvahasta, Bilva, and Vāri, one should apply matured oil mixed with wind-dispelling medicinal herbs. 106.
The essential meaning is:
one should have the child drink well-refined ghee that has been cooked with the milk of a cow whose calf is eight months old;
furthermore, one should constantly fumigate the child with kuṣṭha and sarja resin. // 107 //
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:

one should wear amulets fashioned from the feathers of a blue jay, a vulture, and a peacock, and from the skin of a snake; furthermore, one should provide a strengthening food that restores the complexion and cause the child to be bathed in the middle of a cow-pen. 108.
The meaning of the symptoms is as follows:
the child vomits froth, yawns, looks upward with agitation, and cries; even though he has meat in his mouth, he suffers from a high fever, as if seized by the Mahājvara-Atirudrākṣa spirit. 109.
The meaning of the verse is:
[One should prepare a paste] with nyagrodha, nimba, ahimsra, ambuda, ugragandha, priyangu, sarala, and shatahva. // 110 //
An ointment for the infant should consist of cooked oil mixed with sour gruel, sour curds, and fresh butter;
likewise, one should cook ghee with well-purified medicines that cure wind diseases, combined with milk.
The meaning of the verse: One should cause the child to wear *harītakī*, white mustard seeds, *vacā*, and *jaṭā*.
Here, one should worship the child at the sacred tree with garlands, auspicious foods, sesame seeds, and rice. 112.
The meaning of the passage is: A wise person should bathe the infant, who is afflicted by demons, near a milk-tree;
furthermore, one should always protect him with the guardians who are the specific deities of the Jaina teaching. 113.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

The Vyantaras and those dwelling in palaces (Bhavanavāsins), characterized by eightfold splendor, protect a child afflicted by inauspicious planets when their minds are satisfied by offerings that are clear and well-prepared. (114)

The essential meaning is this: where the best of men have their bodies consecrated by the true mantra of the five supreme beings (pañcaparameṣṭhin), planetary afflictions, calamities, diseases, fire, poison, weapons, and disturbances do not harm them. (115)
The essential meaning is this:

the hosts of Vyantaras and Uragas dwell constantly among human beings, manifesting through their supernatural transformations; they are perceived by their own characteristic marks and are divided into eight or ten classes. // 116 //
The meaning of the passage is this:
the *kiṃnaras* who are their attendants enter into humans by means of illusion—those who dwell in ruined and empty houses, who are impure, unprotected, subject to decay, and unrighteous. (117)
Therefore, men take refuge in those [deities] who assume their forms, dress, and ornaments. (118)
A man who is wise, exceedingly devoted to his guru and the gods, intent on perfumes and flowers, well-nourished,
with bright and unblinking eyes, does not even sleep when afflicted by the gods. // 119 //
The meaning of the verse is: In this world, he who reviles his gurus and deities, who is himself crooked-eyed, fearless, and full of pride;
who is excessively harsh in his sweat (or perspiration) and never finds satisfaction—such a man is afflicted by the asuras. 120.

The meaning of the state is that he, being joyful, sports here in delightful palace-towers, lofty mountains, and sandy banks; and he desires the fragrant garlands of flowers cherished by the Gandharvas, as does a man favored by the Gandharvas. 121.
The essential meaning is as follows:

One with a copper-colored face, body, feet, and eyes, who moves swiftly yet possesses an exceedingly steady nature, is a seeker of boons and a great radiance; such a person shall always be free from the afflictions caused by yakṣas. (122)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

A man who is greedy for milk-rice, sugarcane, molasses, and meat, and who is afflicted by wicked spirits and ancestors, will satisfy his ancestors through offerings of water, food, and other gifts, yet he will also offer even water [in a manner that fails to reach them]. (123)
The meaning of the verse is:

A man who is fond of meat, wine, and blood, who is exceedingly brave, extremely cruel at heart, devoid of even a modicum of shame, very powerful, and a night-stalker (niśācara), becomes a Rākṣasa afflicted by the disease of swelling (śopha). // 124 //
The meaning of the sign is that he will be greyish, extremely harsh, rough-voiced, habitually lacking in cleanliness, and prone to incoherent chatter.
A man who is greedy for dwelling in a dilapidated empty house will be surrounded by piśācas. // 125 //
The meaning of this is as follows:
He who crawls upon the surface of the earth like a snake licks even his own lips with his tongue;
when oppressed here, he becomes angry, agitated by the seizing of a serpent, though desiring only to drink milk and eat rice-pudding. (126)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: those gods, who attend upon the Asuras, roam about during the two twilights on the full moon day;
they generally do so on the eighth day, especially when accompanied by Gandharvas, servants, and sub-servants possessing the aforementioned qualities.
Yakṣas quickly strike down those who follow each step during the fortnight known as Kṛṣṇa;
at night, Rākṣasas manifest and cause fear, while Piśācas enter into the bodies of men during the day. 127.
Having realized this, he himself became one possessed of qualities such as truthfulness, compassion, and self-restraint, and was devoted to the Omniscient One.
Let the physician accomplish what is to be accomplished through the application of medicines possessing the power of his own mantras;
for the *knūra* grahas are said to be more painful, while the *bālagraha*s are indeed difficult to cure. (128)
The essential meaning is this:

those planets, possessing wondrous and divine forms and assuming various specific shapes and guises, enter human bodies; being inconceivable, they exercise authority through their own power out of anger. 129.
The essential meaning is this:
one should subdue them through specific forms of fierce austerity, along with meditations, mantras, medicinal herbs, and perfected yogic applications.
Thus do the virtuous speak for the sake of pacifying those innumerable great grahas. (130)
The essential meaning is this:

he whose self has been consecrated by his own mantras— mantras more potent than the best spells of physicians— is one who dwells in the fragrance of self-restraint, observances, self-control, rising truth, and purity.
One should accomplish those known as the planets with offerings of cooked food, wine, oblations, and incense.
The essential meaning is as follows: *amṛtā*, *kaṭukā*, *tuṃbī*, *bimba*, *niṃba*, and *indravāruṇī*.
[This is prepared] with the three pungents (trikaṭuka) joined with all-pungent fragrances, along with elakākṣī, white mountain-variety karṇī, bhūtakeśī, and the roots of arka. // 132 //
With *tālī*, *tamāla*, *sāla*, *palāśa*, *pārī*,
*bhadra*, *iṅgudī*, *madhuka*, and pairs of *sāra* and *karañja* trees;
With fragrant stones, realgar, mica, black mustard seeds, and so forth; and with the excrement of tigresses, Arka, lions, wolves, porcupines, and cats. // 133 //
With equal parts of fangs, horns, and dung.
In this case, ghee and oil cooked with the well-ground pastes and decoctions of the eight excellent types of urine should be employed. // 134 //
The meaning of the term is "ointment" (*abhyañjana*); there is an alternative reading, *vṛṣa*. [It refers to] eye-salve, collyrium, and drinks.
They say that even old ghee is "paripakva" (fully matured).
The bath is performed with water prepared by boiling medicinal herbs;
likewise, incense and ointment are applied using powders and pastes.

The essential meaning is as follows: by means of all those aforementioned excellent medicines, which are of a similar nature yet consist of things that are distasteful, loathsome, and exceedingly foul-smelling; |||
The physician shall quickly conquer all mental disorders without exception. // 136 //
The essential meaning [is extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (137)
The essential meaning is [the praise of] the one whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the gods, humans, and serpents, the bestower of boons.
Having paid homage to the Lord of Jinas, who is white as the moon and the remover of poison, this single discourse concerning the subject matter of the *Viṣamaviṣādhikāra* is now composed. // 1 //

The meaning of the passage is: A king [should appoint] a physician who is an expert in all mantras, poisons, and tantras, who is of noble birth, free from greed, skillful, and whose wealth is the supreme Dharma.
Having duly performed this [rite], which is purified by the fourfold examination (caturupadhāviśuddha) and endowed with wealth and kinsmen, he [the king] protected his own person. // 2 //
And that person, the meaning of whose horoscope is thus, shall exercise supreme sovereignty, enjoying happiness for a very long time,
bringing about the destruction of all enemy kings throughout the entire circle of the great earth.
Having removed the various afflictions caused by poisons produced by the entire circle of enemies, both one's own and others', through his great-souled nature. // 3 //
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is as follows:
even a wise physician who knows the clear characteristics of those [substances],
and who has tested all his people in well-prepared kitchens and similar places;
Having observed [the disciple] through speech, actions, and gestures, one should act without delay. // 4 //
The meaning of the state [of mind] is this:
he laughs, he speaks, he draws much upon the ground here,
and with a distracted mind, he cuts grass and wood without cause.
Terrified with fear, he looks back at his own person here; he does not utter a reply, his face bereft of its natural luster.
Having removed all the food that was contaminated with poison, he cast it away.
Having fully understood [reality] through the characteristics of the non-erroneous, one should strive for a long time. // 6 //
I shall explain the meaning according to the sequence for those who have approached the true distinctions,
regarding the various groups of diverse and excellent foods provided for others.
And then [he taught] the procedure for the various types of poison and the onset of their toxic effects.
The essential meaning is that here many rows of crows go toward death.
The fire-god, having been granted the command, danced most intensely before him.
It has the blue color of a peacock's throat and is filled with extremely unbearable smoke. // 8 //
The essential meaning is that he wanders about, even though there is excessive pain in his nose and heart.
Food held in the hand quickly causes the nails to break and produces a burning sensation;
once it has entered the mouth, it makes the tongue painful as if it were a stone.
The essential meaning is that [excessive] emesis causes distress in the heart, excessive delusion, burning sensations,
and pain; while excessive purgation causes stupor and excessive distension.
It causes the poison to enter the stomach and brings about agitation of the sense faculties;
I shall now describe the characteristics of its movement through the fluids according to the traditional scriptures.
The essential meaning is that among substances free from poison, there occurs a very variegated and diverse appearance,
possessing excellent characteristics and accompanied by various bubbles and froth.
And furthermore, in the broth of boiled green gram, black gram,
and pigeon pea, there was [a face] fashioned with many dark lines by a most beautiful streak.
The essential meaning is this:
even poison, when mixed with wine and water by a rising dark cloud,
assumes its own characteristic through the agitated lines [of the waves].
Likewise, curd that has acquired a slight yellow tint along with its white luster, or that which is beautifully copper-colored when placed in milk or buttermilk, [is auspicious]. // 12 //
Furthermore, the essential meaning is this: here, one does not perceive two distinct reflections fallen upon those liquids, nor does one see them as anything other than modified forms.
And it would soon become like food twice served and left stale. // 13 //
The meaning of the passage is:
if the tooth-stick is provided with a tip [that is too large] and possesses unbroken or frayed fibers,
then facial swelling and pain from severe digestive distress will occur.
Just as that [was the case], so too for men, even when there is a collection of face-powders and cosmetics,
eruptions such as smallpox break out despite the application of ointments.
The essential meaning is this:

just as in the external world there are swellings and pains caused by excellent substances suitable for all parts of the body, so too here [in the internal realm] there are swellings and pains caused by manifest kaṣāya, water, clothing, and so forth.
Through the poison of the garland, they arise in the openings of the vital channels of men. // 15 //
The essential meaning here is to be discerned by those who know the defining characteristics, like a garland upon a crown, a head, strength, writing, or a multitude.
There may be cracking of the skin, excessive swelling, heaviness in the feet, and pain; furthermore, footwear and other such items may become infused with poison and thus cause harm. // 16 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
the discharge of semen and phlegm, as well as the arising of boils and swellings in one's own bodily constituents (dhātus), occur here in the pair of thighs, the anus, the scrotum, and the penis.
In the openings of cavities, there is movement through the nose, superior incense, poison, and blood. // 17 //
The meaning is that even powerful blindness becomes cured by the application of collyrium rich in medicinal herbs.
They destroy even their own enemies, for they become [as such] by taking refuge in that [virtue]. // 18 //

The meaning is that the corruption of the sense organs occurs through the application of smoke; for while the application of collyrium produces disorder only in the eyes and not in the other sense organs, it is likewise stated in another treatise:
When the medicinal smoke reaches the nasal passages, the symptoms are a distortion of the senses;
having observed this, there occurs at that very moment a state of aversion toward looking [at objects],
as if one were a cakora bird.
And likewise, the blue bird dies.
Again, the jīvinī-jīvaka scratches the earth; the flock of spotted deer cries out, and the noble peacock suddenly calls. (19)
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is the state of being poisonous in the case of many substances mixed with poison,
characterized by intense series of burning sensations, tearing pains, and swellings.
Having identified the poison, one should eliminate it by means of nasal drops, eye-salves, and drinks combined with emetics and purgatives. // 20 //
The meaning of the situation is this:
having bound poison to the right hand of the king,
a female mouse destroys it.
And even the food of the aged has gone [to waste] here.
Desirous of protecting his heart in this world,
he constantly drank the juice of the *śimbi* plant, extremely cold and mixed with ghee and molasses.
Poison is tested even by means of deer and birds; therefore, kings should keep such creatures near their kitchens.
(There is a variant reading *mudrikām*. According to this reading, [the ring] is consecrated with various medicinal herbs and is a destroyer of obstacles.
One should wear a ring set with precious and semi-precious gems; this is because the word "paribaṃdhya" (having bound) occurs in the verse.
Since the reading "mūṣikā" also occurs in other texts, it has been retained;
"cāṃtagatam" is an alternative reading.
The essential meaning is as follows: having licked a preparation of indralatā combined with madhuka, sugar, and ativiṣā,
and furthermore, ghee processed with the powder of the three pungents (trikaṭu).
The king, free from suspicion, partakes with delight of even prepared poison along with flavorful food and drink, and thus remains at ease.
The essential meaning:
Now, the entire treatment for the various types of poisons, along with the network of diverse classifications, has been compiled from the traditional scriptures.

I shall proclaim here for the sake of the wise that which has been declared through a few true paths by those whose wealth of speech is meager, yet who have well understood the full extent of reality.
The essential meaning is this:

everything that exists here in the world is said to be of three kinds—those endowed with their own qualities, those that nourish, and those that destroy; there is nothing other than these two [categories].
The entire [world] is the cause of suffering; therefore, that which nourishes it is detrimental to the self. // 24 //
The essential meaning is this:
a heap of poison, honey, wine, meat, and other such things that cause extreme evil becomes a destroyer of existence;
yet that very thing [when transformed] becomes a destroyer of cyclic existence.
On this earth, those who perform neither [of these] would become groups of non-eaters. // 25 //
The essential meaning is this:
even one whose conduct is endowed with right conduct and discipline, if his mind is ruined,
wanders about, speaks everything, and acts both on what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Under the sway of desire, a man takes pleasure in his sisters, daughters, and mothers; intoxicated by liquor, he always carries off what is pure as if it were impure. (26)
Now, the drinking of intoxicants here causes most wicked transformations; it is the sole abode of exceedingly harsh diseases and brings about the contempt of men.
It destroys the purpose of both states of existence and is the cause of misfortune. // 27 //
When those difficult points have been stated by me according to the scriptures,
they are set forth individually, together with their defining characteristics and qualities.
The threefold conceptualization—arising from the forest-born, the mobile, and the artificial—is here entirely subsumed by these words for the sake of total benefit. (28)
The meaning of the essential nature here is stable; it is considered to be tenfold,
consisting of excellent, pure roots, shoots, beautiful flowers, and abundant fruits.
With the nectar-like words of Rādhikā and various groups of parrots described [by her], // 29 //
The meaning of the state [of existence] is always like poison from its very beginning, right down to its pure root.
Poison from *viṣadalikā* along with *karaṃbha*, as well as leaf-poison; and poison from fruits, leaves, and fine flowers such as the golden gourd (*kanakasatuṃbikā*) and others. // 30 //

The meaning of the substances here is as follows: *viṣa* (aconite), *sāra* (heartwood), *niryāsa* (resin), *carma* (leather), *cilla* (a type of bird), *dinakara* (mango), *tilvaka*, *snuhi*, and the group [of plants] with excessive latex are poisonous.

The poisons derived from extensive minerals, such as *jalaharītāla*, *gandhaka*, and *śilā*, will be described individually; thereafter, the extremely dangerous *kanda* poisons will be explained. (31)
The meaning is "bhāvārtha";
there is a variant reading "billā," and even the qualities of exhaling, yawning, and convulsing arise from leaf-poison.
From the poison of flowers, there occurs heaviness of the abdomen, delusion, and vomiting;
from the poison of fruits, there is loss of appetite accompanied by swelling and a burning sensation in the scrotum.
The meaning of the symptoms is as follows:
due to the application of medicinal pastes containing bark, *tvak*, *malasāra*, and various decoctions,
there occurs pain in the head, a lack of clarity in vision that is not excessively harsh, and a predominance of phlegm (*kapha*).
Excessive salivation, frothing at the mouth,
vomiting, and excessive purging constitute the specific symptoms here for all types of milk-poisoning.
The essential meaning is that [this applies] to all poisons derived from curd, sour gruel, and minerals for human beings.
Now, those aforementioned poisons are uneven;
they violently destroy a person suddenly and at an untimely hour. (34)
The essential meaning: I shall explain the poisons born from bulbs, which are uneven in their effects, by means of their own specific characteristics,
beginning with the Kālakūṭa poison.
With a superior mustard seed known as Kardama, which rises from the hip. // 35 //
There is the great poison *puṇḍarīka* combined with *vatsanābha* and *nijamūlaka*, and there may also be another, the poison named *hālāhala*, accompanied by *mustā*. (36)
Having understood even the most terrible and fierce poison of the Rāṭaka snake through the power of the Hero’s teaching, // 37 //
Therein, having identified the thirteenfold poison by its characteristic signs, one should treat it;
loss of sensation, excessive trembling, and rising [of symptoms]—this is the characteristic of *kālakūṭa* poison. (38)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Leaping up, wandering about, laughing excessively, and biting others with his formidable claws, he has released himself from the torment of dysentery, which had been drinking away his two eyes in the mire. (39)
The essential meaning is that by means of mustard seed, disorders of excessive wind (vāta), flatulence, colic, and pustules may arise.
One whose eyes, excrement, and urine are yellow, and who likewise has a neck that is extremely motionless, [is one who will die]. // 40 //
The essential meaning is:

by *mūlaka* there is excessive vomiting, hiccups, emaciation of the body, and squinting eyes; by *puṇḍarīka* poison there is redness of the eyes and great abdominal enlargement; and by *ativiṣa* [the same occurs]. (41)
The essential meaning is this:

here, due to the defect of a potent poison, there may arise an intense pain even within the heart at the site of the wound; furthermore, there may occur an increase in swelling of the calves, thighs, abdomen, and other parts, resulting from extensive tissue destruction. (42)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

A man whose limbs are paralyzed, excessively heavy, and trembling, and whose body is struck by *mustā*, becomes one who breathes while wandering about and faints due to *hālāhala* poison, with all his movements ceased. (43)
Tell me, by whom was Bhavārtha carried off—his body overcome by extreme suffering, his sight distracted and stolen away by Vairāṭaka? // 44 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Those poisons possessing the characteristics already described—extremely intense, endowed with fierce potency, and harmful—when combined with their ten qualities and present in excess, kill a mortal before long. (45)
The essential meaning is as follows:
This poison is dry, hot, extremely sharp, rapidly pervasive, causing suppuration, light, intensely agitating, subtle, and clear; endowed with these ten qualities, it kills swiftly. (46)
Its essential meaning is as follows:
by its dryness it agitates the wind (vāyu) here, and by its heat it likewise provokes the bile (pitta) and the blood;
due to its subtlety it pervades the entire body, and because of its sharpness it pierces the limbs and the vital organs (marmas).
The essential meaning is this:

by virtue of its pervasive nature, it quickly reaches the entire body here; by virtue of its agency, it swiftly destroys [impurities]; and by virtue of its quality of drawing out those [impurities], it enters even the excessive *dhātus*, shaking them as well due to its clarity. // 48 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows: It is not possible to stop this [world] here by means of leaping and such methods, because its nature is exceedingly matured.
Even if it causes distress, this world, when purified, will quickly pacify even fierce poison.
The essential meaning is as follows: that poison which has become decayed and worn out, shattered by fire, lightning strikes, excessive heat, frost, or rain,
and struck by potent anti-venoms, becomes known as *dūṣīviṣa*.
The essential meaning is that this other [type], atisāra caused by pride, produces dūṣīviṣa and abdominal enlargement. // 51 //
It also produces other types of flatulence, as well as various kinds of severe disorders that cause a great depletion of the bodily humors.
Now the meaning of the state of the intense poison-velocity of the immobile [poison] is described regarding the specific first impulse:
the tongue becomes stiff and black, there is fear, fainting, pain in the heart, and vertigo. (53)
The meaning of the state [of symptoms] is as follows:

trembling, pain in the throat, intense burning, perspiration, yawning, thirst, and abdominal colic—these are produced by the second impulse of the poison; moreover, there is also a powerful internal groaning. (54)
The essential meaning is:

abdominal colic, dryness of the throat and palate, swelling, yellowness, and a pair of eyes affected by darkness—these arise from the specific third stage of the poison-impulse in all poisons derived from *kanda* tubers. (55)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: vomiting, moaning, abdominal pain, hiccups, and extreme heaviness of the head—
these are the disorders caused by the fourth stage of the poison's onset in living beings due to an extremely potent poison.
The essential meaning is that in the fifth stage of the onset,
there is an excessive discharge of phlegm with a change in color;
indeed, in the sixth stage, the diarrhea caused by all the humors in a disordered state is accompanied by colic and delusion.
The meaning of the state [of the poison] during the seventh stage of its velocity is: the breaking of the joints beyond the movement of the shoulders and the obstruction of the flow of breath.
Having observed that, one who knows the methods for counteracting the effects of poison should immediately pacify the fierce venom. (58)
The meaning of the verse:
One should cause the person afflicted by the poison of the first impulse to vomit after sprinkling his body with cold water;
one should have him drink the medicine mixed with ghee, and in both cases, one should purge him from both ends. 59.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Nasal medication, collyrium, and the drinking of antidotes are for the specific third stage of poison-impulse; all the aforementioned antidotes, excluding ghee, should be employed during the fourth stage of impulse as described.

The meaning of the fifth [digit] is sweet medicine; furthermore, in the sixth, one should apply remedies accompanied by decoctions, as well as treatments for dysentery, nasal drops, collyrium, and very potent [medicines]. (61)
The essential meaning is:
one should apply sharp collyrium or even a nasal squeeze (avapīḍa) to the head, or [make] a "crow's foot" mark;
on the seventh day, when the excessive force produced by the poison has subsided, all other measures for neutralizing the poison should be employed.
The essential meaning is that ghee cooked with *pīlu*, *amṛtalatā*, and *śirīṣa* quickly removes poison. (63)
The meaning of the verse is:
with priyaṅgu, viḍaṅga, sunīlī, sārivā, tagara, and pūtikarañja. (64)
Having consumed this potent poison-dispelling cooked ghee, one conquers poisons in this world;
one should employ it for humans through drinking, nasal drops, collyrium, and external applications, using that excellent clarified butter.
And the meaning of the ritual is as follows: having finely powdered sandalwood, ururucaka, amṛtavalī, and cardamom, [one should mix them] with white cow's ghee. // 66 //
It neutralizes all disorders such as difficult poisons, irregular fevers, burning sensations, thirst, and severe fevers.
The meaning of the verse:
Furthermore, the poison known as *jaṅgama* (mobile) is said to be extremely terrible and is divided into sixteen types:
[the venom of] the gaze, the breath, the sharp fangs, the saliva, the urine, the excrement, the semen, and the nails. (68)
Wind, bile, the anus, one's own bones, touch,
stinging insects, flies, and corpses— these sixteen manifest poisons are inauspicious and take away the lives of living beings. (69)
"Bhāvārthaḥ sitaḥ" is an alternative reading.
Those serpents of divine form, possessing the intense venom of their gaze and hissing breaths, have been born upon this earth.
There were fanged creatures— horses, donkeys, monkeys, and vicious dogs— abounding in fierce and potent venom from their teeth.
The meaning of the term *bhāva* refers to those many groups of embodied beings well-known as quadrupeds, such as porpoises and crocodiles;
as well as those with rows of teeth, sharp claws, fierce venom, and snakes, including the *abheka*, the *varga*, the *gṛha-kokila*, and others. (71)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: There are countless swarms of crawling creatures, rich with the intense venom of urine, feces, and bites;
there are various kinds of mice whose semen is poison, and scorpions fierce with their poisonous sting. (72)
The essential meaning is as follows:

those with variegated bodies and many legs—such as gadflies, mosquitoes, wind-creatures, and fierce scorpions—as well as stinging insects, various kinds of worms, and leeches, kill by means of the sharp venom from their mouths. (73)
The essential meaning is that these have been declared to be poisonous substances, and their bile as well would be a potent poison. // 74 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows: flies, gadflies, bees, and so forth, possess intense venom located in their stings;
likewise, the bodies of those inconceivable many insects are themselves poisons in the form of corpses. (75)
The essential meaning is this:

even among mobile poisons, there are ten varieties characterized by specific features and qualities; these, along with all other poisons originating from the entire body, aggravate the humors (doṣas) and possess excessive toxicity. (76)
The essential meaning therein is as follows:
among the mobile poisons, the extremely virulent serpent species here are of five kinds—those with hoods, those with many circles, and those whose bodies are adorned with stripes. (77)
Among those [snakes], those produced by a mixture [of species] have names distinguished by their transformative coloring;
they are non-venomous, resembling parrots or the moon in appearance, such as the *toyada*, *tatsamaya*, and *jāgaraka*. (78)

What need is there to speak of those human serpents who bite with their uneven, sharp, and formidable fangs, for whom the very sight is a breath of intensely virulent poison, and who can only be managed by a collection of medicinal remedies? (79)

Among those, I shall here prescribe the appropriate medical treatment—constrained by the rules regarding what is curable and incurable—for those whose symptoms are produced by their own constitutional defects through the specific force of the venom of the stinging insect. (80)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
intent on protecting her young, intoxicated with passion, and driven by the greed for a mouthful,
[the lioness] [kills] even from a touch or a kick of the foot.
Moreover, those snakes bite because they cause great suffering through their excessive anger.
The meaning is as follows; "bhayabhītavisarpā" is an alternative reading.
In this context, the bite of serpents is of three kinds: *svarpita*, *radita*, and *udvihita*.
Here, the *svarpita* bite occurs by means of one, two, three, or four venomous fang-marks. (82)
That poison, characterized by tooth-marks submerged in it and accompanied by swelling, will become uneven and extremely intense;
one should destroy that poison, along with all its residual traces from the bite, very swiftly with anti-venomous remedies. (83)
The essential meaning is this:

whatever [wound] is streaked with red, black, or white lines, or is swollen, or is otherwise [altered], that should be known as smeared with little poison; having recognized a man here who has been bitten by a highly venomous [snake], one should act with haste. (84)
The essential meaning is this:
even a man bitten by a snake, if he remains composed and possesses a wound with clear blood, and if that wound is free from swelling, it is called "devoid of poison" (nirviṣa). // 85 //
The essential meaning is this:
due to contact with that [object], which is caused by its impact, there arises this manifold [sensation] produced by the agitated wind.
The meaning of the signs is as follows:

those hooded serpents bearing umbrellas, plows, moons, excellent wheels, svastikas, and goads move swiftly; when enraged, these venomous snakes, accompanied by the wind, manifest their power before long.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
Those who move slowly on this earth, appearing like very long [serpents] variegated with many-colored circles (maṇḍalas), and who abound in fiery venom, are born here as Maṇḍalins. 88.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Those serpents on earth which are variegated like fine paintings, resplendent with their own luster, and possess shimmering brilliance, are produced by phlegm (kapha) and are designated as *vararājīmantas*. 89.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

For those who enjoy [the fruits of their karma], those [serpents] that provoke the wind (vāta) are the maṇḍalins who release much bile (pitta); while those endowed with bodies adorned by the king of life-force (jīva) produce an excessive and fierce phlegm (śleṣman). // 90 //
The essential meaning is this:

those snakes arising from the combination of two [humors], which cause the provocation of the group of two doshas, and which possess all the symptoms produced by the provocation of vata—these occur in this case of snake-bite poison. (91)
The essential meaning is this: having recognized those [poisons] manifested by me, one should purify them with appropriate medicines and mantras. // 92 //
The essential meaning:
We shall describe the disorders caused by the force of the fierce poison of the hooded snake (*darvīkara*), characterized by their preeminent symptoms.
First, the poison quickly vitiates the blood, turning it black; likewise, in the second stage, it does the same to the flesh. (93)
Heaviness of the eyes, excessive pain in the head, and similar symptoms constitute the disorder produced by the third stage of the poison's onset;
however, when it reaches the internal organs (koṣṭha), the poison quickly causes excessive salivation of phlegm, characterized as the specific fourth stage of the poison's onset.
In this fifth stage, kapha itself becomes aggravated and, having opened the channels, produces severe hiccups;
in the sixth stage, it causes a burning sensation, a gripping pain in the heart, and fainting; and when the seventh stage arises, it releases the vital breaths.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
likewise, in the case of circular poison (maṇḍalīviṣa) as well, the blood becomes vitiated by the poison from the very first stage upon being drunk;
it causes the flesh, eyes, face, and hands to turn pale, and in the second stage, it also makes the mouth bitter.
In the third stage of the poison's onset, there is thirst; in the fourth, a violent fever; in the fifth, a burning sensation;

and in the sixth and seventh stages, as the intensity of the poison increases further according to the stated sequence, there occurs the destruction of memory followed by the release of life. // 97 //
The essential meaning is that in the first stage of its onset, poison even in women vitiates the blood,
making it appear reddish and slimy.
Even if the flow of saliva is very abundant, that occurs in the third [stage]. // 98 //
In the fourth [period], it causes stiffness of the neck and severe pain in the head;
in this fifth [period], it quickly brings about an obstruction of speech.
In this context, even a drop of poison falling into the throat causes the destruction of life in the sixth stage;
in the seventh, that same effect occurs even from an abundance of phlegm.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
this poison, consisting of four hundred and fifty mātrās, when it enters its own seat (the body) with ferocity,
likewise directed by the vital wind (marut) into the other constituent elements (dhātus), itself produces seven different stages of intensity.
The meaning of this is that such poison, though endowed with its own qualities, destroys all people just like a weapon or a thunderbolt; it perishes as quickly as a horse.
Therefore, I shall speak according to my own power, following the system of the unspoken.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

For one bitten by any snake, having bound the limb above the site of the bite and tied four fingers together, one should excise the flesh and release the blood; or, having excised it elsewhere than from the site of the bite, one should cauterize it with fire or suck out the venom. (102)
The essential meaning is this:
just as all poison becomes non-poisonous through mantras, so too it cannot be remedied by medicines alone.
Having quickly provided protection for the life-force through mantras, the wise person should subsequently employ medicinal treatments. (103)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

A wise man, having released the blood from all the veins above and below the bite by means of a weapon or a ligature, should likewise, when this virulent poison has pervaded the entire body, apply [the remedy] to the five parts located at each of the five [limbs]. 104.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
when the corrupt blood has been extracted, that which is called its poison quickly attains total non-toxicity.
Afterwards, the one afflicted by poison, having been sprinkled with cold water, should drink the medicinal remedies along with curd, ghee, and milk. (105)

The meaning of the verse is as follows: In the first stage of the *darvīkara* [cobra] venom, the weapon is the surgical instrument; in the second stage, it is the extraction of blood and the administration of anti-venoms (*agada*).

In the third stage, there should be the drinking of anti-venom, nasal drops (*nasya*), and collyrium (*añjana*). In the fourth stage, even the anti-venom must be properly administered by means of emesis (*vāmana*). (106)
In the fourth, fifth, or even the sixth stage of poisoning, the wise physician should drench the body of the victim, who is afflicted by poison, with cold water;
having smeared him with applications of cooling substances, he should then purge him upward with strong [emetics].

Even in this seventh stage, the wise physician, having administered a sharp nasal drop (nasya) and collyrium (añjana), should create a small wound on the head shaped like a crow's foot; he should then apply a thick skin-graft there.
The essential meaning is this:
during the initial impulse of this [poison], one should not administer weapons [surgery] too forcefully to those adorned with [protective] circles.
Having caused him to drink a medicine mixed with ghee, one should quickly and properly induce emesis during the second stage.
In the same manner, it should be applied during the third stage of the poison's velocity; however, for the remaining stages, everything else is exactly as previously described.
Even when bitten by those with striped markings, one should first thoroughly incise the wound deeply with a sharp instrument.
In that case, having induced vomiting, the vitiated blood should be purified by means of a gourd with an internal wick for the sake of eliminating the poison;
or, one should cause the patient to drink an anti-poisonous medicine (agada) prepared with that [blood], or a gruel (vāgū) cooked with it, immediately.

One should quickly treat the remaining poisons of hooded snakes (darvīkara) with the remedies prescribed for their respective potencies, using strong purificatory therapies for the upper and lower tracts, potent nasal medications (nasya), and all other direct treatments such as sharp collyriums (añjana). // 112 //
The meaning of the passage is this:
one should recognize that a wound which has black discharge, is black in color, accompanied by burning, and where putrid flesh is falling away,
is "poisoned-pierced" (digdhaviddha)— that is, a wound in which poison has been administered by cruel means such as arrows.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

Seeing a mortal person accompanied by a dark discoloration, overcome by fainting, and with limbs afflicted by the fever of intense burning, one should know that poison has been administered there; for the black flesh in this wound is sloughing away.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: Having removed that putrid flesh which is moist and having drained the blood by means of leech applications, this patient afflicted with a wound rich in poison should be purified; one should sprinkle him with cold decoctions of milk-exuding trees.
One should wrap a cloth soaked in well-ground, poison-neutralizing cooling substances and apply it over that wound.
One should act in this same manner for a wound caused by a sharp thorn, or even when this poison has manifested directly as a pitta-type disorder.
The meaning of the verse: Equal parts of mājjiṣṭhā, madhuka, trivṛt, surataru, drākṣā, the two types of haridrā,
bhārṅgī, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, hiṅgu, and salt should all be powdered together.
This medicine has been prepared to destroy all poisons, like an enemy of serpents. // 117 //

The meaning of the passage: pāṭhā, hiṅgu, the three fruits (triphalā), the three pungents (trikaṭuka), vakra, ajamodā, agnika, rock salt (siṃdhūttha), viḍa salt, along with viḍaṅga, and sauvarcala salt— all these should be powdered.
Having placed all this mixed with cow’s ghee inside a horn, it remains there; when applied with one's whole being, it destroys all poisons whatsoever. (118)
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
sthauṇeya, suradāru, the two types of candana, the two types of śigru, guggulu, tālīsa, kuṭa, nara, kuṭaja, ugrā, arka, agni, and sauvarcala.
Having powdered kuṣṭha, satkratu, rohiṇī, and trikaṭu, and having placed them together with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) inside a cow’s horn, one shall neutralize all poison. // 119 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
Tālīsa in abundance, along with viḍaṅga, kuṣṭha, viḍa salt, and saindhava; bhārṅgī, hiṅgu, mṛgādanī, sakiṇī, pāṭhā, paṭola, and vacā.
Having ground these together with powdered long pepper, goat’s milk, ghee, and water, one should administer this antidote. // 120 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows: Mañjiṣṭhā, Madhuśigru, Śigru, Rajanī, Lākṣā, Śilāla, and Iṅgudī,
along with Pṛthvīkā, Aṃśuharā, and Reṇukā— these should be taken in equal parts, powdered, and mixed together.
If that [elixir], having been stirred with all groups of urine and all salts and placed in a horn,
should kill even a superior man, the *saṃjīvana* [remedy] would bring him back to life.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
white Aparājitā,
Karṇikāra, Kiṇihī, Śleṣmātaka, and Kaṭphala.
One should also avoid the *vyāghrī*, the *meghaninādikā*, the *bṛhatikā*, the *aṅkolanīlī*.

Having stirred [the medicine] with the juice of bitter bottle-gourd and *sacālinī* fruit and placed it in a horn, in whichever house it is kept, there shall be no snakes, nor how could there be insects or malevolent planets? 122.
The essential meaning has been declared: these formulations entirely destroy all poisons arising from wind and phlegm;
they are likewise highly effective, even for poisons originating from bile, when combined with very cooling substances.
Sugandhika, kāyastha, fruits, grapes, and the bark of lavanga will also be mentioned;
as well as śyāmā, soma-rasa, ādārī, kuravaka, bilva, amlikā, and pomegranates.
[One should offer] white aśmantaka, tāla leaves, madhuka, excellent kuṇḍalī, sandalwood, along with kunda, indīvara, sindhuvāraka, kapittha, and indrāhvā flowers.
This verse is not found in manuscript *ka*.

Drenched in all kinds of milk and ghee, mixed with equal parts of sugar, and prepared with every effort, these quickly pacify the poison of the maṇḍala, just as the ten dharmas [pacify] karma. // 124 //
The meaning of the passage is: [one should worship] the flutes, conchs, paṭaha drums, bherī drums, and mṛdaṅga drums smeared with unguents, by means of their sounds.
May they quickly render poisonless those men who have consumed poisoned nectar;
and may even the trees that cause paralysis, upon seeing his face, become deliverers through the mere touch of him day after day. (125)
The essential meaning is that it should be situated pervasively within the spokes, like a virtuous person because of its pleasant touch, or like semen.
Because their fangs are curved like fish-hooks, they are called *bhujaṅga*s; from them they extract and release a most terrible poison that provokes all the world's maladies. (126)
The essential meaning is this:
having recognized that a man has been entirely smeared with extremely hot poison released by those expert in the science of *ativisa*, one should sprinkle him with cold water.
The wise physician should quickly treat it with plasters and poultices of *ruṣṇālā* that are highly effective against poison. // 127 //
The essential meaning is this:
when the limbs are compressed by flatulence, the patient here produces stool that is fleshy and resembles the color of a palm fruit;
he constantly spits foam from his mouth, and even the digestive fire does not burn the heart of the afflicted one.
Now, having acquired the instructions from a realized master, I shall explain separately those cases of being bitten that are incurable. (128)
The meaning of the [astrological] signs is as follows:

when bitten under the well-known constellations, there is swelling at the site of the bite that is very black and excessively red; furthermore, there are four marks of the fangs upon it, appearing like dark blue blood. (129)

Elderly men overcome by the afflictions of hunger and thirst, children with emaciated limbs, those whose bodies are struck by excessive bile, heat, and fire, and those suffering from the disease of indigestion— [all these were gathered].

One should avoid those bitten by a snake whose noses have perished, whose faces are extremely distorted, whose joints are severely shattered, who suffer from stammering or loss of speech, and whose bodies have become rigid—even if the bite was on the neck. (130)
The essential meaning is this:
blood does not flow from those who have not been wounded, even by the most manifest tremors;
nor does a man experience constant horripilation when drenched with cold water.
A wick-like growth, born of phlegm, spreads incessantly from the mouth, as does blood, both upwards and downwards.
Having opened the mouth of one who is asleep or unconscious according to the prescribed method, one should avoid those bitten by snakes.
The meaning is:
these are medicines for destroying the many poisons arising from scattered foot-dwelling insects.

Having understood the threefold nature of the humors (doṣas) and the method of the path, and following the sequence of what is curable and incurable, this has been clearly explained; now, relying on the doctrine of the Great Victor (Buddha), I shall speak of it directly.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
And mortals, within the fierce dens of wild beasts, torn by the mouths, teeth, and claws of those predators,
were overwhelmed by great agony accompanied by swelling and blood arising from intense thirst.

Furthermore, other non-human beings, possessed by fierce and powerful poisons arising from wind and phlegm, and afflicted with violent insanity, bite other mortals who are even more harshly enraged. (133)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
If those bitten by venomous serpents should at some time possess qualities conducive to recovery and exhibit auspicious signs,
they perceive those very [serpents] as reflections appearing in a mirror, a lamp, sunlight, or water.
Out of an even greater fear of water than that caused by the sight of the sound and touch [of waves], they flee;
they avoid even the eight clearly visible bodies, having perceived them as particularly ominous signs of death.
The essential meaning is this:
where there are those known as "mice" (rats), fierce and manifest in many forms,
when men are struck by their teeth or nails, the vitiated blood flows from the wound.

It may produce swelling at the pericarp [of the eyes], eruptions, circular patches, glandular swellings, fainting, thirst, severe fever, and other such ailments rich in pain, arising from the three types of vitiated humors (doṣas). // 135 //
The essential meaning is this: those who have been bitten by creatures known as *daṣṭā* and *mūṣaka*, or by the *nṛpataru*, *madana*, *aṅkola*, and *kośātakī* plants,
should be properly emeticated and purged according to the sequence of their own predominant humors (*doṣa*), even if they suffer from leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) or indigo-disease (*nīlī*).

A powder made from *vyāghrī*, *śvetā*, *punarnavā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), *bṛhatī*, *siṃdhuvāra*, and *arka* should be drunk with the alkaline water of *śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, *kiṇihī*, and *kiṃśuka*. (136)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
for each part of curd, ghee, and milk, there should be four parts of decoction made from *vajrā*, *arka*, *alarka*, *gojī*, *nṛpataru*, *kuṭaja*, *vyāghrikā*, and *naktamāla*.
Ghee cooked with equal parts of the pastes of *kapittha*, *nīlī*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), *karajī*, and *rohiṇī* is an antidote to poison; it quickly pacifies the venom of rats. (137)
And other meanings of the term *bhāva*— namely those beginning with "fainting" (*saṃmūrchita*) and so forth, which arise from fire, wind, and water— are said to be of three kinds.

For those [diseases], the method of pacification according to their respective defects is proclaimed—whether they are curable or incurable—by means of medicines and other remedies that are peerless, unfailing, and capable of neutralizing all poisons. (138)

The essential meaning is as follows: in this world, when the regions of men are bitten by spiders, scorpions, fierce insects, and the like, their blood becomes afflicted by the aforementioned defects due to the mild, moderate, or intense nature of those creatures' venom.
Mandalas, swellings, pustules, and tumors with intense inflammation arise;
as well as severe diseases such as ringworm, vitiligo, itching, kiṭibha, and hard ear-niches (satkarṇikā). // 139 //
The meaning of the passage is this: by consuming insects that possess the quality of being devoid of food due to ignorance,
humans incur various diseases and many manifest, great calamities.

One should bring about their pacification through the application of excellent medicines prescribed for neutralizing *dūṣīviṣa* poisons; otherwise, it would lead to other [undesirable] results. Now I shall describe all the medicinal drugs that remove poison. (140)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: [the roots] of *arka*, *aṅkola*, *agni*, *aśvāntaka*, *ghana*, *nicula*, *pragraha*, and *aśmantaka*;
of *śleṣmātakī*, *āmalakī*, *arjuna*, *nṛpakaṭuka*, *śrīkapittha*, and *snuhī*.
Of the Māsphotā, Pāṭalī, Siṃduka, Taru, Ciri, Bilva, and Arimeda trees. // 141 //
Of *gojī*, *sarja*, *urubhūrja*, *asanatara*, *tilaka*, *plakṣa*, and *somāṃghrikā*;
of *ṭuṃṭūka*, *aśoka*, *kāśmarya*, *amarataru*, *śirīṣa*, and the two types of *ugraśigru*.
One should cook all the ashes here of uṣṇīkā, rañjaka, āruṣkara, varasāra, sarala, and the two types of palāśa, along with those of nakta and ahna, using six parts of urine as the liquid medium.

Having cooked that [substance]—filtered through a cloth made of pure white cloth soaked in its urine—according to the procedure for alkaline preparation, one should grind together tagara, rucaka, and asafoetida with cloths. This fine powder, when applied in every way, is the direct destroyer of all poisons. (143)
The meaning of the verse is: having ground [the ingredients] until dry and mixed with ghee and molasses, it should be placed inside a cow's horn.

When administered through various applications such as nasal drops, collyrium, ointments, and diverse methods of drinking, it directly destroys all poisons—whether from stationary sources (vegetable/mineral), mobile sources (animal), natural, or even artificial. (144)
The essential meaning is this:
having observed that which has come to pass—the mortal state—one whose bodily fever has subsided and whose senses are serene.
Then, with the decoctions of the roots of the *nyan* group, one should administer all the uncooked preparations, such as the *peyā* (gruel) and so forth. // 145 //
The essential meaning is:

one should avoid sleep during the day, excessive sexual intercourse, over-exertion, excessive exposure to the sun, anger, as well as oil, kuluttha, sesame seeds, wine, sauvīra, buttermilk, and sour gruel.
Having abandoned all food in cases of intense poisons, one should employ cooling treatments; however, in cases of insect poisons, every kind of powerful sudation and ointment should be applied. (146)
The essential meaning is this:
among mortals whose bodies are afflicted by form and who are subject to those intense impulses.

Having torn it apart with the falling blows of sharp, raised weapons, he destroys it; just as one who is to be cured might eliminate his own internal poison through great mantras and tantras. // 147 //
The essential meaning [is extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (148)
The essential meaning: Having paid homage to the Jinas beginning with Vṛṣabha and ending with Vīra,
who are the teachers of the path of Dharma— the cause for crossing over the great ocean of terrible saṃsāra— [I shall compose this work].
I shall describe in their entirety the various medical treatments of the Ṛbhus, along with their associated groups of procedures.
From that essence comes flesh, from flesh comes fat, and from that, bone.

From the marrow, that which is called pure semen is produced; here, there are seven types of constituent elements (dhātus), and from the influence of the elements being either warm or very cold, the specific disorders (doṣas) arise. // 2 //
The essential meaning is that,
according to this view, even the five auspicious marks are free from injury.
The groups of one's own residences, joined with the tendons and divided by eight, are said here to cause afflictions. // 3 //
The meaning of the subject matter includes also [the arts of] massaging, anointing, drinking, taking food, piercing, and sewing. // 4 //

[He is skilled] in emesis, purgation, and strong purgation by means of powders following the mantra for evacuation, as well as in the application of medicinal pastes, fumigation, and the pacification or agitation of the humors. // 5 //

It also provides protection against the diseases of the anus, urinary tract, and poison; it is nourishing, potent, alkaline, and sweet; and it even wards off more than ten million worms and other afflictions.
It was spoken with alkaline great medicines for the sake of pacifying the entire multitude of diseases. // 7 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
excessive anger, sexual intercourse, sitting for a long time, walking, standing, exertion, harsh speech, grief, heavy eating, and riding in vehicles also [cause disease]. (8)
Having quickly removed all unwholesome things that produce many disorders, she remains present.

I shall now set forth the *Sameka* necklace, which is like water perfected as a medicine for quelling one's own faults; it bestows everything and is enjoined by the incomparable scriptures for the increase of the fire [of wisdom]. 9.
A person should bring about the essential welfare of men through nectar and other substances that increase the digestive fire.

Just as one intent on effort gradually increases a fire by means of small amounts of grass and wood until it becomes much greater when surrounded by a multitude of dry fuels, so too [should one proceed]. // 10 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
hot water, and likewise boiled water that has cooled, in appropriate measure; gruel, along with *vilepī*, *dūṣa*, excellent *dhūpya*, and *khalāna*, whether prepared or unprepared.

Then, one should administer a diet consisting of very little ghee, moderate ghee, or more ghee than food, throughout all the days, according to the sequence of the three fires, based on the calculation of the divisions of three, two, and one.
The essential meaning is:

those afflicted by burning sensations, thirst, excessive heat, intoxication, and liquor; those suffering from severe hemorrhaging (raktapitta); and even those overcome by addiction to women or extreme fainting, should be treated very effectively with cooling foods.

One should always treat those men who have been purged with ghee mixed with turmeric, who suffer from diseases of wind and excessive strength, and whose impurities are moistened, with even more intensely hot substances.

The essential meaning is as follows: those afflicted by diseases caused by wind (vāta), who are excessively dry and emaciated, who engage in excessive sexual intercourse, and who are devoted to hardships through the special consumption of large quantities of food, drink, and so forth;

For those whose *kapha* is predominant, who suffer from abdominal distension, urinary disorders (*meha*), or excessive obesity, one should treat them with very dry, frequent, and small meals containing fats. (13)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: In this case, one should lead the patient on a diet of increasingly parched grains for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire (*agni*).
One should gradually proceed from a mild and balanced fire by means of light foods, beginning with one or two mouthfuls at a time. (14)
The essential meaning is that for those who are impoverished, devoid of fire, or afflicted by disease, [the rite] prescribed for the six seasons is even more inferior.

It has been taught by the Victors that [this regimen], which pacifies the humors, brings about extreme nourishment, and serves as a cause for strength and virility, is suitable for those in good health and provides sustenance. (15)
The essential meaning is that one should [attain] the qualities produced by the medicinal action according to the number of medicines and the number of times they are administered.
I speak also of the destructions accompanied by the piercing of vital points (marmans) and the withdrawal [of the breath]. // 16 //
The essential meaning is that it possesses the qualities of being an aphrodisiac, a digestive, and a laxative, and its dissolution flows both downward and upward.

Those who know all the rites performed by the masters of every medicine declare that there are poisons that purify both parts [of the body], those that cause purgation, and even medicinal poisons. (17)
The essential meaning is this: medicine taken in the morning is powerful for all those who are strong, acting as the cause for destroying all diseases;
moreover, when taken before food, it ensures rapid digestion and brings about well-being.

Furthermore, this medicine, when administered by a knowledgeable physician, destroys the hosts of diseases located above, below, and in the middle of the body, as well as those situated within its own core. (18)
The meaning is this:
just as medicine that stimulates the digestive fire is drunk between meals,
so too [the practice] is performed at midday, situated between the two regular times of eating.
That which is to be given here as food is declared to be called "with devotion" (sabhakta) by virtue of its own qualities. // 19 //
The meaning of the passage is that a specific medicinal preparation of mung beans should be consumed at the beginning and the end of the meal.
In this regard, it has been stated repeatedly and again and again that medicines are found among the householders. // 20 //

The essential meaning is that one should also employ the powder contained within the morsel for women with weak digestive fires, for the purpose of stimulating digestion and nourishment, according to the sequence of considering the ten medicinal substances and their appropriate times. (21)
And according to the Ācārya’s system, the meaning of the essential nature is also the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), consisting of paste, decoction, powder, and oil.
I shall declare the entire fruit of all the scriptures through the characteristics of the *gānis*. // 22 //
The meaning of the passage is that one-eighth remained, which was completed by others, namely Śrutakīrti Kumāra and Nandi.
The method for the ripening of the astringent [taste] was established of old by those beginning with Ripra. // 23 //
The meaning of the passage is that it refers to ghee combined with half as much milk as remains after one quarter has been consumed, and with half as much ghee again.
