Among these, the essential meaning is praised as that which is established by the various conceptual distinctions within the systems of all the masters.
And even those who know the scriptures are made smooth by their own names and qualities, which are as radiant as the day.
The essential meaning is that one should prescribe a mild cooking for a medicated oil (sneha) that possesses the quality of superior discernment (*viveka*) regarding the medicinal paste (*kalka*).
Due to the abundance of the viscous (*picchila*) paste that is distinct from the oil, it becomes smooth (*cikkaṇa*) in this world.
Having observed that [surface] to be rough and very slippery, they say it is "over-burnt. (26)
The meaning of the essential substance is as follows:
sixteen *kuḍuba*s of oil constitute the measure for liquids;
the powder should be like a cat's paw; and the excellent paste (*varakalka*) here should be the size of an *akṣa*.
They do not speak of any excess when there is a collection of many medicines for pacifying [the disease] of men. // 27 //
The meaning of the essence is that all flavors, joined with three, are calculated as sixty-one and a quarter.
Furthermore, one should employ a physician here who possesses qualities purified by their actions and thereby achieve success. // 28 //
The essential meaning and detailed explanation of the different *rasas* (flavors) is as follows: [It is] that which,
when properly administered with the best of dual medicines, destroys the entire collection of disorders.
Having reflected on the lifespan and understood it through many groups of desired signs, one should accomplish [the practice]. // 29 //

I shall explain the essential meaning elsewhere for those men who know reality, who desire to destroy all enemies in the form of karma, and who long for the attainment of the stainless bride of liberation. (30)
The meaning of the essential nature, having been determined by one who has reached the further shore of the scriptures through his own mind alone, should be declared;
for the wise man [discerns it] by its being contrary to and distinct from the activities and transformations of dreams. // 31 //
The meaning of the state [of dreaming] is as follows:
if one, agitated by fear, climbs trees with thorns while in a dream,
or even falls headlong from the slopes of mountain peaks into the interior of a terrifying cave;
That which arises from palm trees and the like brings about the cause of killing those people. // 32 //
The meaning of the omen is that one will go toward the wild beasts and deer, having swiftly mounted [a vehicle] and headed toward the southern direction.
Wearing yellow garments, she laughs repeatedly and seems to dance all around. // 33 //
If a man is led away here by those of extremely hideous form,
he beholds even heaps of cotton, sesame, lime-paste, pits, and iron.
The essential meaning is that one should abandon all philosophical systems that have been reflected upon by oneself if they are fruitless. // 35 //
The meaning of the essential import is this:

a healthy person soon encounters a great accumulation of diseases and becomes afflicted; thus I shall describe the groups of dreams for one who understands the distinctions among the vast multitude of maladies. (36)
The essential meaning is that he beheld hosts of dreams: temples of the Lord of Jinas, and charming friends and kinsmen.
And even the ascents bring happiness to those men who behold them. // 37 //
The meaning of the passage is:
[he saw him] with his slender body trembling, or else with all sensation having passed away.

One should abandon a person whose natural disposition has been cast aside, whose lips are harsh with black teeth and their own saliva, whose eyes are fixed, sunken, bloodshot, and distorted, and whose gaze is upturned. 38.
The mind perceives everything as having a distorted form and arising from a multitude of afflicted conditions;
it hears distortion, and it smells a scent that is likewise distorted.
The physician should abandon even that weak patient who himself finds all tastes devoid of flavor and calls them tasteless, who feels no pleasure in touch, and who laments.
The meaning of the state [of the breath] causes the drying up of the subtle body and brings about death. // 40 //
The essential meaning is this:
he whose form, taste, smell, complexion, and face have become perverted, yet who produces cool tears from his eyes even without any ocular pain; [that person is possessed by a spirit].
By those [omens] that are white, black, or reddish, occurring without cause, and accompanied by a roar. // 41 //
The essential meaning is this:
whether one sleeps day and night or does not sleep at all,
[the mark is] a vast head formed by the high protuberance of the forehead being touched.
Even a conscious man falls [to hell] through idle chatter. // 42 //
He who [sees] even the entire world enveloped in smoke, frost, and water,
and he who [sees] the surface of the earth scratched and disturbed by its fissures.
And that man who sees the sun scattered with dust as his own body, and who does not feel pain caused by fire and other such things; (43)
He who does not perceive the enemy that is the reflected image, and he who seeks to purify gold by means of the methods used for beeswax— [both are deluded].
And he who perceives the sun at night, the moon as possessing the brilliance of fire, and the wind as manifest within embodied beings; 44.
Upon whose forehead lice swarm in great numbers,
and upon whose head a mass of dust settles without cause;
He whose chin was submerged and whose large testicles were hanging down.
And he whose voice is lost, deficient, or distorted; // 45 //
For him, even that which is vast as day becomes like night, and even that which is exceedingly subtle becomes vast.
For whom softness is as if hard, and even cold is as if not cold; for whom every object may indeed possess contrary qualities. (46)
Having avoided those men who are like hosts of wicked and many misfortunes,
one should examine them well by their actions, personal character, and qualities.
May he, the preeminent among all physicians, who is skilled in the specific diagnosis of diseases, constantly cure those ailments that are most easily curable. (47)
The wise man, having abandoned these aforementioned persons who have met with misfortune, as well as those afflicted in their vital organs, should proceed.
Having understood this, the physician should begin its treatment;
I shall now describe the characteristics of the vital points (marmans) with great care. 48.
The vital point (marman) known as Bhāvārtha is located between the big toe and the middle toe;
death occurs here quickly by means of the [injury] called Ākṣepaka.

The meaning is that the *kūrca* is above both [the *pāda*] from the middle of the foot; otherwise, there might be confusion regarding its name in this case of injury.
Below the ankle, there is a mass at the top of the foot (kūrcaśīrṣa) causing extreme suffering;
there is swelling in the ankle accompanied by stiffness, numbness, and pain.
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is the heel; death occurs from blood loss and so forth in the *indravasti* when it is located in the upper half of the calf.
In the joint of the shanks and thighs, however, at the knee, [the arrow] is called Amogha;
if it is wounded there, there is lameness and pain.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
Above the knee, at a distance of three finger-breadths, is the *āṇī*; there is pain [there]. If this [vessel] is injured, there is swelling and enlargement of the thigh.
Between the thighs lies the vital point (marman) called urvī;
from the discharge of blood from this, there occurs swelling and wasting of the thigh. // 52 //
The meaning of the verse:

Above the two thighs and below the groin, at the root of the thigh, or likewise in the *rohitākṣa* region, there occurs hemiplegia, swelling of the leg, hemorrhage, or death for living beings due to intense pains. (53)
The meaning of the term is as follows:
between the scrotum and the groin, there is the vital point (marman) called viṭīpāka, which destroys semen.
There are eleven such points on one thigh, and likewise on the other thigh and on the pair of arms. (54)
The essential meaning is that, specifically in the feet, there are the ankle, the well-formed knee, and the two joints; thus, there are exactly forty vital points (marmas) here in the limbs. 55.
The meaning of the passage: Now I shall explain, according to their specific characteristics, all the vital points (*marmas*) situated within the abdomen and the chest.
If the anus, the bladder, or the region of the navel is wounded, death occurs instantaneously for men. (56)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

A wound located in the chest, situated on the path of the stomach (āmāśaya), or between the breasts—that is, in the heart—causes immediate death. Furthermore, others maintain that even if it is two finger-breadths below the breasts here, death occurs instantly.

In those with a predominance of *kapha*, death occurs for men due to the provocation of *kapha* at the vital point (*marman*) at the root of the breast; likewise, at the vital points two finger-breadths above the breast, death results from the provocation of blood, known as the *stanarohita*. (58)
The meaning of the passage: Now, above the shoulder-joints (aṃsakūṭa), on one's own two sides, there are two vital points (marman) called kapālaka;
death results from injury to these when blood becomes excessively putrid, while in the other two, which carry the wind (vātavahe), death occurs in the same manner.
According to the opinion of Āpastamba, there are two special vital points (*marman*) called *stambha* located on both sides of the chest at the level of the primary channel (*pradhānanāḍī*).
From injury to these, embodied beings meet death here through the sounds of their own wind-filled bellies and coughing. (60)
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is concealment (*apalāpa*) according to another treatise.

On both sides of the spine, at the base of the back, are the two kaṭīkataruṇa bones.

The meaning of the term *bhāvārtha* refers to the thick outer portions on both sides of the back, as well as the vital points (*marman*),

there is straightness from both ends of the bamboo pole down to its very base;

situated on both sides within the nasal cavity, following the path of the channels, these two vital points (marman) are located; when they are struck, there is a loss of the sense of smell.

Even though they cast their daily side-glances from the outer corners of their eyes—those very spots called the "outer angles"—they produce blindness in men at that very vital point by striking them there. (68)
The meaning of this is that death occurs immediately from those two [lines], or else when they are on the upper part of the eyebrows at the vital points (marmans).
The two upward-throwing [hand gestures] are also placed above those very same hairlines.

among the tongue, nose, ears, and eyes, which satisfy their respective [objects],

The essential meaning is that these five types [of beings] are joined together by means of bones, sinews, marrow, formidable veins, and their own flesh.

the hips, the collarbones, the shoulder-blades,

The minor vital points (marmas) of the sinews have all been described above; now I shall speak of the vital points of the joints.

The two *maṇibandha* [wrists] from the two *krakāṭikā* [temples], likewise the *kukuṃdura* [shoulder-joints], the joints of the thighs, the one called *apālaka*, the *sthapanī*, the *phaṇa*, the nipples, the primary roots, and the *nīlamanyaka* are vital points (*marman*). (75)

Those who know the specific details of the vessels and vital points (marmas) declare them to be: Śṛṅgāṭaka, Aṃsa, Sirādhimātṛkā, Urvī, Bṛhatī, Ūrjitapārśva, Saṃdhi, Hṛt, Nābhi, Apastambha, and Lohitākṣaka. // 76 //
The palms, the heart, the *indra* (perineum), the bladder, the anus, the navel, the breasts, and the *rohitaka*—
this entire collection of manifest flesh-marmas has been set forth by the Victors.

The essential meaning is that the throat, head, vessels, anus, heart, bladder, thighs, navel, the two temples, and the junctions of the channels (śṛṅgāṭaka) are always sites where [injury] immediately takes away life; so says the Lord.
The chest, along with the vital points (marmas) of the heart and indrabasti, the kṣipras, and the sīmantakas;
likewise, the two joints of the flanks and the bṛhatīs—these indeed destroy [the patient] after some interval of time.

The meaning of the [relevant] state is that for living beings, the *utkṣepa* (upward throw), the *sthapanī* (stabilizing pose), and the *suviśalyaghna* (remover of arrows) are [performed] at the vital points (*marman*); likewise, with the two *manyā*s (carotid regions), the two *phaṇa*s (temples), the two *nitaṃba*s (hips), and the two *vidhura*s (shoulder-blades), together with the two *kūrpara*s (elbows). The two *krakāṭika* [temporal] regions and the two *taruṇa* [shoulder-joint] vital points cause impairment through various causes; along with the *sakarnashirsha*, *maṇibandha*, and *gulpha* [wrist and ankle], these eight types of vital points bring about pain for embodied beings. (80)

for those who possess vital breaths, there are twenty-nine [fatal points] that take life instantly;

men whose vital organs have been struck by injuries from the [hostile] side are sustained through various groups of medicines and the practice of methods prescribed by skilled physicians, though only occasionally.

pierced here as well, struck in the middle, and pressed against the sides.

Having learned the essential meaning from the venerable Ācārya Nandi, who was a knower of all the scriptures, and having understood the defects and the fierce diseases born of those defects,

The essential meaning is the procedure for pacifying the fierce poison of planetary afflictions as proclaimed by Svāmin and established by the renowned Siddhasenas.
Regarding the medical treatment for children, that which was taught by the venerable Daśarathas through the *Meghanāda* [treatises],

The meaning of the content is "Siṃhasena" according to the Ka manuscript; here,
even the entire eightfold path has been explained in detail by Samantabhadra through the power of his extensive speech, with particular distinction.

The meaning of the passage is as follows:
Having introduced the birthplace in the Kaliṅga country of Veṅī, [the poet describes it] as being full of mountain peaks,
where siddhas and vidyādharas delight amidst the spreading canopies of burgeoning trees and creepers.
On the delightful Rāmagiri, adorned with caves, shrines, and temples resembling the caverns of Mount Mandara, I have composed this beneficial treatise for the sake of all living beings. (87)
The essential meaning is this: day and night I remember that which uproots all karma. // 88 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows: Having mastered the science of medicine, the wise sage achieves health,
which is the sole cause of perfected happiness.
One whose body is afflicted by diseases caused by one's own faults binds karma due to the various transformations of those personal defects. (89)
The essential meaning is this:

a wise man of steadfast character is neither the creator of dharma nor the destroyer of artha, neither the enjoyer of kāma nor the faller from mokṣa; for by the destruction of that [ignorance], he would no longer be a mortal. (90)
This is the Bhāvārtha, a treatise composed by the eminent teacher Ugrādityācārya; it is a weapon that pierces the vital points of ritual actions.
By mortals proficient in all rites, having understood this, the four goals of life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—are attained. (91)
The essential meaning—
manifesting with extreme clarity from the true substance, honored and cultivated by the distinguished,
its own conduct strengthened by the conquered heroic efforts— is comparable to the path of the Jina.

May this Āyurveda—the procedure for the observances of the world—enduring until the moon and stars perish, remain for the sake of the ultimate welfare of all living beings, containing the essence of all the principles of reality established by the Lord of Jinas. 92.
May the entire world-mother (the earth) endure for a very long time, shining with incomparable and supreme festivities;
may the Dharma of the Jina prevail, the uniquely pure abode of all radiant and worthy beings.
May the sovereign of kings, who is devoted to the Jaina path, protect the entire earth; may this venerable and auspicious medical science of the Lord of Jainas endure for all living beings. 93.
The essential meaning [is extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all its subject matters.
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (94)

therefore, I shall set forth the definitive medical science, which possesses manifold meanings and brings about welfare; for "medicine" (vaidya) refers to the practice of healing, and not to some other distinct object arising from knowledge.

having understood which is the most effective means of treatment regarding what is curable and incurable, the physician should treat them.

even for those very wholesome actions that have been well-performed, neglect may occur;

The essential meaning [is derived] from these great compositions of poetic rasa, which are favored by the learned and refined.
For many eons, I shall speak at length with numerous verses concerning the supreme bestowal of longevity.

it is smooth, very white, extremely unctuous, easily grasped, and spreads with little pain; such is the alkaline (*kṣāra*) substance which possesses these qualities, and by means of this alkaline, the following [conditions] should always be avoided.

One whose vital points (marmans), sinews, vessels, nails, bones, and eyes are extremely tender, who has little flesh on the joints, and who suffers from diseases of the channels (srotas) as well as of the vital points, and who has an aversion to food—[in such a person, there is no hope of recovery]. The meaning of the verbal root [is understood] as something additional to the activity, by virtue of its application even to primary and secondary weapons.
In cases of fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, worms, and poison, one should always apply it externally to the affected channel.

he may successfully treat even when they are located within the veins, ligaments, bones, and joints.

In the flesh as well, there is slight pain accompanied by slight swelling, blackishness, contraction, dryness, and ulceration; this is considered to be the summary of its characteristic signs. (20)
The meaning of the verse is:
even in the limbs, it is intensely covered by moist silk down to the very pores of the skin.

It is also highly effective for wounds that are extremely deep, for those with hard, protruding flesh, and for conditions such as tumors (granthi), swellings (arbuda), skin tags (carmakīla), moles (tilaka), and dark spots (alāka). (21)
When the fever has subsided, the burning sensation manifested by the eight enemies—the *karmas*—is destroyed;

The meaning of the passage is as follows:
those for whom fire-therapy is prohibited include those of a bilious (pittaja) constitution, those with excessively perforated ulcers,
those who are emaciated, those with internal hemorrhaging, those who are exhausted, and those who have a foreign body lodged within.

Furthermore, I shall describe step by step, according to their specific characteristics, the treatment for those persons who are to be sweated, those afflicted by numerous clusters of ulcers, and even those who have been burnt. (23)
The essential meaning is as follows: if it is indeed so, then fourfold [classification] has been declared therein for them in due order.

I shall describe the characteristics [of the patient], as well as the excellent medical treatment for the fourfold [diseases], and the prescribed regimen for food and so forth, which is always approved by the venerable Lords of Jinas. (24)
"Avyadhyā" is an alternative reading. The meaning is:
whatever other sesame-colored [substance] exists that is hot, excessive, and neither too intense nor stable.
More painful than the heat itself is its long-term subsiding, characterized by the state of being badly burnt. // 25 //
Fainting, excessive thirst, heaviness in the joints, emaciation of the limbs, sagging of the muscles, and compression of one's own veins, sinews, and bones.
From time, it grows with worms; once long-established, it becomes extremely discolored.
This is the characteristic of an excessively burnt (vidagdha) ulcer; now I shall describe its treatment as well. // 26 //
The essential meaning is this:
fire, having reached even that which is oily or dry, burns it quickly; this is wonderful.
In that very place, various eruptions and other afflictions, accompanied by excessive pain, shall always arise.

Having recognized that it has been suddenly touched by fire, a beneficial application of warm medicinal substances possessing heating qualities should be repeatedly and properly applied here to alleviate the burning sensation. (27)
This is mentioned by the word *pluṣṭa* (consumed) in another text.
The meaning of the verse is:
one should diligently smear [the image] with mercury, or with red ochre mixed with *tugā* resin. // 28 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

even for one who has been badly burned, one should treat the eruptions with sprinklings of pleasantly warm milk, smearing with clarified butter, and even with cool ointments; furthermore, one should cause the eruptions to burst.
Therefore, the physician should apply cold medicinal herbs mixed with ghee to the burst sphoṭas, or even cover them with cool leaves, and thus make the abscess perfectly cold.

Having understood the essential meaning and having applied cooling measures extensively, the physician should remove even the hanging flesh from a severely burnt area, as well as the tendons and other tissues.

Having thus removed all that is impure and non-impure, one should wash [the wound] with milk, or cover the ulcer with leaves growing in the forest; then one should perform the treatment prescribed for non-ulcerated [wounds].
The meaning of the verse is as follows: even for the healing of a burnt wound that has been properly treated and is fit for the application of medicinal powder,
one should use unblemished, non-stale *śāli* rice grains that have not lost their luster, along with lac, at the appropriate time.
And one should repeatedly pulverize it with well-ground batvak leaves until a definitive consistency is reached.
The essential meaning is as follows: regarding vitiligo, one should apply various medicinal ointments that produce diverse colors as previously described;
furthermore, one should consume a diet that is unctuous, pleasing, and very cooling.
This entire procedure for fire has been declared; now I shall describe the application of surgical instruments (śastrakriyā).
Surgical instruments are said to be of two kinds: primary instruments (śastra) and secondary instruments (anuśastra), according to their respective methods.
The essential meaning: first, I shall briefly describe all the various types of surgical instruments,
[as well as treatments] by means of alkali, fire, crystal, *urasāra*, nails, glass, skin, leeches, and so forth.

Even among those [patients], for women of the royal court, children, the very elderly, and others who are afraid of medicinal drugs, the application of leeches—which consists primarily of substances—is said to bring about great relief. (33)
The essential meaning is this:
when blood is excessively vitiated by pitta, or by pitta along with kapha,
one should extract it using a horn, leeches, or a heated gourd.
Thus they speak in succession, all of them by means of all [the methods];
therefore, I shall describe therein the procedure for aquatic creatures according to their true characteristics.
The meaning of the term *bhāva* is the water-impurity of those very same water-born beings.
Or rather, it may simply be called "āyuḥ";
in that context, they are described as *jalā* and *yūkā*, and likewise as *samyagjalūkā*.
Painful are the wicked poisons that are the very venom of one's own body; let their characteristics be observed. // 35 //
Their dwelling (*oka*) is in water, thus they are *jalaukasas*;
their life (*āyuḥ*) is in water, thus they are *jalāyukas*. This is the meaning of the suffix.
Among them, that which resembles a heap of collyrium, possesses a thick head,
is called "black," and is a poisonous leech, should be avoided by those suffering from the afflictions of leeches.
That which possesses a naturally uneven belly, resembling a fish called *varmī*, dark in color, and mottled, is known as *karburā*; it is poisonous and always censured by the lords of sages. (36)
The essential meaning is this:
she was named Lagardā because her large, extremely dark face was covered with hair;
she was like the twilight sky, adorned with streaks of light resembling Indra’s bow.
A snake that is extremely venomous, dark-colored, yellowish in luster, and whose body is variegated with various kinds of spots is indeed a miserable sea-serpent (sāmudrika) to be avoided. (37)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: like the two horns of a cow, and likewise like the testicles, it is firm in its lower part;
it is swollen, thick at the tip, uneven due to poison, and resembles a cow’s hide or the ring finger.
Vomiting, fainting, exhaustion of the limbs, and intoxication are clearly the symptoms [of this condition]. // 38 //
The essential meaning is this: knowing their poison to be like the venom of a serpent, a physician should apply the powerful medicine prescribed in the *Viṣatantra* concerning the domain of poisons.
It destroys all other extremely malignant and fierce poisons when used as nasal drops, ointments, and so forth. (39)
Thus have I correctly described the poisonous leeches along with their essential characteristics;
I shall now likewise describe the six non-poisonous types in brief, according to their defining traits.
That which has a brownish-yellow (kapila) color on its sides, belly, and mouth, appearing as if smeared with lac, resin, and vermilion, is itself called Kapilā; it resembles a mung bean in size. (40)
The essential meaning is as follows: Piṅgalā has a body that is slightly reddish, very round, and tawny, with a tawny face;
she who possesses the scent of a bell-shaped mouse is indeed a mouse.
That which drinks quickly here, moves swiftly, has a long and extremely sharp mouth,
and whose body is like liver in color and smell, should be known as the Śaṅkumukhī.
The essential meaning is this:
she whose belly and face resemble a red lotus, and whose back is like a mung bean,
is indeed here known as Puṇḍarīkavadanā, both by name and by her very form.
She who is measured as being eighteen finger-breadths in length, renowned for her virtues as Śyāmā Sāvarikā, would be among the animals here. (42)
The meaning of the term is that on the back it is of a glossy, mudra-like color and tawny.
In another text, it is said:
"In those [regions]— in Sumālavya, in the region of Sapāṇḍu, in Sahyācala-Ādityaka,
in the collection of lands between the Kāverī and Taralā, and in the three Kaliṅgas of Veṅgī."
In Pauṇḍraka as well, and especially in Viśaṃṣa, there are many leeches that eat excessively;
one should quickly apply those that drink [blood] and are free of poison, and then remove them.
The meaning of the passage is:
when the pond is full, covered with moss, and marked by mud interspersed with lotuses.
In the cold season, having provided water and other necessities along with cool lotus stalks,
one should constantly offer [the food] every seven days, continuously manifesting whatever [deity] is desired.
The essential meaning is this:

just as a physician, having observed a patient suffering from various diseases that can be cured by the release of impurities, administers treatment by prescribing cold liquids during the cold season; so too [is the case here].
Having thoroughly rubbed that limb where the pain is located with powdered cow dung or ground earth,
one should repeatedly apply leeches to it after immersing it in very cold water.
Washed successively with the pastes of *vāmyā*, *sadrājanī*, white mustard, and *vacā* mixed with water,
and then rinsed with pure water, they are treated with the paste of mung beans mixed with water.
Or again, [the ritual] should be performed on a foot smeared with butter or upon a wound inflicted by a weapon. // 46 //
The meaning of the term is as follows:
the *ṇai* refers to the *cūṣaṇaka* leech, while the *vidāvara* leech is the *svayaṃgrāhikā*.
Having drunk that [mixture] and fallen down, one should then apply *saṃkuḍika* to her, and having smeared her face with *saindhava* salt and oil, one should press her or cause her to vomit. // 47 //
The essential meaning is this: having placed that vomited matter into a jar filled with water, one should nourish it;
and having recognized even the excessive flow of blood, one should stabilize it with medicinal drugs.
Having reflected that she might become a teacher, one should immediately cause her to be released from the salt.
Afterward, having repeatedly washed the meaning of the state with cold water here, one should discharge the disease;
or, having thoroughly sprinkled it for a long time with milk or ghee, one should proceed gradually.
Furthermore, one should cause it to coagulate thoroughly with powders made from linen that have been completely dried. // 49 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

with extremely pure *lodhra* flowers, with cow-dung made from excellent cows, with wheat and *dhātrī* fruits, with conch shells, with collections of oyster shells, with *arimeda* trees, and likewise with *granthi* wood.
Having quickly powdered the *rā* plant, one should staunch the blood by binding it with the strength of the bandage. // 50 //
The essential meaning is as follows: those children who are stout, emaciated, thin, wounded, crippled, or of inferior nature;
those who are intent on eating little, dependent on others, or excessively prone to sleep and lethargy.
And all those leeches should not be nourished by the physician with nourishing treatments. // 51 //
The meaning of the subject matter has thus been correctly set forth in detail according to the authoritative treatises; therefore,
I shall now briefly state the compendium of these treatises.

One who knows the treatises on weapons and is skilled in their application should have various weapons made of iron, adorned with diverse decorations, commissioned by smiths renowned for their expertise in great works.
The meaning of the terms is as follows:
that which is to be cut (chedya) is said to be the excessively grown leaf; one should apply that which is to be scraped (lekhya);
here, that which is to be split (bhedya) is known as the lotus petal; and that which is to be pierced (vedhya) refers to the bone with a hatchet.
Then, the "Surgical Instrument" (Śastra) and the "Probe" (Eṣaṇī) were spoken; likewise, the "Remover of Arrows" (Śalya-eṣaṇī) was constantly recited. // 53 //
The essential meaning is this: command that the worldly arrow, unknown to Kaṅkamukha and the others, be brought forth.
One should quickly extract the foreign body from that very spot where the pain is most intense. // 54 //
Having carefully examined the meaning of the situation, as one would a needle for the act of sewing, one should sew the head of the thigh— whether straight or crooked—
with it into the abdomen, which is already known to have many wounds.
One should heal it externally with medicines for pressing, squeezing, and healing. // 55 //
The essential meaning is this:
even regarding the eight types of karma such as those to be excised, whenever a physician desires for the patient the performance of a particular karma,
he [prepares] medicines, instruments, surgical tools, houses, cold water, hot water, fire, and so forth.
Then, having combined the unctuous substances with six types of attendants to achieve completeness,
and having ascertained that the food is suitable, he should first feed the patient.
Even with the greatest effort, one may remember the meaning of the text here, yet a physician renowned for his surgical practice [remains superior].

One should quickly extract the stone through the anal passage from the left side; having cut away the hemorrhoid according to the prescribed method for one restrained by attendants, one should wash it away with water.

The essential meaning is this: having recognized that the patient here has been properly lubricated and fomented, well-prepared, and constrained by appropriate therapeutic measures, one should then clearly grasp the suitable instrument for his vein.
One should release the blood from a wound by gradually lowering the stream;
having slightly removed the pressure of the instrument, one should staunch the bleeding through the strength of the bandage.
The essential meaning is this:
one should overcome excessive bleeding that has escaped through the veins by means of astringent remedies.
One should read "vāpayet" as an alternative reading;
[this practice] would bring about wind-related diseases, consumption, dyspnea, coughing, hiccups, and so forth, as well as anemia, insanity, headache, and even death before long. (59)
The essential meaning is as follows:
when the blood is excessively increased, one should first effect its pacification;
then, one should have the patient drink cow's milk that has been boiled and subsequently cooled, every day.
One should feed the patient prepared substances here that pacify heat and cold, and which stimulate the digestive fire.
The meaning of the verse is:
A learned physician should protect the patient, who produces a continuous flow [of urine] and nourishment of a radiant complexion.
Health, lightness of the body, gentleness of mind, and firmness of the self and the senses. // 61 //
The essential meaning is:
blood that is excessively frothy, reddish, clear, and flows very rapidly due to wind (vāta) is vitiated; blood vitiated by its own bile (pitta) is bluish, excessively yellow, or black.
It is undesirable when it is putrid, constantly infested by all kinds of worms, mosquitoes, and flies; when it is stained by an excess of phlegm, thick, and exceedingly slimy. (62)
Even that which appears as flesh may emerge after a moment or a very long time due to phlegm;
it is cold, has the luster of red ochre, and when innate, resembles an *indragopa* insect.

Seeing that blood—which is extremely non-congealed, free from intervals, devoid of discoloration at all times, and composed of the life-force—one should protect it well so that it remains inexhaustible. (63)
The essential meaning is that [this] does not apply when one has not sweated, nor when one has consumed unctuous or dry food, nor when one has ingested a great deal of tasteless food.

If one has not yet eaten, blood-removing food that is very liquid, small in quantity, and extremely cold, as well as cold water, should be drunk; having recognized that condition, one should treat him accordingly. (64)
The essential meaning is this:
those who have lost blood, those afflicted by dyspnea, cough, wasting, fever, or the fatigue of travel;
those who are emaciated, parched, or wounded; and those distressed by old age, childhood, or consumption—these should be avoided, provided they are not of pure body.

During times of distress, one should cause those women who have miscarried due to the exhaustion of their bodies from female occupations and fasts, those whose embryos are destroyed by kicks or blows to the flanks, and those men whose semen is depleted or who have been poisoned, to undergo an induced miscarriage.
The essential meaning [is extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. // 66 //
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter from the beginning, titled "The Treatment of Karma," in the section on the *Uttaratantra* of the *Kalyāṇakāraka* composed by Ācārya Ugrāditya.
The rule for the primary established doctrine, which is the medicine for the various types of well-known difficult diseases, shall now be set forth. // 1 //
The meaning of the passage:

Furthermore, diseases arise for embodied beings during the procedures involving clarified butter, the consumption of [medicines], or the application of various medicinal herbs; this occurs either due to the physician’s specific ignorance regarding what is beneficial or because he fails to attend to the patient himself.
Because of that transgression. // 2 //
The essential meaning is this: the consumption of ghee is always a rejuvenative (rasāyana) for a person when properly administered;
yet that very same thing becomes a cause of harm to men through either under-dosage or over-dosage. // 3 //
The essential meaning is:
even when ghee is undigested, loss of appetite, fever, urinary disorders, intoxication, skin diseases, and fainting may arise;
therefore, one should drink warm water with rock salt, or the physician should induce vomiting with lukewarm water. (4)
The essential meaning is as follows:

when the body is light, there is a desire for food, and the mind, speech, urine, feces, and vital breath [function properly]; the occurrence of eructations, purity, and clarity of the senses—these indeed are the signs of well-digested [food]. (5)
The essential meaning is as follows:
Therefore, one should drink gruel prepared with *kustumburu* and *nimba*, or according to the state of the humors (*doṣa*).
One should provide suitable light food, warm, along with wholesome soups of *kulattha* and *mudga* beans, or with *sattū* (flour). (6)
The essential meaning is this:

a person intent on nourishing the body should himself drink ghee produced from sesame seeds, gradually increasing the dose with effort for three, five, or seven days; thereafter, it may be consumed habitually as it becomes suited to one's constitution. (7)
In the case of Pitta-type fever, one should drink ghee with sugar; in Vata-type fever, one should drink it with rock salt and warm water.
Those who know the medical tradition prescribe the three pungents combined with alkali for diseases arising from the nature of phlegm (kapha) in their proper sequence.
The meaning of the verse is: If a man is devoted to the afflictions, possessed of great strength, himself stable, and exceedingly devoted to coldness;
During the season, one should drink that ghee alone; indeed, drinking it plain is beneficial for those who desire their own welfare. // 9 //
The meaning of the state [of the sun] is how much measure it attains; that indeed is drunk when [the sun] has reached the middle of the day.
It is truly excellent because of the absence of intoxication, fatigue, exhaustion, burning heat, fainting, and extreme loss of appetite. // 10 //
The meaning of the passage is: [one should avoid administering it] to one who is delicate, a child, obese, extremely weak, thirsty, averse to clarified butter, or suffering from extreme anorexia.
One should have him drink ghee here, which is well-heated, prepared according to the proper method, and accompanied by devotion. // 11 //
The essential meaning is this: one should drink ghee combined with long pepper (pippalī), rock salt (saindhava), and buttermilk (mastukā), which is supreme for warding off dryness (raukṣya).
One may easily consume milk with sugar, or simply milk, or even barley-gruel with a small amount of rice.
Having milked [the cow] with white, black, and ghee-colored [rays], and having caused it to drink the draught, a person is liberated from harshness.
This excellent ghee, even when cooked with the liquids of horse gram (kulattha), jujube (kola), sour gruel (amlapayas), milk, and curd, acts swiftly [as a remedy]. // 13 //
The essential meaning is this:
among kings, the elderly, the weak, and those who are powerless, as well as among those whose fires of suffering are great yet whose faults are few.
The physician should administer here the most excellent unctuous formulations proclaimed [in this work], even for a moment. (14)
The essential meaning is that extremely parched and solid feces pass out with great difficulty, and even food that has been eaten is not digested properly.
The ripening of karma arrives; indeed, his chest burns, his limbs become discolored, and his belly is filled with wind. // 15 //
In this world, such a person becomes extremely weak, possesses a very feeble digestive fire, and has a parched body.
After that, I shall describe the auspicious marks of a person with supple limbs; listen to that in brief. // 16 //
The meaning of the word *bhāva* is "among the bulls"; there is an alternative reading, *vṛṣeṣu*. Its meaning will be: those who are righteous, that is to say, those whose nature is peaceful.
However, in this context,
the reading "nṛpeṣu" appears to be appropriate. (Sanskrit)
The inevitable production of oiliness and impurity, the aversion to ghee, and the sinking of the limbs occur here.
And having become characterized by an especially smooth quality, I shall likewise describe the characteristic of excessive unctuousness. // 17 //
The meaning of the state [of the disease] is:
burning in the anus, excessive discharge of stool, loss of appetite, drooping of the face, and the upward movement of phlegm.
Diarrhea, excessive burning sensation throughout the limbs, and delusion are the symptoms of a person who has been excessively oleated. // 18 //
The essential meaning is this:
one should drink warm water with ginger; one should quickly cause [the patient] to eat rice with a soup made of mudga beans.
Alternatively, one should administer a clear gruel (yavāgū) combined with cumin, asafoetida, and rock salt. // 19 //
The essential meaning is this: ghee is a captivating elixir for men; therefore, those who drink it here with diligent effort [attain their goal].
For them, water cooled by snow is always beneficial, as is gruel made with barley and a small amount of rice that has been cooled by snow.
Having carefully observed the groups of diseases arising from [excessive] affection, the procedure for one afflicted by diseases arising from sweating is now stated.
Sweating is in every respect the most beneficial for humans on this earth; yet, even when it is applied [properly], diseases may still arise therein. // 21 //
The essential meaning is this:

indeed, many diseases are pacified through the power of correct application, yet here too, they may arise from improper application (ayoga) or excessive application (atiyoga). Since various groups of ailments can thus manifest, the determination of the proper degree of sudation (sveda) is highly recommended here.
The essential meaning is that sweating is declared to be fourfold, categorized by heat, steam, binding, and great liquefaction.
Heat (*tāpa*) consists simply of warming with cloth, fire, or the palm of the hand; likewise, steam (*ūṣma*) is produced by means of hot bricks, stones, or heaps of grain. (23)

The essential meaning is as follows: here, the process known as "binding" (bandhana) occurs through the use of warm medicinal herbs, as well as milk-porridge (pāyasa) and the like that have been thoroughly cooked, and by means of coverings of leaf-garments;
whereas the process named "liquefying" (dravana) occurs through excessive fomentation (sveda) with warm sour gruel (sauvīraka), water, ghee, oil, and milk. // 24 //
The essential meaning is this:
it is beneficial when wind and phlegm are mixed; it brings benefit to the body through the application of unctuous substances, whereas here it burns when applied dry.
The essential meaning is this: for the *vāta* and other humors, which are constantly situated within the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), become naturally dissolved through the application of oleation;
then, having attained liquidity by means of sudation, they return to their own places in due order, becoming healthy and established in their own respective abodes within the abdomen. (26)
The essential meaning is this: here, through sweating, the digestive fire constantly attains increase; sweat is the cause for destroying the great maladies of phlegm and wind.
When applied properly, it quickly generates perspiration in an excessively dry body and even produces a desire for cold.

The essence of sweating provokes pitta and blood, directly bringing about eruptions, vertigo, intoxication, fever, burning sensations, and fainting; when applied excessively, it swiftly brings these on, so the wise physician should employ extremely cooling measures in that case.
The meaning of the verse is:
[I bow] to him whose body was not consumed by the fire of hell, yet whose limbs here were incessantly afflicted by drops of cold water.
One should bathe the patient with warm water to kindle the digestive fire in the stomach and then feed the teacher soft food that stimulates the fire.
The essential meaning is that,
having described the procedure for sudation, there follows, in due order, the treatment for the great diseases arising from improper purification.
Here, it will be prescribed according to the rules of correct procedure by means of the Siddhayogas, which are the authoritative compendiums of medicinal substances related thereto.

The meaning of the passage is that this same reading is found in two or three manuscripts; however, it appears somewhat inconsistent with the context. Since this is a section concerning the "sweat-born" (svedaja) beings, the reading "prāṇātipāta" (taking life) seems more appropriate here.

This means: regarding the state of life-threatening danger (*prāṇātipāta-avasthā*) caused by the excessive application (*atiyoga*) of sudation (*sveda-karma*)—which gives rise to the diseases mentioned in the preceding verse—the procedure for that situation is prescribed in this verse. It is possible that this textual variation arose due to a scribal error:
"When the humors (*doṣa*) have been diminished, they should be nourished; when all [humors] have become agitated, they should be properly pacified."
"They should be maintained in health, constantly protected, increased when flourishing, and immediately purified when corrupted," so it was said by Siddhasena. // 31 //
The essential meaning is that emesis is for purification, while purgation is for successful restoration; thus it is established by the perfected ones.
We shall now explain specifically that vomiting which has been prescribed for those two by the path of the Siddhānta. // 32 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

having reflected thus, "Tomorrow I shall perform the emesis properly," the wise physician should quickly feed the patient during the afternoon; I shall now also fully describe those who are fit to be fed. (33)
The essential meaning is this:

those who are afflicted by many intense and emerging defects, who possess a keen digestive fire, and in whom the strength of the vital essence (sattva) predominates—those whose bodies are seized by great diseases should be nourished by those expert in the world. (34)
The meaning of this is as follows:

On the following day, at the common time for administration, having observed the appropriate dose in the morning, one should indeed cause them to vomit by means of medicinal pastes (kalka), decoctions (kaṣāya), powder formulations (cūrṇa-yoga), or unctuous substances (sneha) and so forth. // 35 //

The essential meaning is this: emetic formulations are employed with substances that are foul-smelling, unsightly, and of repulsive appearance, as well as with nauseating drugs and those other than those one is accustomed to;
whereas purgative formulations here are used with substances that are pleasing to the mind. (36)
The essential meaning is this: even children, the very old, those afraid of medicine, women, and those afflicted by weakness—
having caused them to drink those auspicious medicines enriched with milk and other such substances, one should protect them.
One should cause them to drink. // 37 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows: "One should cause [the breath] to flow"—this is an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*).
Having quickly observed nausea, salivation, and perspiration, the wise man, seated upon his seat (*pīṭha*), [should proceed].
One should touch one's own throat with the stalks of the *gandharvahasta* and *utpala* lotus petals for the purpose of generating speed. // 38 //
This is the essential meaning: when the morbid humors have been expelled through the administration of medicine, when the bile has subsided from the heart, chest, and stomach;
when the body and mind have become purified and light; when the bodily functions are properly established; and when the phlegm has been thoroughly vomited out. (39)
The essential meaning is this:
having quickly purified the head-ache (śirobalāsa) with gargles, collyrium for the eyes, and medicinal drops,
and having washed it with warm water in the afternoon, one should properly feed the patient with various meat soups (yūṣa).
The essential meaning is this: when pacification has been thus performed, diseases caused by phlegm (kapha) are destroyed;
for when that root, the phlegm, is removed, they vanish like clusters of water-born plants when the water is gone.
Having understood the entire scripture that prohibits the non-attainment of the two [goals], the physician [should act] with medicines.
The essential meaning is this:

a physician should first purify the upper part of one who is extremely impure, and only then the lower part; otherwise, a mass of diseases will always suddenly afflict that mortal whose digestive fire has been suppressed. (42)
The essential meaning is:
"Tomorrow I shall thoroughly purge this patient—who has been lubricated, sweated, and well-vomited—with purgative medicines"; thus, even before the forenoon, he should first [prepare himself].
One should also administer the drinking of prepared warm water, which facilitates the liquefaction of waste matter.
The essential meaning is this:
having carefully considered [the patient] on another day when the food has been digested and the sun is bloodless (i.e., not red),
one should administer medicine after observing the digestive fire and the progression of the disease, which may be slight or harsh.
The digestive tract (koṣṭha) is of three types: soft, hard, and likewise intermediate;
it is soft due to vāta, hard due to kapha, and intermediate when all the doṣas are in equilibrium. (44)
The essential meaning is this:
here, [the intensity] is considered mild when the soil is very soft, and sharp when it is extremely hard;
likewise, by the wise and skillful, the medium measure is established even in that which is called "medium."
One should not desire to forcibly remove impurities that have not yet been reached, nor should one apply bile-based medicines in such a case.
Or even if it has already arisen, one should not suppress it, for excessive suppression brings about obstruction.
The essential meaning is as follows:
when, in due order, the wind (vāyu), water-like impurities (kapha), bile (pitta), and the arising phlegm (kapha) have been expelled through the medicine,
and these have passed away, then, by following the movement of the wind, one becomes properly purged.

This person, whose body is pure yet afflicted by fatigue and exhaustion, carrying a light frame, being contented yet intensely thirsty and possessing digestive strength, should drink barley gruel when emaciated. (46)
The meaning of the state [of being] is expressed by the suffix -kta; one should drink it neither with mere cleverness nor merely according to one's power and reasoning.
The benefits of both emesis and purgation have already been proclaimed;
having understood their defects and qualities through the rules of prohibition and prescription, the wise physician should administer them.
The essential meaning is this:

that purificatory medicine which is excessive in its nature of sharpness, heat, and subtlety goes upward even while undigested, due to the predominance of its [corrective] qualities; thus, emesis occurs properly.

The meaning is this:

for one with weak digestive fire who has been treated with unctuous therapy, a very sharp medicine administered when the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha) is soft will pass through too quickly and thus fail to cleanse all the morbid humors (doṣas).
The medicine drunk here in the morning is digested by midday; it purifies thoroughly until nothing remains—this is the view held in the eternal Jaina scripture. (49)
The essential meaning is this:
one should gradually eliminate even very great and excessively fluctuating defects;
and even when they have diminished, one should repeatedly pacify those that are still active and not small, and continue to practice.
In this world, one should remove the humors (doṣas) when they are fully ripened and mobile, employing every means for everyone;
for if not extracted, those accumulated humors quickly destroy the person entirely.
The essential meaning is this: one who is of a moist constitution (snigdha) and drinks purgative ghee excessively causes the doshas, which have become mobile and displaced from their sites,
to be restrained again by the power of the unctuous substance and thus become stable in their own locations.
All those things that bring happiness become loosened by the binding of the evil messenger. // 51 //
The essential meaning is this:

for one who knows the specific compartments and has correctly identified the six compartments, one should administer a purifier that removes the humors; likewise, for one who is not so informed, having observed [the condition], one should give something gentle and mild.
And that vigor which is captivating and free from affliction—that is the medicine. // 52 //

From the digestion of that [medicine], there is the removal of minor doshas and the arising of excessive wind-pain. // 53 //
Furthermore, there are others: shifting of the humors, cardiac displacement, and likewise obstruction.

either a very large amount of pleasant-smelling incense was offered, or a purgative medicine was administered.
If the vomited matter moves upward, or if there is an increase in the humors (doṣas), or even the onset of extremely severe diseases,
one should thoroughly purify that vomited material with very sharp purgative medicines.

In that case, one should again cause that [patient], who has already experienced undesirable results and possesses an aggravated state of the humors, to vomit once more with very unctuous and extremely potent medicinal drugs. (56)

when the portion of the *āmāśaya* (stomach) is likewise filled with foul-smelling and loathsome substances,

and being unable to subdue the remaining host of humors, becomes the cause of great disorder.
It causes fainting, vomiting, loss of appetite, thirst, impure eructations, pain, and nausea;
therefore, one should induce emesis with water boiled with *ahi* and *ugra*.
The meaning of this is:
[it applies] to one who is small, of little strength, and whose entire great defect has been set in motion.
In that case, one who has been improperly purged downwards should be vomited using warm water;
even for one with a sharp digestive fire, that [unpurified matter] is digested like food and should be quickly cleansed. (59)
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
If a small amount of medicine with few therapeutic qualities is drunk but not completely digested, it will not expel the morbid humors (doṣa) through vomiting;
consequently, there will be an increase in pain and disease in the head.
Nausea may also occur here; one should emetic that patient who is very strong, even if the humors have moved downward.
From purification, heaviness is removed; from wind in the chest, there is pain in the anus.
One should quickly purge that person with very mild, strong medicinal purgatives; for a man who has been deprived of treatments such as oleation, extremely dry medicine should be administered.
If cold water is given to one who is engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman, it provokes wind (vāta);
that [wind] causes excessive colic, or else produces symptoms such as vertigo and fainting.
The essential meaning is: the physician who has administered an oil prepared with these medicinal pastes as an unctuous enema (anuvāsa).
Whether it be very little or even a great deal that has been ingested, it does not move upward or downward. (62)
Flatulence, gripping pain in the heart, thirst, burning sensation, and fainting;
Having first applied oleation to that patient, one should induce emesis; likewise, having applied unctuousness to the lower part of the body, one should perform purification.
For one who has vomited well, all the great morbid humors (doṣas) that have arisen within the body are completely expelled.
One should then completely purify it of all striking, piercing, and other such defects.
If the purgation is poorly performed, excessively purgative, or has not yet begun to take effect, one should quickly drink well-prepared warm water for the sake of optimal purification. 64.
When the body has been sweated, the morbid humors (doṣas) immediately rush out with great force once they have attained a liquid state.
When even a very small accumulation of humors has passed and the wholesome medicine has been digested, that is a specific instance of insufficient administration (ayoga).
And one should prepare that medicine so that it leaves no residue. // 65 //
Having understood that the patient’s strength is slight, that his defects have been eliminated, and likewise that the remaining [doshas] are minimal,
one should then administer the correct dose for further purification in the proper sequence.
Even if one has not administered an enema or an oil enema, one may perform the procedure of purgation if it is highly beneficial. // 66 //
"Separation" (*viyoga*) is an alternative reading; this is the meaning of the term.
The men of the earth are intent on obstructing their impulses; the wives of servants out of shame;
the merchants out of greed; and other worldly people likewise do not seek their own true welfare.

Furthermore, those diseases that are extremely parched, characterized by constipation, or likewise obstructed, may become difficult to purify; therefore, one should first apply oleation well and then perform purification.
The meaning of this is:

if an excessively sharp medicine is administered to a person who is well-oiled and has undergone sudation, and whose digestive tract is extremely soft, it will cause over-action; through vomiting, there may be an excessive discharge of bile.

If there is an excessive discharge of phlegm due to an improper administration of purgation,
it results in the depletion of blood as well, and indeed, the agitation of the wind (vāyu) arises.
One should perform emesis with [the appropriate substances], followed by the administration of extremely cold milk, ghee, and decoctions. // 69 //
Furthermore, it should be treated according to the procedures for diarrhea, with wholesome medicines and diet.
There was also the destruction of the pair of eyes of pride and the cessation of the movement of the tongues. // 70 //
And I shall also provide for their medical treatment here, in due order.
In that case, if there is excessive flow of blood, one should perform the procedure for profuse hemorrhage;
and if the tongue protrudes, one should rub the tongue with powdered rock salt and the three pungents (tri-katu) and then press it back.
If the tongue were to enter within, then just as others would eat sour things before them,
one would repeatedly consume the entire category of sour foods oneself, eating inexhaustibly.
When the eyes have been anointed with ghee, one should gently press them in a playful manner;
once the jawbones are well-stabilized, one should apply fomentation using medicinal herbs that alleviate excessive phlegm and wind.
In cases of hiccups, eructations, thirst, and so forth, one should apply the appropriate remedy even when consciousness is lost;
one should quickly cause the patient to hear the sweet sound of a flute in the ear, which restores awareness.
Then one should contemplate one's own flesh as being like washed water, and subsequently, that very flesh as being mixed with blood.
And the physician should apply the remedies for these, according to the sequence already stated, by means of medicinal drugs.
One should press that anus which has protruded and been sprinkled with warm oil;
and having constantly performed the treatment for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi), one should administer the medicine. // 74 //
I have indeed fully explained the correct medical treatment for the group of disorders involving the tongue as their objective;
therefore, let the vital blood be examined by its characteristics.
Even when washed with warm water, it does not become excessively soiled; furthermore, in this context, it destroys blood during sleep, except when it is associated with pitta. (75)
The essential meaning is that "taking life" is characterized by the blood of a living being; knowing that [blood] has flowed, one should apply extremely cold treatment.
And one should constantly employ cooling medicines that promote healing.

Furthermore, that dryness resulting from indigestion and the intensification of the wind (vāta), along with the medicine that has been drunk, causes distension here by creating an extreme obstruction of the wind, feces, and urine. (76)
If excessive piercing pain occurs in the bladder or the rectum, one should apply oleation and intense sudation;
furthermore, one should administer various medicinal suppositories and fire-stimulating enemas.

When a very mild digestive fire, weakened by previous depletion, consumes excessively dry medicine, it suddenly vitiates the wind (vāyu) combined with bile (pitta) and brings about [the disease]. // 77 //
Then follows the most intense cutting pain, followed by the torment of heat;
next comes the obstruction of urine and feces within the womb, from which a loss of appetite arises.
One should administer an asthapana enema with milk mixed with oil, ghee, and liquorice (yaṣṭimadhuka);
one should perform an anuvasana enema daily with milk and ghee, and feed the patient on milk. // 78 //
The meaning is this:

for one whose stomach is extremely dry and harsh and who has many morbid humors (*doṣas*), a small amount of mild medicine administered to remove those humors is insufficient; therefore, the humors become further provoked.
Discharge of bile and phlegm, occurring continuously and without pain, causes constant oozing. // 79 //
The essential meaning is this:
one should pacify that disorder of excessive discharge here with astringent medicines—
both those already mentioned and those to be described later— by means of stabilizing and restorative treatments.
One should consume a very small amount of mixed rice, distinguished by its warmth, while savoring it well. // 80 //
The essential meaning is this:
a person who is either excessively unctuous or excessively dry, having drunk a purificatory agent here,
forcibly expels waste that has not yet arrived and retains waste that has already arrived.
Within that [condition], phlegm (śleṣman) flows accompanied by a burning sensation, colic, and an abundance of white, very red, or black matter; it is manifestly a purgative (vāhikā). // 81 //
The meaning of the passage is that one should subsequently cause the patient to drink non-frozen water prepared with fire and medicinal herbs.
Having brought about the approach to the heart of ignorance, there are likewise faults here. // 82 //
Furthermore, causing pain in the heart, a person— constantly biting his tongue along with his teeth—
becomes exhausted while gazing upward, or else faints due to extreme emaciation.
One should cause those who have attained perfection through the arising of desire to dwell here together constantly. // 83 //
One should quickly cause that patient to vomit even with rice-water mixed together.
On the next day, having purified his body, he partakes of very cool drinks and other refreshments. // 84 //
The mass of dissolved morbid humors in the channels forms a concretion;
it then obstructs the feces, urine, and flatus, and likewise suppresses the digestive fire itself.
One should purge him with emetics and likewise administer non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), and then have him undergo a period of restorative confinement (anusaṃvāsa).
The meaning of the verse is as follows: that cutting pain which was described in the case of purgation is prescribed [as occurring] in emesis;
downward discharge occurs in the upper part [of the body], and the expectoration of phlegm is observed [to occur]. (86)
Diarrhea flowing downwards, and likewise upwards by itself, as well as dry eructation—these fifteen complications have been described in order, along with their medicinal remedies. // 87 //
The meaning of the verse: Furthermore, in this case, when the proper application of good conduct is correctly performed, many inconceivable great virtues arise;
likewise, when the improper application is caused by a bad physician, many inconceivable evil qualities also arise. (88)

The meaning of the positive injunctions and prohibitions has already been explained; hereafter, the treatment for rectal disorders will be described using expert and pleasing medicines, categorized according to the application of the nozzle and the enema bag. (89)
The meaning of the verse:
Now, in this case, if the eye is moved, rolled back, or turned sideways, resulting in an injury to the rectum, the physician should apply treatment as for a wound and perform fomentation there. (90)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Similarly, when a medicinal preparation containing oil is thrown upward and, accompanied by air, is expelled from the body in an instant along with froth, it quickly pierces the groin if heated; one should then administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) or subsequently a unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
The essential meaning here is that when [the fire] has subsided, it indeed burns more intensely as it falls headlong; furthermore, the falling liquid quickly consumes the substrate.
This is the essential meaning.
In the same way, due to the fault of directing [the gaze] obliquely, one should not move toward fluidity; rather, one should apply it straight.

If it is afflicted by a very subtle and difficult-to-perceive *duścittara*, it will not become fluid; one should therefore avoid that as well. // 95 //
The essential meaning:
hereafter, the symptoms of disorders of the enema (basti) will be explained; one should avoid them as well. (96)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

likewise, when the rectum is thick and has an internal opening, it does not become firmly closed; thus, avoiding those who are very weak, [the physician] should extract the fetus once it is pressed and pierced, as it emerges quickly as a fluid through the wide-open passage. (97)

Now, if the bladder is too small or excessively compressed, the liquid becomes thin; therefore, the physician should avoid these [conditions]. Likewise, from excessive squeezing, the liquid flows out rapidly through the mouth and the two nostrils. (98)

Having thus understood this, let the procedure be performed immediately: purge him with very strong purgatives, sprinkle him with very cold water, and then, with great effort, cause the fluid to flow downward. (99)

If the liquid is discharged due to slight pressure, or if it is repeatedly pressed with wind (vāyu), it causes flatulence and excessive pain; therefore, administer an excellent enema that subdues vāyu. 100.

When applied after a long time, it merely suppresses the onset of disease, leaving the afflicted person in a state of distress; likewise, a small dose of medicinal oil, though containing many beneficial ingredients, will be entirely ineffective if used continuously.
In the same way, when it reaches an excessive degree, it brings on dysentery at that very moment. // 102 //

In cases of dysentery (pravāhikā) as well, the same therapeutic procedure applies. Medicines that are very cold or very hot, those that increase vāta or pitta, those with an excess of salt, and liquid substances cause distress to the rectum. (103)
Now, in this case, purification enemas (saṃśodhana-basti) and excellent purgatives (virecana) are administered by those who are certain [of the diagnosis]. The underlying meaning is as follows:
furthermore, when there is excessive pressure even in the downward-facing (avaśīrṣa) enema, the procedure for the upward-facing (uttara) enema is also described by the wise.

this is the intended meaning.

here, one should extract the arrows from those whose bodies are bent,
or from the groin itself, or from another location.

And for those two, the physician who knows the truth of their departure and arrival should carefully administer an enema.

The essential meaning is as follows:

Now, furthermore, the countermeasures for improper application and other such faults will be explained according to their characteristics through medical treatments; here and in the subsequent [sections], there shall be a discourse on further discussion, and thus I shall speak sufficiently on what has been stated and what remains unstated. (108)
Even a very cold enema, or one with insufficient medicinal ingredients, or even one administered in too small a dose, produces a state of non-uniformity (ayoga).
Furthermore, the enema may ascend into the abdomen, or there may be distension and excessive pain. (109)
In this condition, the wise prescribe a very sharp enema as appropriate, and purgation is also ordained.
When there is indigestion, overeating, or an excess of waste products, even a large enema, though cold and cooling, is indicated. (110)

In this case, when administered, it produces sensation and excessive distension; therefore, it is given here as a primary enema (*pradhāna-basti*) according to the excellent treatises on enemas (*vasti-śāstra*), for it subdues wind, stimulates the digestive fire, and acts as a powerful purifier. The meaning of the verse is that it is also extremely effective when there is excessive heat or an excess of salt.

Likewise, from the excessive use of very sharp, sour, and pungent substances, there arises in men the great disease known as *parisrāva*.
And that [pitta], having produced weakness and a sense of exhaustion in the limbs here, causes the paittika [disorder] to flow out.

The essential meaning is that from the use of a very sharp enema, or even from an oil enema (anuvāsana), there may arise dysentery (pravāhikā) due to excessive administration; these are the complications.
For one who is passing [the stool], there is a burning sensation like a piercing colic, and there occurs the discharge of blood-stained, blackish, and excessive phlegm. // 115 //
The essential meaning is that one should feed [the patient] with very unctuous ghees combined with cooling medicines, as well as excellent oils and milk. (116)

When the enema is administered during strong wind (vāta), it is excessively oppressed by its sharpness and causes it to move toward the heart; that very [condition] brings about fainting, intoxication, burning sensations, heaviness, excessive salivation, and various kinds of pain. (117)
The essential meaning is that one should purify [the patient] with groups of medicines for the three doṣas through non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), and then administer unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).
Furthermore, this applies to one whose nature is dominated by wind (vāta) and who has become excessively dry, or again, to one who has fallen into a very painful bed. (118)
When an enema containing only a small amount of medicinal potency is administered to one who is aggravated, it causes a severe stiffness of the limbs that is very difficult to treat;
therefore, in such a case, the treatment for Vāta disorders must be applied with medicines that are highly effective against excessively aggravated Vāta.
Now, for a person whose humors are slight, whose abdomen is soft, or whose body has been well-fomented— (120)
A very sharp enema, when administered too hastily, produces a truly remarkable state of over-action (atiyoga).

The meaning of the passage is this: even in cases of excessive hemorrhage, that which flows forth is indeed preceded by the vital principle (jīva).
The essential meaning is that,

Although the procedure for the enema has already been described here, I shall provide it [again]. // 123 //

when one who knows the scriptures has performed this excellent purgation,
it is for the sake of one who has been brought [to health] and whose strength has been generated over seven days.
