one should administer it according to the person's age and strength. // 124 //
The essential meaning is this:
the quantity [of liquid] prescribed for well-known decoctions and gruels is the same as that for fats; however, the Noble Ones have stated that for fats, it should be half of that amount.
One should not administer an enema to a person who has not eaten, for it would fall into an empty bowel and cause disorders. (125)
Therefore, having quickly fed him what is appropriate for that,
one should properly administer an oil enema along with the rising sun.
Due to ignorance, that very same [practice], when joined with excessively clever devotion, directly causes fever; therefore, it should be applied only in that specific way.
The essential meaning is this: for one who has been given a very large quantity of food that is excessively unctuous,
the physician should not administer an oil enema (anuvāsana), even if it is well-known [to be effective].
Fainting, thirst, intoxication, and fever are said to be caused by this; thus, this unctuous substance is employed for these two types [of disorders]. // 127 //
The essential meaning is this:

having observed the sequence of diet, one should treat the intoxication of disease with milk and even with superior groups of medicinal compounds containing a high proportion of parched grain flour (*khala*).
Having fed that patient with appropriate food reduced by one-quarter, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) according to the prescribed method.
The medicinal substance does not pervade upward once it has acquired the potency of the oil; therefore, one should first purify that [channel]. (129)
The essential meaning is:
having administered a non-unctuous enema two, three, or even more times to that person who possesses powerful and greatly aggravated bodily humors, one should then administer an unctuous enema.
Having himself reflected upon the path of the doshas, he should then properly administer a niruha enema to that patient whose body has been lubricated.
The meaning of the passage is this:
having recognized him here as one whose body is impure due to exceedingly powerful impurities, and whose limbs are visibly tormented by the vital winds (prāṇa).
The essential meaning is as follows: having well-anointed [the image] and bathed it here with waters of bliss,
one should feed it according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures.
Combined with the powder of rock salt and bright śatapuṣpa, that is the properly administered oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared according to the rules. // 132 //
The person whose enema has been administered with oil prepared according to the prescribed method should lie on their back with limbs raised,
moved, and comfortably extended.
Striking the buttocks with the palms of the hands is prescribed. // 133 //
One should raise and lower the bed three times in this manner for the purpose of spreading and circulating the oil.
He should say to him: "Wait here for just a hundred moments on the side of Sudakṣiṇā’s thigh. (134)
Thus, having been appointed to perform the well-arranged rites of hospitality,
you may now rest here at ease for the removal of impurity.
One should tell him, "Stay," according to the rule for each step, as he proceeds toward the evacuation of impurities in whatever manner possible. (135)
The meaning of the verse is this: one should stand having completely expelled the wind residing within the entire body through the second *dvasti* (the *samyak* [correct] *dvasti*).
When administered according to the prescribed rite, the third [ingredient] brings about luster, complexion, and strength; the fourth [ingredient] likewise;
and this great fifth [ingredient], when employed here, provides blood that is truly and perfectly pure. (136)

The sixth is the oil enema (snehabasti), which moistens the flesh and the vital essences; the seventh is that which one should administer as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), followed by unctuous enemas on the ninth, tenth, and eighth days respectively. (137)

The essential meaning is this: by employing even three hundred and twenty-four such highly unctuous enemas, a mortal becomes immortal in nature; through his own qualities, he becomes a second [Brahmā] who is yet without a second.
One who directly realizes Kāma—the one who steals the heart, mind, and eyes of all embodied beings—shall live for a thousand years with a divine self-body and endowed with powerful strength. 138.
That which possesses the essential nature of oleation, is accompanied by strong wind, and is associated with feces— this,
when administered according to the prescribed method as a great unctuous enema (mahāsnehabasti), acts with perfect efficacy due to its specific qualities.

Indeed, when the *sneha* (unctuous substance) is very small and is itself overwhelmed by the great mass of manifest *doṣas*, it does not move at all but remains stationary; this occurs due to the various distinctions among the *doṣas* that bring about affliction. // 139 //
The essential meaning is:
in Vāta, the mouth becomes astringent, and there is an irregular, rough fever accompanied by intense pain;
through Pitta, the mouth becomes pungent, and likewise there is a fever with abundant Pitta and a yellowish appearance.
In the case of *śleṣman* (phlegm), the mouth becomes sweet, as do excessive salivation and cold fever; furthermore, vomiting and excessive salivation occur.
Therefore, in this condition, a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) is beneficial for the purpose of breaking up the morbid humors (*doṣa*).
The essential meaning is this:
when a properly prepared and beneficial unctuous enema (snehabasti) is administered to one who has consumed a full meal, it returns mixed with food;
consequently, there occurs oppression of the heart, dyspnea, and cough.
Hoarseness of voice, loss of appetite, obstruction of the movement of the wind (vāyu), and heaviness in the abdomen may also occur;
after performing a fast accompanied by its appropriate regimen, one should administer digestive stimulants (dīpana). // 141 //
Let him duly bestow the essence of existence, as well as fierce [medicines] and after-potions, for the sake of their happiness and welfare. (142)
The essential meaning is this:

when the *sneha* (oleaginous substance) is excessively forced upward with great force, it gives rise to dyspnea, pain in the sides, cough, loss of appetite, vomiting, dizziness, heaviness of the head, and excessive sleepiness. These symptoms pervade the patient.

Having prepared an unguent for the face and an ointment for all the sense organs of the body, the noble one should apply it; and knowing the procedure, he should administer it by means of a method that causes intense pain. (143)
The essential meaning is that one does not return here to this manifest body, which is known to be devoid of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
If the oil remains in the abdomen, it causes heaviness, a bad taste in the mouth, flatulence, and colic;
in that case, an asthāpana enema is beneficial, followed by a mild anuvāsana enema at the conclusion of the treatment.
The essential meaning is this:
when food is very little, an oil enema (snehabasti) that is small in quantity and well-prepared with wholesome ingredients does not cause the exhaustion,
loss of taste, heaviness of the head, or extreme weakness of the limbs that would otherwise arise at that time.
He was a jewel, possessed of great vigor and heroic strength, surrounded by medicinal herbs, and the sole knower of what ought and ought not to be done in every matter.
The essential meaning is this:

if an unctuous substance (sneha) that is excessively hot, too sharp, or combined with water and wind is administered in an excessive dose, it flows out with immediate force; therefore, there is no benefit, and one should act [to remedy it].
When the enema has been properly administered repeatedly over several days and nights, it is withdrawn;
or, like food that has been digested, the enema becomes weak in its potency. (146)

Thus has been described this enema with unctuous substances (snehabasti), which is rich in a multitude of various benefits and endowed with true therapeutic efficacy; hereafter, the grand non-unctuous enema (nirūha), though already mentioned, shall be explained in detail.
The meaning of the verse is:
having quickly performed the evacuation of urine and feces by one whose body is distressed by intense heat and who has surrendered his self; // 148 //
One who knows the prescribed sequence should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) here according to the method already described. // 149 //
The essential meaning is this:

when the movement of urine, feces, well-balanced bile, phlegm, and wind is clearly observed here, as well as the alleviation of pain and lightness of the body—this indeed constitutes a successful enema (sunirūha). (150)
The essential meaning is: the suppression of disease,
the extreme purification of impurities, and the satisfaction of one's own senses, self, and mind.
Indeed, this very same set of excellent characteristics has been declared for both oil enemas (snehavasti) and decoction enemas (nirūha). // 151 //
The essential meaning is this:

in that condition, enemas consisting of a paste, decoction, oil, ghee, and rock salt (saindhava) of drugs that alleviate Vāta, combined with sour substances, administered lukewarm, provide relief for a body in which the Vāta has become aggravated. (152)
The meaning is as follows; "vyādhitāniha" is an alternative reading.

Enemas prepared with water boiled from milk-yielding trees, lotuses, blue lilies, *kākolī*, and other such herbs, and then well-cooled—mixed with sugar, ghee, and milk—are beneficial for aggravated *pitta*. (153)
The essential meaning is:

Enemas consisting of *rājavṛkṣa*, *kuṭaja*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), *ugrā*, alkali, and water, combined with urine and salts such as *saindhava*, are lukewarm and destroy the greatly aggravated *kapha* in the thighs. (154)
The meaning of the term is as follows:

these enemas (bastis), consisting of purifying liquids, well-prepared pastes (kalka), fats (sneha), and rock salt, are renowned by the name "purifying" (śodhana); they are specifically prescribed for the purpose of purification. // 155 //
The essential meaning is that enemas (bastis) consisting of alkali and urine, intensified by a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā), mixed with pungent medicines,
and combined with salts such as ūṣaka and others, produce a thin scraping action. // 156 //
The essential meaning is:

having prepared astringent *aśvagandhā* and excellent *vajralatā*, combined with the remaining sweet medicinal herbs, these enemas—rich in buffalo and cow urine, curd, milk, and ghee—are known as "manifest nourishing" (*prakaṭabṛṃhaṇa*) enemas. (157)

The essential meaning is that enemas (bastis) prepared with the milky trees, sweet medicinal herbs, cooling substances, water, and excellent pastes— smeared with sugar, sugarcane juice, milk, and ghee— are uniquely distinguished as pacifiers [of the disease]. // 158 //
The essential meaning is:
enemas prepared with the pastes and decoctions of uccaṭā, ikṣuraka, gokṣura, yaṣṭīmadhu, māṣa, and guptaphala, combined with abundant ghee, sugar, and milk, are excellent aphrodisiacs. (159)

The essential meaning is that enemas designated as "slimy" (picchila) are prepared with groups of slimy plants such as *śelu*, *śālmali*, *vidārī*, *badarī*, *airāvatī*, and others, along with mature urine, ghee, milk, and *sukarkara*. (160)
The essential meaning is that enemas prepared with the decoction and fine paste of *satpriya* (a type of *priyaṅgu*), *ghanavāri* (liquorice), and *samaṅgā*,
combined with goat’s milk, are always declared to be constipating (*sāṃgrāhika*). (161)
The essential meaning is this:
for childless men and women, an oil enema prepared from the fat of a hundred black bulls matured by the power of [herbs] bestows most excellent and truly noble sons. (162)
The essential meaning is as follows: here, the preparation of jaggery and oil will be described for the purpose of removing the dangerous humors (doṣas) of women. // 163 //
The essential meaning is this: regarding the enjoyment of food, drink, beds, and seats, there is no rule for their avoidance;
rather, whatever one desires may be employed at that very time, provided it is prepared with molasses or oil and is productive of fruit. (164)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: Here, "gauḍatailikam" refers to a decoction enema (nirūha) in which jaggery and oil are present in equal amounts;
when combined with decoctions of the roots of various seed-bearing trees, it removes irregularities of the bodily humors. // 165 //
The essential meaning is this: jaggery derived from sesame is the same as that [from sugarcane], and it is likewise when combined with its decoction; so too is jaṭilā.
This enema, combined with long pepper (piṇḍī), madana fruit, and rock salt, is known as the Vasuyuktaratha. // 166 //
The meaning of the verse: A decoction enema (basti) prepared with devadāru, śatapuṣpā, surasā, hiṅgu, saindhava, jaggery, sesame oil,
and the decoctions of the roots of citra, bīja, and taru, is a destroyer of even the most severe colic.
The meaning of the essence is this:

a prepared enema (siddhabasti) rich with the decoctions of kola, sata, yava, and kulattha, combined with pippalī, madhuka, and saindhava salt, and mixed with aged, high-quality jaggery and sesame oil; this is the one that bears successful fruit. 168.
Regarding the meaning of the term *bhāvārtha*:

prepare a well-administered enema (*basti*) many times with ancient jaggery, sesame seeds, and equal parts of honey, combined with a decoction, using various medicinal drugs to remove the diverse types of *doṣas*. (169)
The meaning of the term is "produced from sesame"; there is an alternative reading, *tilajaṃ*.
O men, apply the groups of enemas mentioned here, as well as some from the superior groups of vehicles, continuously and with great respect toward the best of men, without any hesitation. (170)
This essential meaning should be applied in every way to those who are extremely gentle, as well as to those groups with very few faults and those who are exceedingly happy. // 171 //
The meaning of the subject matter [is as follows]:
from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence (padārtha).

For this [teaching], which resembles a conch shell, has issued forth from that which shines with the two banks of the means for accomplishing the welfare of both states of existence; it is the sole benefit for the world. (172)

Having paid homage to the glorious Lord of Jinas, who is worshipped by the lords of gods, we shall explain the procedure for the urethral enema (uttara-vasti) as taught [in the scriptures], including its specific characteristics, administration, and dosage, for the purpose of eliminating seminal and menstrual disorders and manifesting the underlying defects. // 1 //
The essential meaning is this:
as was stated by way of the illustration of the cluster of *mālatī* flowers, the enema (*basti*) was then administered with a fine nozzle.
In brief, I shall explain the procedure for the remediation of all defects pertaining to the semen and menses of men and women. // 2 //
The meaning of the verse is: [the practitioner] should remain in the utkaṭikāsana posture, having voided urine and excrement.
Having drunk gruel mixed with ghee and milk upon a plank reaching up to his own knees, which is provided with a pillow; (3)
And here, having drawn up the urine, one should likewise equalize it with that [substance].
Having pressed the thighs together, one should experience bliss gradually. // 4 //
The meaning of the essence for men should be exactly one *prakucamita* of oil;
for women, half of that, and for the first [category], half of that is prescribed.
The liquid [substance] is double that measure, spread out. // 5 //

The essential meaning is as follows: having understood that the introduction of the liquid has been prescribed by the authoritative means of knowledge, one should then slowly withdraw the tube from the eye;
and once it has returned [to its place], having observed it well, one should feed the patient here at midday with food consisting of milk and various soups.
The essential meaning is as follows:
one should likewise administer three enemas known as *uttarabasti* containing the aforementioned substances, as well as four others;
for the sake of pacifying the many excellent disorders of semen and menses, I shall now describe the two seeds and the preeminent groups of diseases. (7)
The essential meaning is this:
semen and blood that have been struck by the humors such as wind (vāta) and the rest should indeed be known by the symptoms and sensations produced by their own respective defects.
The corpse, which is foul-smelling by its very nature, arises from an abundance of blood and humors;
it is characterized by numerous knots and is produced from phlegm and wind.
The seed becomes exceedingly thick and putrid,
produced by the disorder of bile and blood.
However, there may be a smell of excrement produced by a combination of humors (sannipāta), which arises from depletion due to wasting or from excessive sexual intercourse. // 9 //
The essential meaning is this:
among those [diseases], the seed-diseases (bījaroga) produced by the three doṣas are indeed curable,
as are those that are like a corpse or pus, though they are all difficult to treat.
The odor of feces is indeed most difficult to cure directly; however, those caused by the three types of *doṣas* through unctuousness (*sneha*) and other treatments are easily curable.
The meaning here is that the prescription of the following remedies will indeed serve to ward off the preeminent defects of semen and menstrual blood.
One who has purified himself should drink ghee, which is renowned as the most excellent essence, when the semen is tied up with a corpse. (11)
The essential meaning is as follows:
one should drink ghee prepared with the ashes of *palāśa*, *khadira*, and *arjuna* when the semen (*śukra*) has a thick, slimy, pale-white appearance like a knot;
and one should drink that which is prepared with *hintāla*, *tāla*, *vaṭa*, and *pāṭala* when one's own seed resembles excessive pus. (12)

The essential meaning is as follows: in cases of foul-smelling urine, one should drink the excellent *siddha-ghṛta* (medicated clarified butter) prepared with *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *agnimantha*, *abhayā*, and *musta*.

In the event of a decline in semen, one should increase it through the aforementioned aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*) great formulations and by means of the procedures for *rasāyana* and *rasāyana* elixirs. // 13 //
The essential meaning is this: in these five [conditions] consisting of disorders of semen and blood, one should employ the procedure of oleation and so forth along with the uttarabasti;
likewise, in cases of various disorders of the menses, one should perform various purificatory measures for their cleansing.
[He abandons] the afflictions along with their underlying tendencies. // 14 //
One should drink medicinal pastes (kalka) combined with sesame oil according to the prescribed method, as well as wholesome foods, gargles, fumigations, and ointments.
One should administer purificatory treatments (saṃśodhana) according to the proper procedures for the female genital tract to destroy disorders of the menstrual flow (ārtava). || 15 ||
The essential meaning:

For those suffering from abundant glandular swellings caused by the obstruction of phlegm and wind due to menstrual disorders, one should drink a decoction of *devadāru*, mango, *sarala*, *aguru*, and sandalwood, resembling foul-smelling pus and marrow; or a decoction of *kuṭaja* along with the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*) for similar conditions. (16)
The essential meaning is as follows:

here, semen that is exceedingly pure, moistened by the purification of the seed, fragrant, sweet, possessing the luster of a crystal stone, resembling honey, and like sesame oil—such pure semen becomes the supreme cause for an excellent son. (17)
The meaning of the essential nature is as follows: pure menstrual blood is like a cluster of *maṇiśilā* juice and *haṃsapādi* mud, or like the blood from a rabbit's body;
it resembles lac-dye and has the luster of bright saffron, yet when washed, that excellent seed does not lose its color.
The essential meaning is this: here, from the predominance of pure menstrual blood (*ārtava*), a girl is produced; and from the excess of semen (*śukra*), it brings about a son.
When there is equality between the two, it quickly produces a state of neuter-ness (*napuṃsakatva*); for that [result] arises specifically from the particular transformation governed by karma. (19)
The essential meaning is this:
a man who has observed the vow of Brahman, whose own semen is more pure and even purer than the pure menstrual blood of his wife,
should bathe and, with great effort, approach his own wife from the fourth day onwards for a period of at most one month.
For among those who are established [in their vows], one who desires a son [should act]. // 20 //
Regarding the meaning of the state [of pregnancy]:
experts declare that the period when menstruation is seen lasts ten days; even if it is not actually seen, they say it lasts sixteen nights.
Immediately upon conceiving a fetus from an excellent husband, there appear auspicious signs such as lassitude, fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, and a movement in the abdomen. (21)
In each and every one of them.
This is an alternative reading. The meaning is:
for two months, she who is pregnant should be given daily [a preparation] enriched with sweet and cooling medicinal herbs and combined with fresh butter.
In the third month, one should have her constantly eat śāli rice with well-prepared cow's milk. // 22 //
In the fourth month, she should indeed be properly and repeatedly fed with curd; in this fifth month, with cow’s milk by the worshipful one;
and in the sixth month, as in the fourth, and then in the seventh month, when the hair begins to grow, one should have her eat both milk and solid food.

One should drink every day an appropriate dose of ghee cooked with the decoctions of *yaṣṭī*, *ambuja*, *ambuvara*, *niṃba*, *kadaṃba*, *jaṃbū*, and *raṃbhā*, along with curd and milk, for the pacification of bodily heat; hereafter, the remedy for the eighth month is described. (24)

The meaning of the passage is as follows: one should then administer [the treatment] with oil prepared according to the *balā* formula, combined with clarified butter (*ājya*) and mixed with curd and milk,
or with oil processed with the eight sweet medicinal herbs (*aṣṭamadhura-oṣadha*).
When cooked,
it is beneficial when administered as an anuvāsana enema.
Therefore, for the benefit of the woman, perform now both the enema (basti) and the urethral/vaginal enema (uttarabasti) with the prepared oil;
when this is done according to the rules even in the ninth month, it pacifies all defects entirely, and she will give birth easily.
The meaning of the symptoms is as follows:
there will be excessive pain in the waist and in the region of her own back, and phlegm along with urine will flow excessively.
Recognizing that she has recently given birth, they should anoint her with oil and bathe her with warm water. (27)
She should lie down after approaching him in that manner; having observed that the woman has reached her time and is intent on delivery, she should assist her gradually and gently with effort.
Then, by removing the obstruction directly and firmly, she causes her to give birth easily. (28)
The essential meaning is:
having purified that [womb] which has become clean through water, *cāṃbuka*, rock salt, and clarified butter, one should enter it even though its limbs have not yet been fully developed.
Having cut [the cord] bound with eight soft and long fingers' breadth of thread, place it around the neck smeared with oil. // 29 //
"Nāli" is a variant reading according to the Sūtra. The meaning is as follows:
perform all that has been prescribed here in this Susaṃhitā for the sake of nourishing the child.
One should cause that woman who has recently given birth to drink a gruel (yavāgū) that is well-smeared with oil, enriched with fats, and made very warm with a sour flavor. // 30 //

The meaning of the verse is as follows: one should seize her with the hand and draw away another woman who is clinging to her; then one should have her drink a preparation of an abundance of *lāṅgalakī* paste.
Having smeared the soles of the feet, the navel, and the region of the abdomen, one should fumigate the vagina with the oil of snake-skin. (31)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: Having thus performed the rites so that she may be comfortable and give birth easily,
the midwife should then diligently provide her with massages, abundant nourishment for the birth canal, drinks, and so forth, for one month, in order to ward off powerful winds.
The essential meaning is this:
one should properly conquer even that severe colic caused by vitiated blood known as āṛkasa,
using enemas (basti) according to rule, as well as urethral/vaginal enemas (uttarabasti), with well-known medicinal groups that dispel vāta.
The meaning of the state [of health] is the removal of diseases caused by difficult afflictions, many humors, and suppressed poisons.

The enema known here as *uttara* (urethral/vaginal) conquers all disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yoni*) and the seminal fluid (*śukra*), as well as those affecting the vital points (*marman*). // 34 //

The essential meaning here is that the treatment for the complications of the application of smoke-inhalation (*dhūma*) will now be fully set forth. In this context, smoke is of five types: those used for the administration of oleation (*sneha*), emesis (*vamana*), and strong purgation (*ativireka*).
By them. // 35 //
The meaning of the ritual:
having wrapped the arrow, which is eight finger-breadths long, with a cloth,
one should smear it with pure guggulu resin and sarja-nāma.
When administered as medicated smoke, even one that is very dry becomes oily within the body due to its being infused with oil. // 36 //
"Nasyaiḥ" is an alternative reading;
"sūtreṇa" is another alternative reading.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

[The treatment] for the *prāyogika* type involves *elā*, *lavaṅga*, *gajapuṣpa*, and *tamālapatra*; for the *vamana* (emetic) type, it involves emetics; for the *vairecana* (purgative) type, it involves the various head-purgatives (*śirovireka*) already mentioned; and for the *kāsanaka* (cough-destroying) type, it involves the well-known medicinal herbs that cure coughs. (37)
The essential meaning regarding the preparatory [medicinal] application is as follows: here, the nozzle should be forty-eight finger-breadths long and filled with a mixture of ghee and oil;
for the Lord of Jinas, it is thirty-two [finger-breadths], while for the other two types of purgatives, it is indeed sixteen.
The essential meaning is this:
if there is an excessive discharge of oil through their mouths, one should remove it from the nose;
likewise, one should properly eliminate the other type of induced purgation (prāyogika) through the nose, and the other [emetic] type through the mouth alone. (39)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

One should expel through the mouth itself that thick smoke which was inhaled through the nostrils; likewise, one should release through the nose that which was taken in through the mouth. However, those who are experts in the specific doctrines of the Jaina scriptures do not approve of the reverse.
The essential meaning is as follows:

those afflicted by fainting, intoxication, vertigo, burning sensations, thirst, heat, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), exhaustion, potent poisons, grief, or fear; those suffering from anemia, urinary disorders, blindness, upward-moving wind, or abdominal enlargement; and those whose bodies are weakened by old age, childhood, or purgation—[these should not be treated with emetics]. // 41 //

Those who have been treated with medicinal enemas, those with wounds on the chest, those suffering from ulcers, those carrying fetuses, those who have suddenly consumed liquid substances, those who are emaciated, those whose diet consists of meat, and indeed those men deficient in phlegm (śleṣman)—these are to be excluded from the use of medicated smoke (dhūma). // 42 //
The meaning of the essential point is as follows:

after bathing, or even after eating food, or after sleeping excessively, or after engaging in sexual intercourse, or after discharging impurity, or after sneezing, or after vomiting, or for the purpose of cleansing the teeth, a person should daily employ the preliminary rite (prāyogika) prescribed by the Buddha. // 43 //
The essential meaning is this:

since the provocation of the humors (doṣas) occurs directly during eight specific occasions, "smoke" (dhūma) is prescribed as the sole cause for its pacification; thus it is explained in the Jaina doctrine, and by that statement, there is the alleviation of the pain caused by the ingestion of poison. 44.
The essential meaning is this:
by that, the sense faculties become pure, the mind becomes serene,
and there shall always be firmness in the rows of teeth and hair.
It shall be a destroyer of glass-like phlegm and its discharge. // 45 //
The essential meaning is that it causes lethargy, catarrh, heaviness of the head,
foul odor in the mouth, and diseases arising within the oral cavity.
When properly administered here by those skilled in the methods of yoga, over-application, and contraindications, medicinal smoke destroys [diseases].
The meaning of existence is yoga, which is the cause for the destruction of excessive disease; conversely,
non-yoga is directly the cause for the increase of disease.
Excessive application (atiyoga) here consists of the over-application of suitable medicinal substances;
this should be carefully considered in all procedures involving manifest actions with medicines. (47)
The pathophysiology is as follows:

during the stage of atiyoga (excessive administration) of *dhūma* (fumigation), there occurs an excessive ringing in the ears, pain in the head, weakness, a burning sensation, thirst, and excessive tearing. One should satiate the head with nasal drops of clarified butter (*nasya-ghṛta*) and thus conquer that condition.
The essential meaning is as follows:

the dosage for the preparatory [purgative] is here the amount that causes the falling of the stool; for the remaining [types], the limit should be set by the complete expulsion of the morbid humors (*doṣa*).
Having drunk the medicine, one should drink gruel made from sesame and rice, and then inhale the smoke well-known from emetic medicines. (49)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Having performed the smoke-inhalation (*dhūma*) according to the rules, I shall now perform the application of gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*) and the taking of medicinal boluses (*kavalagraha*) for the purpose of cleansing the mouth.
That which is called a *gaṇḍūṣa* consists of holding a liquid; however, that which is known as *kavalagraha* may also consist of dried medicinal herbs. (50)
The meaning of the essence is that one should stir the paste with salt, sour substances, and pleasantly warm water.
One should hold that [liquid] steady; therefore, one should proclaim it as "drava" (the flowing). // 51 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows: As long as the medicine remains enveloped by phlegm, the mouth should remain full and motionless;
when the medicine flows over the eyes and reaches the nostrils, one should release it completely. (52)
The meaning of the verse:
Having grasped another [meaning], one should again transfer it by means of sequential progression and then release it properly;
once the defect has departed—just as the heaviness of the head has vanished—one should carefully apply effort so that the loss of voice residing in the face is well-removed. (53)
Others say that nothing else should be used beyond what is necessary, as it causes excessive drying of the throat and serves as a cause for complications such as thirst;

however, bold practitioners maintain that groups of substances—alkaline, sour, oil, ghee, urine, and decoctions—should be administered according to the specific distinctions of the patient's own doshas.
The meaning of the verse: The measure prescribed here for the liquid used in gargling is "half the mouth" (mukhārdha); there is nothing else besides this.
When the mouth is full, that liquid should be swirled within; if it is less than that, it will not remove the defects completely. // 55 //
The essential meaning is this:

therefore, for the sake of removing all defects without exception, that liquid [medicine] should be administered in a dose equal to half the capacity of the mouth; likewise, one desiring the removal of every defect should prepare a bolus with dried medicinal herbs according to the rules and chew it thoroughly. 56.
The essential meaning is as follows:
having thus described [the procedures], I shall now speak of the nasal medication (nasya) known as *kavalagraha*, which has indeed been taught in the *Saṃhitā*.
Nasal medication is properly of four types, yet it is twofold: that intended for oleation (*snehana*), and the other, which is head-purgation (*śirovireka*). (57)
The essential meaning is this:

that which is prescribed for the purpose of nourishment, which increases the strength of the throat, blood, head, shoulders, and chest, and which bestows a favorable gaze, should be administered in cases of injury from wind (vāta), headache, and conditions affecting the voice, teeth, hair, beard, and the harshness or roughness of the skin. (58)

The essential meaning is that this treatment known as *susnehana* is exceedingly beneficial for men in cases of ear diseases, cataracts, hoarseness of voice, dryness of the mouth, premature graying of hair, and even in the loss of youth; it is also highly effective for oral ailments arising from *pitta* and *vāta*. (59)
The essential meaning is this:

that which constitutes head-evacuation (śirovirecana) should be employed for the multitude of diseases arising from phlegm (kapha) above the clavicle; one should administer both types of nasal therapy (nasya) to those who have not eaten, during the appropriate time when the sky is cloudless, using methods such as warming the hands.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
Having properly steamed the regions of the cheeks, throat, ears, and forehead, one should place [the hands] slightly delayed upon the head;
then, in this manner, one should duly apply comfortably warm drops into these two nostrils, which possess two excellent openings with their tips raised. 61.

One should administer eight measures of oil; here, the first prescribed dose is given individually, while the other three doses should be administered in a sequence doubling each time within the three types of beautiful vessels. // 62 //
The essential meaning is this:

indeed, this nasal medication (nasya) is prescribed for the purpose of producing excellent oleation, as is the continuous and correct application of pratimarśana. In that regard, it should be performed according to the rules during the specified times when the [previous] period has passed. // 63 //
The essential meaning is this:

when a man has risen at dawn and performed the ritual rinsing (avamarśa), it completely removes the impurity accumulated during the night— whether it has entered through the nose or the mouth— as well as powerful sleep, provided it is practiced at the time of departing from one's dwelling.

This [betel], when applied to the teeth after rinsing the mouth with cold water, removes the excessive affliction caused by wind, heat, smoke, and dust that have reached the nose; it bestows firmness upon the teeth and great fragrance to the mouth. (65)
If performed by one who has risen from excessive sleep during the day, this *pratimarśana* (nasal drop) alleviates pain and removes excessive [dosha];
having dispelled the residual drowsiness as well as the heaviness of the head, it brings comfort even to that afflicted person. (66)

The essential meaning [of this teaching], when applied by a person distressed by the fatigue of the path, dispels that very fatigue; likewise, even for one who has always well-uttered [the mantra], this [mantra], when consecrated, immediately pacifies all suffering of the limbs situated upon the body, just as a rain cloud does. (67)
The meaning of the underlying principle is this:
even in a man who has vomited, [the medicine] when administered as an emetic quickly and completely removes the phlegm stuck in the throat;
furthermore, the contemplation (*avamarśa*) of one who has already tasted it produces a direct longing for the food and, in this world, brings about the purification of the channels of hearing.
The essential meaning is this:

having been prepared in the evening, this [mixture] constantly provides men with the comfort of sleep at night and ensures a pleasant awakening. It is also stated that the prescribed measure for its application is the introduction of clarified butter (ghṛta) into the mouth via the nostrils. 69.

From this [practice], the intended result shall arise; moreover, through constant reflection upon it, the mouth becomes fragrant, one's own teeth and hair become firm, and all diseases arising from the ears, eyes, face, and nose, as well as those located in the upper throat and above the collarbone, shall perish. (70)
Thus has the meaning of the [preceding] section been declared; hereafter I shall describe the examination and the supreme head-purgative (śirovireka).
That which reaches the nose is known as *nasya*, and likewise, head-purgation (*śirovireka*) is performed with dry medicinal substances. (71)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: one should add this quantity prepared with a purgative liquid, four drops at a time;
thus made, it constitutes the first dose, and thereafter the doses follow in a sequence of doubling each time. (72)
The essential meaning is that three measures are fixed for the three types of *tripuṭa*;
they should be applied for the purposes of excitation, purification, and thorough pacification.
The physician should determine the dosage according to the increase of the humors,
for it is through the dosage that the purification of the humors indeed occurs in this world. (73)
"Bhāvārthaḥ karoti" is an alternative reading.

When this head-purgative (śirovirecana) is properly administered by those who know its application and its contraindications, it brings about purification and even the cleansing of phlegm that has become powerful. (74)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: there is a channel whose opening resembles the two teats of a goat;
it has a symmetrical form and is provided with two hollows according to the excellent rule.
Having constructed the yantra according to the rules, with the face turned toward the excellent peak,
the intended meaning is that the three yogas should be performed here according to the procedure, just as in the case of smoke.

In the same manner, everything regarding the procedure for the administration of *rasana* has been declared; one should likewise perform the treatment for the complications arising from excessive use of *dhūma*, as well as that concerning the excessive application of *nasya*. // 76 //
The essential meaning is that one should apply [the practice] through the sequence of being skillful, virtuous, and matured.
I shall now describe it in detail, yet characterized by few syllables. // 77 //
The meaning of the state [of being] is distinct from those [elements], characterized by specific qualities, and produced through the connection of skin and flesh.

Swelling may be uneven or even, extensive or small, and it may be accompanied by a sense of rigidity; it arises from Vāta and the other [doshas], from blood, from all of them combined, or from an exogenous cause. (78)
The essential meaning is this:
from those [factors], swellings arise due to the emergence of specific defects, qualities, and the absence of defects;
among these, the swelling produced by blood is like that produced by pitta, being exceedingly black.
Now, the excellent characteristics of those [tumors] as they appear in the raw, inflamed, and ripened stages will be described. // 79 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

due to the power of his faults, through the conjunction of adverse circumstances every day, or because of being devoid of proper external and internal practices, he has himself come to a state of pacification [of his faculties].

That swelling which is hard, with little pain, endowed with a very firm consistency and a color similar to the skin, characterized by low temperature and being extremely cold, is known as the swelling called *āmā* (unripe). // 80 //
The meaning of the state [of the disease] is as follows: that which is of many kinds, extremely severe, with excessive heat, and highly agitated;
and that which is predominant, discolored, hideous, and equal to a distended bladder.
There is also an alternative reading, "avikaḥ.
That which is scorched (vidagdha) is known as being like one pierced by thirst, causing extreme loss of appetite and difficulty in eating. // 81 //
The essential meaning is this:
that which is slightly painful, very soft, bloodless, and small by itself,
and is characterized by the wise through itching, flaking of the skin, pricking, wrinkling, depressions, and so forth.
That which is cold, free from complications, appetizing, and ripe is called *saśopha* (with swelling) and *amṛta* (nectar-like). // 82 //
The essential meaning is this: one should not be deluded by thinking that one is unripe simply because one has not seen the signs of complete ripeness; enough of this.

Furthermore, where the physician [finds] the swelling to be cooler, with skin that is smooth and of normal color, he should quickly cleanse it after dispelling all delusion and removing the swelling. (83)
The essential meaning is:
if it is improperly digested by the digestive fires, one should further cook it with binding substances.
Having bound [it], even the binding is said to be extremely loose, tight, or even.
The essential meaning is that the joints, the eyes, and the ligaments are said to be loose; the face is even;
and the limbs, ears, throat, penis, testicles, back, thighs, sides, and chest are [even].

The physician, skilled in the science of medicine and prepared for medical treatment, should apply [the medicinal substances] firmly to the buttocks, head, thighs, knees, hips, belly, and likewise to the armpits. 85.

There, one should prepare a lotus known as a blue water-lily (nīlotpala), a bud, and a water-lily (kuvalaya), along with mud produced therein,

A mortal would become lotus-faced, most beloved, and though old, suddenly possessed of youth.

The meaning of the verse:

Thus, according to the method of the path of the aphorisms, I have accomplished this black ritual application (kṛṣṇaprayoga),
which has its subject matter taught by the perfected ones (siddhas) and is transmitted through the lineage of the established tenets (siddhānta).
One should give for the sake of youth; therefore, out of compassion, I shall explain that which brings about this goal.
The essential meaning [of this work] has been drawn from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon both banks by accomplishing the welfare of beings in both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (109)
The meaning of the subject matter:
Having prostrated before Jinavallabha, the renowned Lord of the Three Worlds,
who removes the pride and arrogance of those uplifted by the lack of primary wealth;
The science of medicine has been expounded in its entirety for the Lord of men,
for the purpose of preserving the body and bringing about a multitude of great benefits.
The essential meaning here is that for men, the preservation of the body leads to an increase in lifespan;
furthermore, the strength of the senses and the physical vigor of men flourish.
Beyond this, we shall explain the further processing of the rasa. // 2 //
The meaning of the essential nature,
through its specific sequential order, is fully capable of bringing forth the entire collection of objects.
The complete dissolution of the vital essence (rasa), death, and extraction and binding—this is declared as the threefold procedure; indeed, its fruit is likewise threefold. // 3 //
The essential meaning is this:
indeed, Mercury (Rasa) when in a state of swoon (mūrchita) removes malignant diseases by itself;
but when dead (mṛta), it is considered to inevitably bestow the enjoyment of wealth and grain.
When the bond of searching for what has been described is accomplished here, it is said that one then attains incomparable mastery over the sky, as well as freedom from old age and death. // 4 //
The essential meaning is this:
one certainly dies by means of cow-tethers that have a taste like the kapittha fruit.
By means of the Palāśa seed and its juice mixed with well-ground cumin,
or by means of Kucī seeds, the destruction of mercury occurs instantaneously.
The patient, according to the measure of his humors, should daily drink the essence of the processed mercury along with matured milk and jaggery.
Immediately after that, one should employ the "Squeezing of the Woman's Limbs" (aṅganākaravinardana).
The meaning of the essential point is this:
by this method, the mercury permeates the entire body;
through the power of the application, the permeation of the mercury is clearly understood.
From the rubbing of gold [on the body], there arises superior vigor and freedom from disease;
furthermore, the practice of elixirs (rasāyana) should always be applied daily.
The essential meaning is this:
indeed, mercury becomes a true elixir (*rasāyana*) only when it is clearly bound;
it is not consumed when merely processed with other liquids or groups of metals.
That connection with the irreproachable rasa is clearly established here. // 8 //

The meaning of the passage:

at an auspicious moment when the ascendant is joined with its own lunar strength and the proper karaṇa.

The essential meaning is as follows: having followed the Lord of Jinas as the presiding deity, and having established the Lord of Yakṣas and the boon-granting Goddess Ambikā, who resides at Āmrakūṣyāṇḍa;
The five excellent mantras of the beloved Guru consist of four times six [units].
One should daily undertake the worship of all those who are beloved by the Victors without exception.

Having received this previously performed initiation, which is characterized by devotion to the most eminent perfected one and accompanied by the nine planets, the wise man should undertake it for the sake of attaining mastery over mercury.
The meaning of the verse: Then one should purify mercury (rasendra) combined with very beautiful bricks,
having thoroughly ground it with the juice produced from breasts upon a stone mortar.

One should cook [the meat], which has been well-washed and placed in a large vessel suspended over a swing of sour gruel (*kāñjika*), enriched with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), sour gruel, the group of salts, and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*).

The essential meaning is as follows: here I shall describe the transference of the bound, purified, and perfected king of essences (rasarāja). [The ingredients are] honey, crow-dung, a tube, earwax, and buffalo [gall].
The milk of a woman, human blood, and the excrement of a bat, combined with the powder of *śṛṅgī* and *ṭaṅkaṇa* and beeswax, causes one to transfer into another person who resembles a pigeon. (54)
Thus has this commentary, titled *Dīpikāntā*, which is bound together by the authentic and radiant scriptures on the womb (*yoni-śāstra*),
been explained with due reverence by those of tranquil minds for the sake of pacifying all diseases of the entire body. Its essential meaning is as follows.

By the lords of sages, who were like fierce suns, possessed of excellent conduct through their constant practice of great generosity, and who—having acted with skill and having already given wealth here—now desired to give even more, though they themselves were free from worldly desire; (55)
The meaning of the subject matter [is as follows]:
from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon the two banks that accomplish the welfare of both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water droplets for the sole benefit of the world. (56)

Having prostrated before the Lord of Jinas, who is worshipped by hosts of Indra-like sages and gods, I shall explain the essential meaning of those [meditations] which dispel the afflictions of embodied beings and bring about the destruction of even slight conceptual constructions. (1)

First, I shall explain the essential meaning of the *bhāvārtha*, which is fearless and free from conceptual construction for human beings, bestowing fearlessness upon them; thereafter, I, who am devoted to supreme effort, shall speak for the sake of men. (2)
The essential meaning is this:
indeed, *abhayā* (harītakī) bestows fearlessness and auspiciousness; by the power of constant practice, it is a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).
Combined with salts, it destroys *vāta*, and when joined with ghee, it truly and wonderfully conquers *pitta*. (3)
In this world, *bhāvārtha* combined with ginger removes phlegm and cures all diseases caused by the humors;
when taken with sugar, it overcomes severe complications, and when taken with *abhayā*, it is like a self-possessed person. (4)
Regarding the essential meaning: the pure *āmalaka* fruit, the best of fruits, is declared to be "fearless fire" (*abhayānala*).
From the Himavat it is cool (*śiśira*) for embodied beings, yet through its specific variations, the *abhayā* possesses the quality of being very hot (*uṣṇaguṇā*). (5)
The meaning of the term is "fearless," yet it is called *vibhītaka* because it possesses both qualities; thus it was well-spoken by the Jinas.
As for *triphalā*, its name is true to its meaning, for it bears here the three fruits born of the three aims of life.
The essential meaning: Triphalā is the nectar for humans on earth; triphalā removes all diseases. Triphalā sustains youth, and triphalā brings firmness to the body. (7)

Triphalā is called "triphaṃlā" by the wise; it produces marvelous intelligence, effects the purification of impurities, kindles the digestive fire, and is fully capable of carrying away all transgressions.
The essential meaning [of the verse]:

Take equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā), iron (ayas), honey (mākṣika), long pepper (māgadhikā), embelia (viḍaṅga), and the pollen of *bhṛṅgarāja*; add three times as much *vāluka* salt. This nectar-like preparation, when drunk with milk, destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha). // 9 //
The essential meaning:
Drink the three myrobalans (triphalā) combined with cow’s ghee, or the three myrobalans together with sugar;
or the three myrobalans mixed with lalitā and atibalā, or the boiled three myrobalans with *śilājatu*. (10)
The essential meaning is this:

indeed, that man who constantly drinks the three myrobalans (triphalā) combined with yogic formulations shall possess stable intellect, strength, senses, and vigor, and will attain a long life and supreme, unsurpassed well-being. (11)
The essential meaning is that even a very dark cloud is reduced to an exceedingly fine powder by a beloved woman.
Having prepared each one individually with decoctions of the three fruits (triphalā),
this [medicine] bestows all forms of fearlessness upon embodied beings.
The meaning of the verse:

Now, one who drinks this [preparation] derived from *śilodbhava*, processed with great effort using the heartwood of *khadira* and fully cooked with *triphalā*, removes even the most stubborn varieties of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). (13)
The essential meaning is as follows:

If one drinks even *śilājatu* with *śilodaka*, and always uses the bark produced from stone, as well as *nimba*, *kuṇimba*, and *suvṛkṣaka*, it is the supreme remedy for destroying all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). (14)
The essential meaning is this:
even a wasting disease (kṣayagada) may be destroyed in a mere instant by milk boiled with the paste of *śilodbhava* bark and mixed with powdered *magadhajā*, combined with excellent white sugar. (15)
The essential meaning is this:

even one who is very weak becomes exceedingly strong by constantly consuming milk-porridge (pāyasa) cooked with water mixed with the powder of excellent bark from stones; this occurs within a single month.

Furthermore, O blameless-eyed ones, quickly prepare with the finest ghee this clear collyrium made from a mixture of powdered stone, *mala*, and bark, along with a good quantity of lac; apply it to your eyes. 17.
The essential meaning here is: Drink the bark of *śilodbhava* mixed with the powder of the three fruits (*phalatrika*) along with water;
this is taught as the supreme means for emaciation, while [the same preparation] combined with ghee, sugar, and milk serves as a nourishing tonic. (18)
The essential meaning is this:
by consuming a paste of *upalavalkala*, the entire multitude of diseases shall go to destruction;
likewise, [diseases are destroyed] by *triphalā* with sugar, ghee, and beautiful *viḍaṅga* combined with *magadhajā*. (19)
Regarding the essential meaning:

as has been extensively illustrated by means of the preparation of the bark-paste of the *balvaja* grass, I shall now describe further [the preparation] of beautiful *śilājatu*, which is likewise endowed with few variations. (20)
The meaning of the passage is this: here, during the summer season, these mountains have their bodies scorched by the rays of the sun, which are like the fire of a cloud.

With their own horns—like mountain peaks, hardened and firmly set as they burst forth—they discharge streams of ichor; the three worlds become filled with that abundant vigor which surpasses all else.
The essential meaning is this:

one should properly cultivate, in their respective order and according to fixed numbers, the sources of tin, lead, iron, copper, excellent silver, and fine gold, each succeeding one being more superior than the preceding.

Here, mercury—the essence of mountains—is a medicine that produces gold and removes all diseases when combined with triphalā, water, milk, and ghee, [administered] against disorders arising from excessive phlegm, bile, and wind. (22)
The essential meaning is this:
although it is like lac, here it may be five-colored or golden;
in its application, it is comparable to mercury, possessing the best of tastes, and it penetrates all six metals.
By means of the ritual procedure prescribed in the Vedas, it produces gold directly from that very moment, without any deficiency.
The essential meaning is this:

having discerned that these non-venomous snakes have been devoured by birds, one should consume milk, ghee, and pure sugar that has been thoroughly stirred together and eaten by those birds; thus, it shall become inexhaustible.
A man who has conquered his enemies, possesses powerful virtues, and excels in valor should avoid [these]. // 24 //
The essential meaning is as follows: having personally identified various types of stones that possess shapes resembling the fruits of diverse trees,
one should repeatedly cook them with their respective fruits and juices until they are well-matured and then grind them into a fine powder.

Having prepared [the medicine] together with milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice, and having eaten food made from excellent śāli rice with ghee once it has been digested, a mortal will become immortal through its own inherent qualities. 25.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:
three *gavyūtis* from the well-known city of Kolipāka,
in the eastern direction, there is one additional black stone of *bhallātaka*.
Having understood all this through these and other means, one should remove the pure stone powder. // 26 //

One who has purified their body and whose conduct is pure should worship this in a sanctuary of the Siddhas, using one āḍhaka of that powder, one āḍhaka of excellent ghee, and one āḍhaka of bhallātaka oil.
Having ascertained the dosage for that excellent medicine, Droṇa should consume it daily in gradual succession;
likewise, he should remain in a room as described until the medicine has been digested.
A man who eats the finest rice of the *śāli* variety mixed with ghee and milk shall always remain refined by such acts as bathing, anointing, and the application of unguents. (28)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: Su-carita, having himself consumed that medicinal powder prepared in a mortar, his body purified,
dwelt happily upon the surface of his bed within secret, windless chambers.
A man who is constantly devoted to the most truthful vow and daily recites the syllables of the Jaina mantra conquers the host of diseases exceedingly, becoming long-lived and powerful. (29)
The essential meaning is this:
the powder of *bhallātaka* stones, ground with cow's milk and burnt in three *puṭa* applications over a fire of cow dung, is always effective here once it has first been purified.
And when he has grown old, being endowed with the application of beautiful elixirs, he shall become like a god in person.
In the past, having repeatedly drunk ripened water, he purified his own body and soul.
Within six months, even one who is extremely weak shall become strong, and likewise one who is thin or of medium build;
he should always consume excellent rice mixed with ghee and milk.
The meaning of the ritual is as follows:
having bathed, with a body anointed with unguents, wearing garments prepared according to the injunctions, and bringing the offerings as prescribed.
Resembling a lord of mortals and like a celestial being, endowed with strength and truly comparable to the God of Love himself,
he shall live for a thousand years, becoming an internal bond and always transcendent.
The meaning of the terms is as follows:

"vajras" refers to diamonds; furthermore, "vajra-iron" refers to all types of meteoric iron; "vajrorubandhī-phala" refers to the fruit of the *vajra-kapāla* tree; and "vajra-named stone" refers to the diamond-stone (*vajrapāṣāṇa*).
Whatever has been obtained from this, having taken it according to the rite and burnt it with the fire of a bellows,
one should properly cast the resulting fine ashes into water made from *pāṭala* and *vīra* trees.
Having performed seven successive immersions in very hot water boiled with horse gram (*kulattha*),
the wise practitioner should then carefully place [the object] again in milk that is even hotter.
Having reduced it to powder and mixed it with sugar and clarified butter, one who knows the proper dosage should lick it himself;
that man, knowing the right food and place of residence, conquers even well-known diseases. (34)
The essential meaning is this:
having administered for six months the adamantine supreme medicine mixed with clarified butter, once this has been digested,
even food consisting of rice mixed with ghee and milk may be taken along with excellent medicines.
Such a man shall live for a thousand years, always possessing extreme pride,
his strength emboldened by the arrogance of burgeoning youth, and his body as firm as adamant.
The essential meaning is that one should consume it with milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice combined.
Desiring unimpaired strength, irresistible power, superior vigor, and freedom from disease,
as well as a lifespan of a thousand years, a man should maintain his own appearance in a faultless manner.
The essential meaning is as follows: having taken even the horn of a cow-horned mountain goat, dried it, and reduced it to powder,
one should cook it with cow's milk and clarified butter mixed with jaggery, and consume it gradually.
Afterwards, by consuming milk and ghee, a mortal himself attains inexhaustible strength;
even if previously devoid of vigor, he certainly becomes possessed of supreme vitality and exalted qualities. (37)
The essential meaning is as follows:
having prepared edible preparations from castor oil plant, *amṛta*, *hastikarṇī*,
and the splendid *vīra* tree according to the prescribed method, one should consume them daily until [the disease] is quickly destroyed.
Having obtained that vigor of abundant strength, radiant with playful charm, and endowed with fresh youth,
he shall thereafter attain a lifespan of three hundred years, free from disease.
The essential meaning is this: having thoroughly powdered *nāgī* and *satkhalu*, one who always licks this mixture with clarified butter becomes stainless.
A man who remains in the state of most wonderful youth shall live for a thousand years. // 39 //
The essential meaning here is this: I shall briefly set forth the ritual procedures according to the rules,
as described using excellent medicines specifically prescribed for the rainy season and other times, beginning with *Varṣābhū*.
By seeing those peerless [remedies], which destroy emerging diseases and yield perfect results. // 40 //
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

[The preparation] consists of alkaline substances derived from *ikṣuraka*, sugarcane, *tāla*, sesame, *japā*, *mārga*, *nirguṇḍī*, plantain, *arka*, lotus, *citra*, *citraka*, sesame, and *khadyota*, which have been thoroughly cleansed.
"Svarakarṇikā" is an alternative reading.
Then, with the ripe [drugs] boiled in four times their quantity of water until one-quarter remains:
One should cook the inspissated juice (phāṇita) with the pure, shining sugar-candy of his feet until it is not too liquid.
In that [jar], having finely powdered equal parts of the three pungents and the three aromatics (trijātaka), and having added them as a quarter-part,
this mixture is placed in a jar that has been prepared with the aforementioned consecrations.
Another person, having faith, places a covered jar containing a month's supply [of medicine] as a treasure;
by consuming it, he conquers the hosts of diseases and enemies that are inexhaustible, and lives for a long time. (42)
The meaning of the essence is that it is well-prepared and properly placed in a consecrated vessel, even when mixed with fragrant substances. // 43 //
It is most delicious, the abode of happiness that utterly destroys the entire multitude of diseases.
Thus, by drinking this excellent elixir, which is like a wonderful painting, a man who consumes it continuously shall destroy consumption (yakṣman),
as well as hemorrhoids and all diseases that deprive one of strength.

The meaning of the essence is that the patient, having prepared [the medicine] according to the method for the ripening of the passions (kaṣāya) based on what is appropriate or inappropriate, should consume it.
He himself shall live for three hundred years, utterly crushing all diseases; though lacking virility, he shall possess exceeding vigor and fortitude, and be like the God of Love incarnate. (45)

A mortal who practices this yoga of various conceptualizations and mental constructions according to the sequence and rules prescribed in the scriptures attains manifest power, majesty, longevity, vigor, and unimpededness, as well as freedom from disease. (46)

Having understood the meaning of these [treatises], which have been composed by those whose own intellects have extracted the established conclusions through their connection with the well-known attainment of manifest fruits of direct perception,
and having applied themselves here with effort according to the prescribed rule, mortals become such that all their enemies are difficult to restrain. (47)

The meaning of the term *bhāvārtha* refers here to the secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) concerning elixirs and rejuvenators; those men who approach these supreme medicines according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures become eternally happy.

Moreover, according to the method of reasoning already stated by the knower of both existent and non-existent things, [it is established that] this is the truth. What more need be discussed? Let all that exists be constantly cultivated. 48.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: Just as a city protects its inhabitants from the fear of enemies by means of its own defenses and all its resources, so too does the body protect its members from disease through the application of various medicinal remedies.

This administration of medicine here is suitable for those who have performed meritorious deeds; otherwise, the collection of bodies—the abode of dharma and happiness—perishes, being corrupted by many defects. (49)
Such is the essential meaning: thus, there are various medicinal herbs, sufficient for the purpose, yielding the fourfold fruit of success. (50)
The meaning of the essence is one whose pair of feet are cherished and who knows all the scriptures.
I am the exalted lord of sages, whose virtues are worthy of being conversed with;
I am the venerable teacher, the glorious one who delights Nandin, and I am the powerful one. // 51 //
The meaning of this is: by his command, for the sake of accomplishing the distribution of various medicines,
and for the purpose of fulfilling the ascetic practice of being affectionate toward good physicians.
This treatise, extracted from the teachings of the Jina, has been composed with diligence;
it is renowned upon the earth as "The Bringer of Auspiciousness. (52)

This meaning of the essential reality—supreme, unsurpassed, endowed with extensive subject matter, and free from all faults—was previously proclaimed by the best of Jinas; now it has been composed by the Great Guru, the Sage-Indra, who is like a fierce sun among scholars. (53)
Having accurately extracted the essential meaning in brief from the great scripture *Prāṇāvāya*, which shines with the distinguished Māgadhī language that exceeds all other tongues by half a measure;
The venerable teacher of Ugrāditya, who shines with preceptorial virtues, has composed this treatise, the abode of happiness, in the Sanskrit language; this is the distinction between the two. (54)
Its essential meaning is adorned with poetic ornaments, composed of excellent words that are pleasant to hear, and requested by those who know their own welfare;
it bestows vitality, longevity, courage, and manifest strength upon living beings, and is the cause of their well-being.

Having mastered this treatise—which has arisen from profound reflection, is capable of withstanding critical analysis, is known as "The Auspicious," and was composed by the Lords of Jinas—the wise quickly attain happiness exactly as it is. (55)
The essential meaning [is established] here by means of verses,
narratives, and extensive great narratives proclaimed by the Lord of Jinas.
May that lotus-like face of the Moon of the Jinas, the abode of bliss for all living beings, endure as long as the sun, the moon, and the stars exist. // 56 //
The essential meaning [is extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issued from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines upon the two banks that accomplish the welfare of both states of existence, has issued forth like a spray of water for the sole benefit of the world. (57)

Having bowed with devotion to the Victorious One, Ariṣṭhanemi, the Supreme Lord whose stains are utterly destroyed and who possesses the most excellent and auspicious marks, [this work] shall be proclaimed as it was spoken among those established in well-being. (1)

The essential meaning of this secret, which has come down through the supreme scriptures of the great sages who know the ultimate truth, is now declared: this omen pertains only to those whose souls are devoted to sublime meditation, not to those whose souls are deluded. // 2 //
The essential meaning is this:

death is the characteristic of death; it is the exhaustion of the life-force. Since death arises from some means—such as poison—for those who are utterly deluded, I declare that death is a great terror; for whom, then, would it not occur? // 3 //
The essential meaning:
Now, I shall proclaim here the characteristics of misfortune for great-souled ones who have well-cultivated themselves through effort;
for even among those whose age has become advanced and infirm, there is always a constant fear of death that is universally recognized. (4)
The meaning of the verse:

Beings in other states of existence are permeated by the fear of old age, disease, and death; yet, because they do not awaken [to the truth], they are terrified by that very fear of death, and therefore one should not speak of their death here [in this context]. (5)
The essential meaning is this:

those who are bound by suffering and possess fearful minds within the four realms of existence—those who desire liberation, the abode of all happiness—let them listen with ease as it is now being told. (6)
The essential meaning is this:

whatever possesses characteristics contrary to its own prior cold-natured constitution is declared by the Victors to be a fatal sign (riṣṭa); hereafter, it will be explained even more clearly. // 7 //

The meaning of the verse is as follows: If the orb of the moon or the sun appears like the bow of Indra (the rainbow) over the three divisions of the earth, even if it is accompanied by a hole, such a person indeed lives for two years. // 8 //
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Even one who does not see the crescent moon, nor the halo of light, nor the Pole Star (Dhruva), nor the star Arundhatī, nor the path of the wind, nor the rays of the moon, nor the heat of the sun during the day— even such a person shall not [die] within a year.

The essential meaning is this: whatever man beholds the lunar disc shining with radiant splendor and the sun whose mass of brilliance has been dispelled, he shall at some time go to heaven after eleven months. 10.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
One who sees vomit, phlegm, semen, urine, excrement, or semen, or one who sees a rainbow with a brilliant luster,
or one who perceives the brilliance of gold or stars while asleep or even when awake— such a person lives for ten months.
The meaning of the passage is as follows:

Having seen a golden tree that had come from the world of the gods, and having seen deceased piśācas in the city of Bāmbare, he beheld wonderful men hanging down for nine months—some excessively long, some more so, and others bent over. (12)
The meaning of the verse is this:
a man who is exceedingly stout without cause may, for no reason at all, suddenly become thin by himself;
or his very nature may undergo such a change without cause, and he shall live here for eight months and a half. (13)
The meaning of the verse is as follows:
If a footprint, whether in front or behind, meets with fragmentation in mud,
or if it is covered with dust and plaster, or is itself moist, such a person does not live beyond seven months.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

If owls, crows, vultures, hawks, ravens, jackals, fierce dogs, tigers, leopards, and the like, having forcefully ascended to the head [of the person], dwell there, he will certainly perish within six months. (15)
The meaning of this is as follows:
even with mere dust and water, or even with very fine dust, if one’s own head is directly rubbed [with it],
or if a man sees smoke rising from a fire-pit here, he will perish after five months.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

Even when the sky is devoid of clouds, if one perceives the continuous flash of a brilliant, flickering lightning within it, that person shall go to heaven from the region of Yama after four months. 17.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: when one does not see one's own body upon looking at it—just as one might see buffaloes, camels, or donkeys while asleep—and if, having mounted a strong wind during the day, one is seen by crows, even if dead, such a person lives for exactly three months. (18)
The meaning of the verse is as follows: Upon seeing a rainbow situated in the midst of the water, moving visibly for even a moment,
the wise man, having reflected that his own life will last only two months, should personally renounce all attachment to the self.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

When a man does not see the reflection of Alakā, the moon, the sun, or blazing light even when they are directly before him, or if he perceives them otherwise, then after only a month [he shall die]. 20.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

When one does not clearly perceive one's own form here within the circle of vision directed toward another, and when one does not perceive the burning incense, that person will cease to exist after three or five nights. (21)
The meaning of the passage is as follows: when the body emits the odor of a corpse, or when people report sensations for no apparent cause,
or when one perceives what is awake as being a dream— that person lives for exactly twelve nights.
The meaning of the verse is as follows:

when the face becomes pale, weak, and dark, and the lotus-like facial orb becomes flat, and when there is a line like a young insect on the cheek, such a person lives for only seven nights in this world. // 23 //

When the wind (māruta) pierces and excessively afflicts the body, including all the vital points (marman), the person is constantly miserable like one stung by a fierce and venomous scorpion; he lives for only three days. (24)
The essential meaning is this:

if a man is not made to experience horripilation when sprinkled with very cold water resembling ice-cold snow, and does not perceive any sensation throughout his entire body, he shall not live beyond two days. (25)
The meaning of the verse is this:
even one who hears the roar of the ocean at the very edge of his vision might, with great effort, fail to see the light; or else, such a man would live for no more than a single day.

When the meaning of the [mantra] syllables sequentially occupies the foot, the shank, one's own knee, the thigh, the hip, the flank, the neck, the hand, the forearm, the shoulder, the chest, the head, and the skull, [then that person becomes a great yogin]. // 27 //
If one does not see one's own shadow for three, two, or one year,
or for ten, seven, four, or one month respectively, one will live for that duration.
Thinking that a man may live for as many days as there are fortnights, eight, six, three, or even one more, he should renounce his attachment to self. (29)
The essential meaning is as follows:
for the pair of eyebrows, nine days; for the ears, seven days of sound;
for the nose, five days and so forth; and for the eyes, three days of light.
Having become composed, a man who fears cyclic existence should abandon this body according to the prescribed rite. // 30 //
The essential meaning is as follows:
visual delusion, darkness before the eyes, a throbbing sensation in the sight, profuse perspiration on the face,
rigidity of the vital channels (jīva-sirās), and an intense eruption of horripilation in the feet and hands.
And if a blockage should suddenly occur for a man, it is a prominent sign of imminent death. // 31 //
The essential meaning is as follows:

having directly perceived such a distinguished omen, and having abandoned his entire circle of possessions and his wife, he should go toward either the northern or the western direction, once he has correctly identified a vast and excellent region. (32)
In a place free of living beings, on a stainless stretch of ground, undisturbed and devoid of the signs of desire;
at a sacred ford of the Victors, or in a temple, or in a charming lotus grove, or in a forest. // 33 //
Having determined that [auspicious] direction— either east or north—
upon the ground, on a stone, or even in the sand,
and having performed the excellent worship of the Lord of that Field (Kṣetrapati), one should revere the lotus-feet of the Jina.

Having thus worshipped the assembly of Jinas and having bowed down, one of right vision, with fear utterly destroyed, should then practice here the meditation on Dharma that is pure and white, according to one's own strength. (35)

Thus, one who desires meditative absorption—the cause of liberation—and who is honored among men, should contemplate these words of homage, which are the sole perfection of the Jina’s virtues, thinking, "May this also come to pass for me. (36)
The meaning of this is: having daily held fast in their minds, with fortitude and other virtues, those excellent sages [attained that state].
"Satprayābāḥ" is an alternative reading.
Even though the sequences of birth, old age, and death have been described as inherent to saṃsāra,
by contemplating the instability of the body, those who are senior in asceticism should always remain so.
This is the essential meaning [extracted] from the great ocean of the excellent scriptures issuing from the mouth of the Jina,
which is agitated by the multitude of waves consisting of the vast expansion of all categories of existence.
For this [teaching], which shines from both banks by accomplishing the welfare of both [self and others], has issued forth like a spray of water for the singular benefit of the world. (38)
The meaning of the state of being.
